marks.name: Japanese marks, seals, signatures and crests

groups.name: Hizen porcelain: Arita, Imari, Kakiemon, Nabeshima, Hirado
Kutani, Banko and the export marks
Censor and date seals on prints

caveats: A mark names a maker, studio, kiln, publisher, office or person; it does not prove an object genuine or date it: Japanese marks were copied, inherited by later generations and applied to reproductions.
Characters are given as written on the object, old forms included; variants list the other forms.

rows.kana: だいみんせいかねんせい
rows.meaning: Made in the Chenghua (Seika) reign of the Great Ming, 1465-87 (not a true reign mark on Japanese porcelain)
rows.kind: Chinese reign mark on a Japanese object
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue, two columns of three characters, often in a double ring or square
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Used continuously from the 1630s to modern times (Miyaki, Kyushu Ceramic Museum).
rows.what_it_tells: Says only that the maker copied a Ming-style base mark. It does not date the piece to the 15th century and does not say the piece is Chinese. Style, body, glaze and painting date a piece.
rows.cautions: It is the commonest Hizen reign mark. Check the 大 / 太: Arita often writes 太明 (a dot added to 大), whereas Chinese pieces write 大 and differ in brushwork, foot and paste. Meiji and later Arita reproductions repeat the mark; both Chinese and Japanese pieces carry it, and it was already on Chinese porcelain imported to Japan before Arita began (1610s).

facts.text: The 'Daimin Seika nensei' mark imitates Chinese porcelain and was used through the Edo period, from the 1630s without interruption, in steady numbers, down to modern times.
facts.quote: 1630 年代から途切れることなく、一定数の使用を保ちながら近代まで使用される

facts.text: The variant writing 大/太 continues into modern times; at first probably a simple error, but a Swiss-museum piece has dots added to a 大明嘉靖年製 mark in red, so it may be deliberate.
In the 1600-1640s Chinese export porcelain with 大明成化年製 and 福 marks was already coming to Japan, and Arita copied it soon after porcelain began in the 1610s.
Forged Chinese year-marks such as Dai Min Sei-ka nen sei (1465-87) are found on early 17th-century Old Japan; the practice was revived for modern imitation Old Japan made for Europe and America.

facts.text: In the second half of the 18th century it appears mostly on small dishes, with one example on a salt dish.
In the Kyushu museum's century-by-century chart it is shown from the 18th century to the 19th.

facts.text: It is the commonest mark among the earliest marked Shibata pieces (220 of 517).
Chinese porcelain with 福 was imported to Japan before Arita began.
Cleveland: 福 'mark on base' on a Hizen Ko-Kutani-type cup; 'FUKU in square seal under aubergine glaze' on a Ko-Kutani-style plate.

facts.text: The uzu-fuku appears in the 1660s, becomes the main fuku mark from the 1670s into the 18th century, typically with three spirals; degraded forms follow.
facts.quote: 1660 年代から出現し、1670 年代以降から 18 世紀にかけて

facts.text: It falls out of use by the end of the 18th century, is absent in the early 19th, and a typical form returns after the Meiji era.
facts.quote: 明治以降に再び典型的な形の銘が使用

facts.text: Modern revival products use the form closest to the typical one.
facts.quote: 典型例に近い渦福が使用されました

facts.text: In 1930s scholarship uzu-fuku sherds from the Shōkakei (Ogi) kiln were taken as evidence of Sakaida (Kakiemon) involvement, since the mark was seen as mostly Kakiemon's.

rows.date_note: One dealer blog gives 1885 for the trademark registration; Japanese Wikipedia says the 7th and 8th generations used it and the 12th-generation company was given the right in 1919. Fuku-in-square marks from the Edo period are older.

facts.text: Kakiemon is said to have registered the cursive fuku in a double square as his own trademark in 1885; afterwards it was used exclusively and often caused disputes with other potters.
Museum text: fuku is often in a single or double square frame in Arita.

maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: 1670-80s into the 18th century (Miyaki).
rows.what_it_tells: Reading is uncertain.
rows.cautions: The characters cannot be read reliably, so do not translate them.

facts.text: The mark has been read 古へ人 or 古を倣う; it appears from the 1670-80s into the 18th century with finds at the Kakiemon and Nangawara Tsuji kiln sites.
facts.quote: 古へ人」や「古を倣う」と読まれてきた銘

rows.meaning: Gold (seal-script) in a double square
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: It belongs to the Kakiemon kiln-site period; Cleveland dates a Kakiemon-type bowl to the 1700s.
rows.what_it_tells: The reading as 金 is tentative.
rows.cautions: The meaning is uncertain.

facts.text: A 金-like seal-script character in a double square is among the marks at the Nangawara kilns.
Cleveland: bowl 'Kakiemon type' with 金 on base.

rows.meaning: Clove-flower mark
rows.device: A clove (chōji) drawn like a flower

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue or enamel
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Found only at the Tsuji kiln site at Nangawara.
rows.what_it_tells: A base sign whose reading or maker is not settled; do not over-read it.
rows.cautions: Mostly on pieces that stayed abroad, suggesting export wares.

facts.text: The clove-flower mark has been found only at the Tsuji kiln site at Nangawara; surviving pieces are mostly abroad.
facts.quote: 南川原窯の辻窯跡でのみ出土

rows.meaning: Pine in a circle (Arita, Higuchi kiln) / in a double square (probably Shōkakei, Ogi)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Circle form mid-late 18th century (Miyaki).
rows.what_it_tells: The circle form is shown to be Arita; the square form is probably Shōkakei.
rows.cautions: Check the body: Mikawachi bodies were also decorated at Arita.

facts.text: 丸に松 was once taken for Shōkakei (Matsugatani) ware of Ogi but sherds at the Arita Higuchi kiln show it is Arita.
facts.quote: 有田の樋口窯跡の出土陶片にこの銘があり

facts.text: A pine in a double square is known from Ogi sherds and is likely Shōkakei.

rows.kana: ごろうだいふごしょうずいぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Gorōdaifu Go Shōzui (name copied from Ming Japan-order wares)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Later 18th century; derived forms to c.1800s.
rows.what_it_tells: Copied from Ming 'Shōzui' wares for Japan; meaning debated.
rows.cautions: Meaning uncertain.

facts.text: The legend was on Ming porcelain made for Japan ('Shōzui'); Arita copied it from the later 18th century and it degenerated (五→王).
Bowes (1882) records 'Go-ro-ta narabini Sho-zui sin-zo' on Arita ware c.1820.

rows.meaning: Made in the Enpō era (1673-81)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: First Japanese era mark in the Chinese 'nensei' form; the mark was reused around 1800 (Miyaki).
rows.what_it_tells: Japanese-era marks can be later reuses: a piece marked 延寶 may date to c.1800.
rows.cautions: The Kyushu Ceramic Museum warns that some era marks were added later with old era names: '年号銘の中には後世に古い年号を入れたものもある'.

facts.text: 延寶年製 is the first Japanese era mark in the Chinese style, but it is also one of the marks reused c.1800.
facts.quote: 1800 年前後に再使用された銘の一つ

facts.text: The Kyushu Ceramic Museum warns that some era marks were put in later with old era names.
facts.quote: 年号銘の中には後世に古い年号を入れたものもあるため注意が必要

rows.meaning: Made in the Bunka era (1804-18)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Era name; the seal-script version is documented in a 1806 Kakiemon order book.
rows.what_it_tells: Era names on Hizen porcelain are rare; a seal-script 文化年製 is recorded in the Kakiemon family papers (1806, Kishū order).
rows.cautions: Other Japanese era marks (天明, 寛政, 文政, 天保) also occur on Hizen porcelain.

facts.text: 文化年製 in seal script appears in a Kakiemon-family 1806 order book as the 'mark of the Bunka-era product'.
Other Hizen era marks: 寛延, 天明, 寛政, 文化, 文政, 天保 (a few on map dishes), and 明治年製.

rows.meaning: Potter's name: Imaizumi Heibei (7th generation, per Miyaki)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue in a double square
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base near the edge
rows.date_note: Found with 文化年製 on the same piece (Miyaki).
rows.what_it_tells: Maker's brand name on export or modern Arita/Hirado ware; it narrows the date to the years the brand was in use.
rows.cautions: Brand marks were copied by other firms; check body and decoration.

facts.text: The name 今泉平兵衛 appears in a double square with 文化年製, so it is presumably the 7th Imaizumi Heibei.
facts.quote: 今泉家７代目の今泉平兵衛

facts.text: A rare case: the Kyushu Ceramic Museum shows it placed near the foot edge, like a painter's signature.

rows.meaning: Made at Kameyama (Nagasaki, founded 1807)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: The Kameyama kiln was founded in 1807; a copy of the mark is seen on Arita ware (Miyaki).
rows.what_it_tells: Place mark of Kameyama (Nagasaki); also 崎陽住亀山製. A copy on Arita ware is recorded, so check the kiln.
rows.cautions: Place marks can be copied, for example Kameyama marks on Arita ware.

facts.text: 亀山製 is a Nagasaki Kameyama-ware mark (kiln founded 1807, Bunka 4), copied at Arita.
facts.quote: 亀山焼の銘を有田で写したもの

facts.text: Kameyama pieces also carry 崎陽住亀山製.

Another source differs: Gives 1804 (Bunka 1), founded by 大神甚五兵衛 at Kakineyama, Nagasaki; the museum says 1807 (Bunka 4). The dictionary gives the start of the porcelain production, the museum the kiln founding, or one is wrong.
facts.quote: 文化元年（一八〇四）大神甚五兵衛が長崎市の後方にある垣根山で創始

rows.meaning: Tsutsue kiln (Yamauchi, Takeo)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: 1740-80s (Shibata no.35).
rows.what_it_tells: Kiln-name marks are rare in the 18th century.
rows.cautions: Check the body: Mikawachi bodies were also decorated at Arita.

facts.text: 筒江 written vertically is a kiln-name mark of Tsutsue, one of the few place-name marks of the 18th century.

rows.meaning: Sakaida family's Kaki(emon) mark
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: Sakaida Kakiemon family (酒井田柿右衛門)

rows.where_on_object: back of a lotus-shaped handle (one piece)
rows.date_note: 19th century (1800s-1850s group in the Shibata collection; 9th-10th generation per Suzuta).
rows.what_it_tells: Brand or maker's name for export or modern Arita/Hirado ware; narrows date to the years the brand was in use.
rows.cautions: Not the modern 柿右衛門 signature.

facts.text: 酒井田 in an irregular frame with 柿 in a square marks the Sakaida Kakiemon family; recorded on one piece.
The 9th-10th generation Sakaida Kakiemon used '酒柿' on non-export wares as well.

rows.meaning: Made by Higuchi (Nangawara)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Late Edo to Meiji (Higuchi Taihei kiln).
rows.what_it_tells: Black on an unglazed ring; sherds are found at the kiln site.
rows.cautions: Related marks are ヒ, 南川原樋口造, 松甫 and 恵泉館製.

facts.text: 南川原樋口造 / 樋口造 marks are Higuchi kiln marks (the Higuchi Taihei kiln of the Bakumatsu-Meiji period).

rows.kana: ぞうしゅんていみほぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Miho of the Zōshuntei (Hisatomi Yojibei)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue or overglaze red
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: 1841 (Hisatomi's export monopoly) to c.1861 solid, to 1871 uncertain (Suzuta's chart).
rows.what_it_tells: Brand mark of Hisatomi Yojibei, a merchant; the piece may have been made by various kilns.
rows.cautions: Meiji copies exist. 蔵春亭西畒造 (Hisatomi Yohei) continues to 1871.

facts.text: 蔵春亭三保造 is the brand mark of Hisatomi Yojibei (Masatsune) who got the exclusive export right from the Saga domain in 1841; the mark starts 1841 and ends 1861 (his death), uncertain to 1871.
The Kōgei shiryō (1877) says: when selling to foreigners, 三保 was put on each piece.
facts.quote: 外国ニ鬻ク毎器ニ三保ノ二字ヲ銘ス

facts.text: Zōshuntei Miho zō is the first brand mark in Arita; the name Zōshuntei was granted by the 10th Saga lord Nabeshima Naomasa.

rows.kana: ひちょうざんしんぽぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Shinpo of Hichōzan ('Hizen dish-mountain'): Tashiro Monzaemon's brand
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: Tashiro Monzaemon (田代紋左衛門, Tashiroya)
maker.place: Arita, with branches in Nagasaki, Yokohama, Shanghai

rows.technique: painted in overglaze red (some in underglaze blue)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Suzuta's chart gives 1856 (export licence) to 1890 (death of Tashiro Sakusaku); Tashiro Monzaemon died 1900.
rows.what_it_tells: Brand of Tashiro Monzaemon (Tashiroya); 造 tends to be older, 製 newer.
rows.cautions: The characters are 肥碟山 (not 肥蝶山, which is used by 如仙). The mark was copied or adopted by other Arita export houses. Overglaze red marks are known from Arita sherds, but underglaze blue sherds have not yet been found at Arita, so a blue 信甫 mark does not prove Arita. White body from Mikawachi was decorated at Arita under this brand.

facts.text: Tashiro Monzaemon received a trade licence in 1856 and used the brand 肥碟山信甫; the mark ran from 1856 to 1890 (death of his son Sakusaku, who ran the business).
facts.quote: 肥碟山信甫とは安政３年 (1856) に佐賀藩から許可を得て貿易を開始した田代紋左衛門のブランド銘

facts.text: The marks occur both as 造 and 製; 造 is generally older.
肥碟山 means 'Hizen's dish-mountain', an alias of Arita; new traders from 1868 copied the form.
facts.quote: 肥碟山」という名称は肥前の皿山を意味

facts.text: Overglaze-red 信甫造 sherds were excavated at Izumiyama; no underglaze-blue examples at kiln sites, so a blue mark does not prove Arita.

rows.kana: ひちょうざんふかがわぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Fukagawa of Hichōzan (8th Fukagawa Eizaemon)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: Fukagawa Eizaemon VIII (深川栄左衛門)

rows.technique: painted in overglaze red (some in underglaze blue)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: From 1868 (new licence) to 1875 (Kōransha), and possibly to 1877 on Philadelphia entries (Suzuta).
rows.what_it_tells: Early Fukagawa Eizaemon export mark, before the Kōransha orchid mark.
rows.cautions: Similar marks include 肥碟山辻, 肥碟山深江, 肥碟山平林 (Hirabayashi Ihei, 1868-93), 肥碟山川崎, 肥碟山南里, 肥碟山如仙 (written 肥蝶山), 肥碟山武茂, 春信 and 漱月; all belong to traders after 1868.

facts.text: 肥碟山深川 is the mark of the 8th Fukagawa Eizaemon from 1868. It ends with the founding of Kōransha in 1875, though exhibits at Philadelphia in 1876 carried 肥前深川製 and 肥碟山深川製.
facts.quote: 八代深川栄左衛門の銘

facts.text: The Philadelphia Museum holds pieces marked 肥前深川製, 肥碟山深川製, 肥碟山深川造 from the 1876 exhibition.
Bowes (1882) gives 'Nichi-hi-zan Fuka-gawa seisu' and 'Hichozan Fuka-gawa seisu/tsukuru' with illustrations.

Another source differs: Describes a Nichi-hi-zan Fuka-gawa piece as made in 1875, the year the museum says the 肥碟山深川 mark ends; shows the family name used on pieces of the mid-1870s. Not a firm contradiction: Bowes's date is a collector's attribution.

rows.meaning: Made by Kisa of the Toshikian (Fukaumi family)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue or overglaze
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Used from before 1862 (a box dated 1862) to 1879; with the orchid mark in 1875-79 (Suzuta).
rows.what_it_tells: Mark of the Fukaumi family (Fukaumi Heizaemon, Sumino-suke, Takeji).
rows.cautions: The sources do not give a reading of 年木庵; Bowes spells it 'Tosni-ki-an Ki-so'.

facts.text: 年木庵喜三 is the mark of the Fukaumi family, used from before 1862 (a dated box) until 1875; with the Kōransha orchid mark in 1875-79; after 1879 they used 精磁会社製之.
facts.quote: 年木庵喜三製」の銘については図７で示したように文久２年 (1862) 以前から

facts.text: Bowes (1882) records 'Toshi-ki-an Ki-so seisu' on Arita sometsuke.
Another source differs: Reads the maker as 'Ki-so' (Kiso Toshikian), not 喜三 (Kisa); a 19th-century romanisation, so probably a misreading by Bowes.
facts.quote: Tosui-ki-an Ki-so seisu. Made by Kiso Toshikian

rows.meaning: Kōransha's orchid emblem, with the individual factory name
rows.device: An orchid (ran) emblem, gold or red
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red/gold, or underglaze blue
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: From 1875 (Kōransha founded) to the present; the mark with 深川造 is documented for 1875-87, and the shape of the orchid changes over time (the earliest form was not yet fixed in 1875).
rows.what_it_tells: Orchid mark with the name 深川造, 辻製 or 喜三製, showing which of the three partner factories made the piece.
rows.cautions: Kōransha continues today (合名会社 from 1879, 株式会社 from 1970), so do not date a piece by the orchid alone. A gold orchid on a Mikawachi-bodied vase of c.1875 (V&A) reads '於香蘭社 (orchid) 西山製'.

facts.text: Kōransha was founded in 1875 by the Fukagawa, Tsuji and Fukaumi kilns; each marked its own wares with the orchid and its own name.
facts.quote: 蘭のマークとそれぞれの名前をいれる

facts.text: Orchid + 深川造/製 is dated 1875 and seen to 1887; orchid + 辻製 and orchid + 喜三製 limited to 1875-79 (when Tsuji and Fukaumi left to found 精磁会社).
The Kyushu Ceramic Museum shows the orchid mark as Kōransha's (Arita) mark.
Kōransha: 1875 joint-stock society; 1879 reorganised as a partnership company; 1970 joint-stock company (Japanese Wikipedia).

rows.kana: おいてこうらんしゃにしやませい
rows.meaning: Made by Nishiyama at Kōransha (ornamented vase, c.1875)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: Nishiyama Kōzō (西山孝蔵) at Kōransha

rows.where_on_object: base, around the unglazed ring
rows.date_note: c.1875 (V&A, 1877 purchase from the 1876 Philadelphia exhibition).
rows.what_it_tells: Overglaze maker on a Mikawachi body, with 大日本三河内製 in underglaze black.
rows.cautions: This type shows Kōransha's early outsourcing: body Mikawachi, decoration Arita.

facts.text: The V&A vase has 大日本三河内製 in blue (fired black on the unglazed ring) and around it in red '於香蘭社 (orchid) 西山製'; shown at Philadelphia 1876, bought by V&A 1877, c.1875.
Bowes (1882) records 'Dai Nippon. Mikawachi sei, Koransha ni oite Nishiyama seisu'.

rows.kana: せいじがいしゃせいし
rows.meaning: Made by the Seiji Kaisha (Fine Porcelain Company)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: From 1879, when Tsuji and Fukaumi founded the company; a collector blog says it was used for some years after the company closed (possibly 1897).
rows.what_it_tells: Brand or maker's name for export or modern Arita/Hirado ware; narrows date to the years the brand was in use.
rows.cautions: Not the same as Fukagawa Seiji (深川製磁, 1894).

facts.text: Tsuji Katsuzō and the Fukaumi brothers left Kōransha and founded 精磁会社 in 1879; they then used marks like 精磁会社製之.
facts.quote: 明治 12 年以降は「精磁会社製之」等の銘を用いた

facts.text: A collector blog dates the Seiji Kaisha mark to 1879-97, used for several years on lesser wares by later decorators.

rows.meaning: Made by Fukagawa (Seiji): Fukagawa Chūji's firm
rows.device: Mount Fuji over flowing water in a roundel
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue (Fuji-and-water emblem), also overglaze
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: The company was founded in January 1894 (Japanese Wikipedia; the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism); the sources do not say when the Fuji emblem was first used.
rows.what_it_tells: Name of the firm, with the Fuji-flowing-water emblem.
rows.cautions: A different company (Kōransha, Fukagawa Eizaemon) used 深川造 earlier, so do not confuse the two. The firm exhibited at Paris in 1900 as 'Fukagawa Porcelain'.

facts.text: 深川製磁 was founded in January 1894 by Fukagawa Chūji, second son of Fukagawa Eizaemon VIII of Kōransha.
The Kyushu museum shows 富士流水マーク + 深川製 as Fukagawa Seiji's mark.
facts.quote: 富士流水マーク + 深川製

facts.text: A collector blog dates the 'Fukagawa' mark to the mid-1890s to 1920s and 大日本有田深川製 to c.1900-1910.
1910: Imperial Household purveyor; gold medals at Paris in 1900 and St Louis in 1904 (Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism).

rows.meaning: Kōransha company
rows.device: orchid mark
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue or overglaze
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: The years of the written-name form are not established; the company was reorganised in 1879.
rows.what_it_tells: Maker's brand name on export or modern Arita/Hirado ware; it narrows the date to the years the brand was in use.
rows.cautions: A product label 'Koransha' exists on later wares; the orchid also helps.

facts.text: Kōransha is the Arita firm founded in 1875 and reorganised in 1879 as 香蘭社合名会社.
The museum's modern examples show the orchid on Kōransha wares.
Kōransha's own company profile gives its legal founding date as 10 July 1879 (明治12年); the 1875 date is the earlier 合本組織 association.

rows.kana: だいにっぽんみかわちせい
rows.meaning: Made in Mikawachi, Great Japan
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue (blackens on unglazed ring) or overglaze red
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Meiji export period.
rows.what_it_tells: Place mark of Mikawachi (Hirado) ware.
rows.cautions: Both spellings, '三河内' and '三川内', occur.

facts.text: Mikawachi marks of the Meiji export wares include 三川内, 大日本三川内, 三川内福本造 and 平戸産枝栄造; they identify Mikawachi against Arita.
Bowes (1882) records 'Hira-to zo, Mi-kawa-chi' / 'Hira-to sei, Mi-kawa-chi' in red on eggshell cups.

rows.meaning: Made at Hirado (Mikawachi ware)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内) on the base
rows.date_note: Mampōzan marks run from 1871; the end is uncertain (c.1887-90 in Suzuta's chart).
rows.what_it_tells: Place/brand marks of the Hirado export house.
rows.cautions: '平戸三福寿' is an earlier mark (1837-1871).

facts.text: 平戸産枝栄造, 平戸産枝栄製, 満宝山枝栄造 are brand marks of the Mampōzan trading house (founded 1871); 平戸三福寿 is an earlier mark on a British Museum piece (1837-71).
Bowes (1882) no.87-88: 'Hira-to zo / sei, Mi-kawa-chi'.

rows.meaning: Comb-tooth pattern on the foot of Nabeshima ware
rows.device: comb teeth around foot
rows.where_on_object: foot side / lower edge
rows.date_note: Nabeshima kiln pieces of c.1690-1720s are shown unmarked by the Kyushu Ceramic Museum.
rows.what_it_tells: A feature of the foot, not a maker's mark. Nabeshima is normally unmarked.
rows.cautions: Bowes (1882) called it the 'Kushi-de mark' painted at the lower edges of plates and saucers at Ohokawachi; modern Japanese catalogues treat it as a foot pattern.

facts.text: Nabeshima ware normally has no mark or border line inside the foot; the foot is white; the side of the foot bears comb-tooth pattern.
facts.quote: 高台内には銘、界線などを入れず

facts.text: Bowes (1882, p.38) calls the comb pattern the 'Kushi-de mark' of Ohokawachi, painted in blue.
The Kyushu Ceramic Museum shows Nabeshima (1690-1720s) with no mark, like palace-ware.

rows.meaning: Imaizumi Imaemon, successors of the Nabeshima overglaze painters
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: Imaizumi Imaemon kiln (今泉今右衛門)

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Modern mark; exact introduction not established.
rows.what_it_tells: Name of the Imaizumi Imaemon kiln.
rows.cautions: A dispute over the 角福 mark with Kakiemon in the Taishō era is reported; the sources do not date the mark.

facts.text: The Kyushu museum shows 今右衛門 as the mark of the Imaemon kiln, Arita.
Reported dispute: in the Taishō era the Imaizumi family sued over the 角福 mark, later withdrew and called its work Imaemon ware.

rows.meaning: Made by Kakiemon (modern signature form)
rows.device: none (characters only)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: A modern mark; the Kyushu museum shows it as the Kakiemon kiln's mark, and dealer notes place the 'Kakiemon-made' mark after 1928.
rows.what_it_tells: Brand or maker's name for export or modern Arita/Hirado ware; narrows date to the years the brand was in use.
rows.cautions: Do not read as Edo: Edo Kakiemon-style wares carried fuku marks, not the name.

facts.text: The Kyushu museum shows 柿右衛門作 as the mark of the Kakiemon kiln, Arita.
A dealer blog notes that after 1928 Kakiemon XII's own pieces were marked 'Made by Kakiemon'.

rows.meaning: Arita ware (place-of-origin mark)
rows.device: none (characters only)

maker.name: not a single maker: used by many Hizen kilns
maker.place: Arita and other Hizen kilns, Saga/Nagasaki

rows.date_note: 'Arita-yaki' appears as a mark only from the early Shōwa period (Kyushu museum).
rows.what_it_tells: Place and style name: ware from Arita.
rows.cautions: The Edo name for Arita porcelain was Imari-yaki; later marks may use either place name.

facts.text: In the early Shōwa period 有田焼 first begins to be used as a mark; earlier the wares were called Imari ware.
facts.quote: ついに産地の名前を冠した「有田焼」が銘としても使われるようになりました

rows.date_note: Second World War (戦時中); the source gives no exact years.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies area and wartime date, not a kiln name.
rows.cautions: Not all numbers are matched to kilns; Arita records lost.

facts.text: During the Second World War pottery was under government control; Arita guild members stamped 有+number, other Saga guilds 肥+number; the number is a valuable indicator of place and wartime.

other_spellings: crest of the Prince of Satsuma
rows.meaning: Crest (kamon) of the Shimazu lords of Satsuma: a cross inside a circle
rows.device: A cross inside a circle, painted in red, gold or black; usually above a place name or a maker's name
rows.technique: painted in red, gold, black or blue; also stamped or printed on twentieth-century pieces
rows.where_on_object: base, usually above 薩摩 or a maker's name
rows.date_note: Used on genuine Kagoshima wares before 1868 and then, as a trade convention, on export and imitation Satsuma from the 1870s until the present; the crest alone gives no date.
rows.what_it_tells: That the maker or seller wanted the piece taken as Satsuma ware. On pre-Meiji Kagoshima work it points to the domain's patronage; on Meiji and later pieces it is a style label.
rows.cautions: It does not show age or origin. Bowes (1882) says marks were very seldom used in Satsuma itself and the crest appeared only in rare instances. By the Meiji export boom the crest was painted on pieces from Kyoto, Osaka, Tokyo, Yokohama (Ōta) and Seto/Nagoya. Gotheborg records the Shimazu crest with Satsuma stamps on mass-produced pieces made about 1947 for sale to American servicemen and on 1970s-80s imports. Jahn, cited by Wikipedia, says the crest appears regardless of a piece's age or whether it is genuine.

facts.text: Bowes (1882) engraves the crest of the Prince of Satsuma, 'in slight relief, in gold and red', from a tea bowl of choice faience, where it occupies the position of the maker's mark.
facts.quote: CREST OF THE PRINCE OF SATSUMA

facts.text: Bowes notes marks are very seldom used in Satsuma province, and in rare instances the crest or the Prince's name appears.

facts.text: Gotheborg catalogues many Satsuma-style pieces with the Shimazu crest above 薩摩焼 or a studio name, dated from c.1880 through the 1980s, including a mass-produced c.1947 stamped example.

Morse (1901) says most 'Satsuma' sent abroad in the previous thirty years was made for export and 'but little of it has been made in Satsuma'; the Ōta potters near Yokohama contributed to the flood of spurious Satsuma.

rows.meaning: Satsuma (the old province, now Kagoshima); used on export ware as a style label

maker.name: unspecific (Kagoshima kilns and many outside makers)
maker.place: Satsuma province / Kyoto / Osaka / Tokyo / Yokohama

rows.technique: painted in gold, red, black or blue; the last character is often abbreviated to 广
rows.where_on_object: base, under the Shimazu crest
rows.date_note: As a printed or painted export label it belongs to the Meiji export boom (after 1868) and later; Gotheborg dates examples from c.1880 to the 1980s.
rows.what_it_tells: The maker claims the Satsuma style (crackled ivory body, enamel and gilt). Not a place of manufacture.
rows.cautions: Pieces made at Awata and other Kyoto kilns, Osaka, Tokyo, Yokohama and Seto were sold as Satsuma (Jahn via Wikipedia; Morse 1901). The stamp 'Satsuma' in Latin or hiragana letters is twentieth-century. Gotheborg's list notes the last character may appear abbreviated.

facts.text: Bowes records 'Satsuma' within a signed mark on a red-painted vase of 1875 ('Nippon, Nakajima seisu, Satsuma'), Satsuma being named as the style.
Gotheborg lists generic marks reading Satsuma / Satsuma yaki under the Shimazu crest, with the last character abbreviated, and others in hiragana or Latin.
Morse: 'little of it has been made in Satsuma' – the name was applied to export faience made elsewhere.

facts.text: The Kinkōzan family's own account separates Kagoshima clay and decoration (Chin Jukan), Kagoshima clay decorated elsewhere (Yabu Meizan) and work made and decorated outside Kagoshima (Kinkōzan).

rows.meaning: Satsuma ware (the name of the type)
rows.technique: painted or stamped, usually under the Shimazu crest
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Same as the bare 薩摩: a Meiji-and-later export label, not a date.
rows.what_it_tells: The piece is meant as Satsuma-type ware. Japanese dictionaries define 薩摩焼 as the ware of the Kagoshima kilns (Tateno, Naeshirogawa, Ryūmonji and others); 錦手 pieces from them were the export 'Satsuma'.
rows.cautions: Found on Awata/Kyoto, Osaka, Tokyo and Seto pieces and on mid-twentieth-century stamped wares. Compare the full signed marks such as 大日本京都錦光山造 before reading it as a Kagoshima product.

facts.text: Dictionaries describe 薩摩焼 as the ware of the Kagoshima kilns, brocade-style 錦手 pieces being massively exported from the late Edo into the Meiji period.
facts.quote: 幕末から明治にかけて海外むけに大量につくられた

facts.text: Gotheborg examples show 'Satsuma yaki' under the Shimazu crest in the early Meiji (c.1880) through the 1980s.
A c.1947 stamped 'Satsuma' with crest was mass-produced for sale to occupation personnel.

rows.meaning: Great Japan – a patriotic prefix before the maker's name or place
wares: Meiji export wares of every kind
rows.technique: painted in gold or enamel; usually the first column
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The prefix is seen on Meiji export wares, and Bowes (1882) already has it on Kyoto pieces (for example 'Dai Nippon, Dohachi seisu', 1875). Wikipedia and Nilsson say Meiji, and later pieces keep it.
rows.what_it_tells: The piece was made for export in the Meiji period or later. The prefix is a country label, not a maker.
rows.cautions: Later wares copy the whole formula, so the prefix cannot date a piece closer than 'Meiji or later'. A television appraiser declared short forms such as 日本錦光山造 fake (see kinkozan-dai-nippon-kyoto).

facts.text: Bowes translates 'Dai Nippon' as 'Great Japan' on Kyoto marks of Dohachi (scratched 1875) and Yeiraku, and on Seifu.
facts.quote: Dai Nip-pon, Do-Hachi seisu. Made by

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues 大日本清風造 incised on Seifū Yohei III wares dated 1893–1912.
Tokyo National Museum records 「大日本京都 錦光山造之」 in gold on a Kinkōzan jar of 1892.
facts.quote: 大日本京都 錦光山造之

facts.text: The Kyoto Satsuma display list (Sannenzaka Museum 2020) transcribes 大日本明山製 and 大日本京都粟田陶器.

rows.meaning: Satsuma Keida – studio name; 与原彫刻 'carved by Yohara' on the same piece
rows.where_on_object: base or foot
rows.date_note: Meiji export period; no firm dates are recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: Shows a division of labour: one name for the studio, a second for the carver.
rows.cautions: Only one museum record; the studio's place is not stated, and Gotheborg's Keida entry is a reverse transliteration.

facts.text: The 2020 Kyoto Satsuma display list gives the marks 薩摩慶田 and 与原彫刻 on an openwork incense burner with curtain decoration.
facts.quote: 薩摩慶田 与原彫刻

facts.text: Gotheborg lists a Keida entry among Satsuma makers (reverse-transliterated).

rows.meaning: Chin Jukan – hereditary name of the head of the Naeshirogawa (Miyama) kiln family, Kagoshima

maker.name: Chin (沈) family, Naeshirogawa kiln; 12th head Chin Jukan (1835–1906)

wares: Satsuma (Naeshirogawa), including export 錦手 vases
rows.technique: painted (gilt or enamel) or impressed; generation recorded by number in modern use
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: 12th head exhibited at Vienna 1873 and later fairs; the name 沈壽官 has been taken by every head since 1906 (13th 1889–1964, 14th 1926–2019, 15th current).
rows.what_it_tells: A Kagoshima-made piece from the Chin family; the generation matters (12th: Meiji; 13th: Taishō–Shōwa; 14th, 15th: modern).
rows.cautions: Gotheborg (Nilsson) writes the family name as 陳 (Chin); Japanese dictionaries and the family use 沈 (Shin/Chin). The same name is in use today, so an unnumbered signature needs its generation checked. Yabu Meizan decorated Chin blanks, so a Meizan signature on a Chin body does not make it Chin.

facts.text: The 12th Chin Jukan (born 1835, died 1906) showed a large 錦手 vase at the 1873 Vienna exposition; the 14th head took the name in 1964.
facts.quote: 明治6年ウィーン万国博覧会に錦手大花瓶を出品

facts.text: Yabu Meizan decorated Naeshirogawa blanks made by the 12th Chin Jukan for export.
facts.quote: 薩摩苗代川焼 / 12代沈寿官

facts.text: The Kinkōzan family account cites Watanabe's classification: Chin Jukan = Kagoshima clay with Kagoshima decoration.

rows.meaning: Gyokkōzan – art name (号) of the 12th Chin Jukan and name of his post-1877 pottery works
rows.where_on_object: not established
rows.date_note: The Kodansha dictionary says he founded the 玉光山製陶所 after the Satsuma Rebellion (1877); no dates for the mark are recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: If a Satsuma piece reads 玉光山 it points to the Chin Jukan workshop; no object bearing it is recorded in the sources.
rows.cautions: Do not equate with 玉山 (Gyokuzan): Gotheborg identifies a 玉山 signature as Chin Jukan XII (1874–1897), but no Japanese source supports that. How 玉光山 appears on an object is not confirmed.

facts.text: The 12th Chin Jukan's 号 was 玉光山, and he founded the 玉光山製陶所 after the Satsuma Rebellion.

rows.meaning: Gyokuzan – 'jade mountain'; maker or decorator's name on Satsuma

maker.name: unresolved (more than one hand; Chin Jukan XII attribution unverified)

rows.technique: impressed (old faience) or painted in gold (Meiji)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Bowes (1882) shows an impressed Giokuzan on a Satsuma vase 'of considerable age'; the Walters has a 玉山-marked 錦手 vase, dated by the museum to 1860–1900, and gold-painted Gyokuzan marks occur on Meiji export pieces.
rows.what_it_tells: A potter or decorator name only. Whether it is the Chin family depends on the piece.
rows.cautions: Gotheborg claims Chin Jukan XII used Gyokuzan 1874–1897; this rests on that one non-Japanese source and is not confirmed. Gotheborg also dates one 'Gyokuzan' tea set to the mid-twentieth century, and a 'dragonware' ewer 'Satsuma, Gyokuzan zo' to the mid-century.

facts.text: Bowes no.130: 'Impressed upon a Vase of excellent work and considerable age. Gyokuzan (Giokuzan), the name of the maker.'
facts.quote: Giokuzan, the name of the maker

facts.text: The Walters Art Museum's 錦手 vase carries a 玉山 mark (museum dates it 1860–1900).
Gotheborg lists Gyokuzan gold marks (Meiji) and equates the name with Chin Jukan XII, 1874–1897.

rows.meaning: Kinkōzan – 'brocade-light mountain'; the Awata kiln name
rows.device: small oblong or square seal
wares: Awata (Kyoto) faience, tea wares and incense burners
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse dated impressed Kinkōzan pieces 1780–1860 in his Case 27; Bowes (1882) calls other impressed examples 'modern faience'. These dates are catalogue estimates, not recorded years.
rows.what_it_tells: An Awata piece from the Kinkōzan kiln, usually pre-export (to c.1870) tea and display wares.
rows.cautions: Morse says the first Kinkōzan signature came when the family moved from Iwakurayama to Awata; his catalogue also has a piece 'Suga Sobei (imp.)' from 'one of the Kinkōzan generations'. The impressed seal is not the gilt Meiji export signature (see the separate Kinkōzan zō entry).

facts.text: Bowes lists Kinkōzan among the five chief impressed Kyoto marks (Ninsei, Dohachi, Yeiraku, Taizan, Kinkozan) and shows examples on faience (nos. 280–283, p.140).
facts.quote: impressed marks are those of the

facts.text: Morse: Kinkōzan first used its signature in Awata (another account: first generation Kobayashi Tokuyemon working in Awata in 1646); impressed examples are dated 1780–1860.
The Kinkōzan family blog gives the founding as 1645 by Kagiya Tokuemon (鍵屋徳右衛門), with the name 錦光山 gained by the 2nd head.
Kyoto Satsuma glazing was perfected by 1870 and full-scale export began in 1872, credited to the 6th Kinkōzan Sōbei, whose son the 7th developed it further.
facts.quote: began their export in full scale

rows.meaning: Kinkōzan signature painted in red on the export Awata ware
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse (c.1901) says that 'in 1877, or thereabouts' Sōbei Kinkōzan flooded the foreign market with profusely decorated Awata signed with the painted mark in red.
rows.what_it_tells: Early export decoration at Kinkōzan, 1870s–80s.
rows.cautions: This rests on a single early-catalogue statement; the Japanese records transcribe the gilt form instead. It needs Japanese confirmation.

facts.text: Morse: 'signed with the painted mark Kinkōzan in red'; Sōbei Kinkōzan flooded the foreign market from 1877.
facts.quote: signed with the painted mark Kinkozan

rows.meaning: Made by Kinkōzan (造 'made'; 製 'manufactured')
rows.device: often in a square or in gilt seal script; sometimes inside a cartouche
wares: Kyoto Satsuma export vases, plates, bowls, incense burners, koro
rows.technique: gilt painted signature, sometimes with a separate seal
rows.where_on_object: base (inside the foot ring), or inside a painted cartouche or screen on the decoration
rows.date_note: Kinkōzan VI began export wares from about 1870–72; the 7th head (1867/68–1927) ran the firm from 1884 to his death; the firm ended with him (c.1927).
rows.what_it_tells: Product of the Kinkōzan workshop (Awata, Kyoto) made for export. Different painters worked for the firm; 'Kinkōzan zō' names the house, not the painter.
rows.cautions: (1) A television appraiser declared fake a vase reading 日本錦光山造 on the base, saying genuine pieces carry fuller marks such as 大日本京都錦光山造 in clear regular or clerical script. (2) The mark can be elaborate: on a 2018 programme it was hidden inside a painted screen, reading 'Kotobuki Dai Nippon Kyoto Kinkōzan zō', with 錦光山 on a scroll. (3) Kinkōzan made blanks that outside decorators (Yabu Meizan) used.

facts.text: The 2020 Kyoto Satsuma exhibition list gives the signature as 錦光山造 on vases, bowls and incense burners, and as 錦光山造之 on a Kannon-on-dragon vase.
Tokyo National Museum records a Kinkōzan Sōbei VII jar (1892, Chicago exposition) with gold-painted 「大日本京都 錦光山造之」 and a seal 「錦光山造」.
On a 2018 television appraisal the mark normally sits inside the foot ring ('高台の中に「錦光山」').
On a 2012 television appraisal, 日本錦光山造 was judged a fake.
Bowes shows a gold-painted 'Nippon, Kioto, Kinkozan tsukuru' (no.284) on a flower pot of inferior faience.
Kinkōzan VI began export decoration (about 1870–72) with Satsuma techniques; VII made colored gilt (色絵金襴手) his speciality and died in 1927.
facts.quote: 色絵金襴手を得意とし

大日本京都粟田陶器 錦光山製

rows.meaning: Made by Kinkōzan of Kyoto, Great Japan (full export form); also 'Great Japan Kyoto Awata ceramics, made by Kinkōzan'
rows.technique: gilt painted, often with a separate seal
rows.where_on_object: base; sometimes within the picture
rows.date_note: The Tokyo National Museum example is 1892 (Chicago exposition); the television appraiser dates the peak of Kinkōzan export to the Meiji 10s (1877-86).
rows.what_it_tells: The fullest recorded Kinkōzan export form; it matches what a Japanese appraiser on television treats as the reliable form.
rows.cautions: Shorter or garbled forms (日本錦光山造) were called fake on television; forgeries copy the formula, so check the gilt writing, the body and the painting too.

facts.text: Tokyo National Museum, Meiji 25 (1892): inscription 「大日本京都 錦光山造之」 painted in gold, with seal 「錦光山造」.
facts.quote: 大日本京都 錦光山造之

facts.text: The 2020 display list gives 大日本京都粟田陶器 / 錦光山製 on a plate with painter credit 圭山画.
facts.quote: 大日本京都粟田陶器 錦光山製

facts.text: The 2012 appraiser says genuine pieces carry 「大日本京都錦光山造」 written firmly in regular or clerical script.
The 2018 appraisal records the same wording as '寿 大日本京都錦光山造' painted on a screen in the scene.
facts.quote: 寿　大日本京都錦光山造

rows.meaning: Keizan – painter credit ('圭山画' painted by Keizan) on a Kinkōzan plate
rows.technique: painted in gilt after the Kinkōzan signature
rows.where_on_object: base or front
rows.date_note: Meiji; no dates are recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: The decorator employed by Kinkōzan for that piece.
rows.cautions: Only one record is known; Keizan's identity is not established.

facts.text: A plate is marked 大日本京都粟田陶器 錦光山製, 圭山画 (painted by Keizan).
Kinkōzan-workshop plates in museum catalogues carry a workshop signature ('Kinkōzan zu') plus a separate painter's signature ending in 'ga' (painted by), the same pattern as 圭山画 and 一香画.

rows.meaning: Ikkō – painter credit ('一香画') on a Kinkōzan plate
rows.where_on_object: base or front
rows.date_note: Meiji; no dates recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: Decorator credit on a Kinkōzan piece.
rows.cautions: Single record; the reading 'Ikkō' comes from the museum's romanisation.

facts.text: A plate 'summer evening scene' is marked 錦光山造 with 一香画.

rows.meaning: Sozan – painter; '京都素山造' made by Sozan of Kyoto

maker.name: Sozan, painter and openwork specialist (worked for Kinkōzan)

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji; no dates are recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A named Kyoto painter who worked for Kinkōzan and under his own name.
rows.cautions: The 'Sozan' cartouche that appears on Kinkōzan plates may be this painter; do not confuse with Suwa Sozan (諏訪蘇山), the Kyoto potter listed in 1910 London exhibition.

facts.text: A 2020 exhibit is signed 京都素山造 (openwork vase with flowers).
The Kinkōzan family blog calls 素山 an unknown genius painter who painted Kinkōzan works.
A Kinkōzan plate with Sozan cartouche is shown on Cefiro's Satsuma page.
素山 was the 号 of Yanagida Tajirō (1865–1925), a painter from Ishikawa employed at the Kinkōzan works from c.1897; the best Kinkōzan pieces often carry a 素山 signature.
facts.quote: 錦光山窯の作品でも優れたものに素山銘のものが多い

rows.device: small impressed oblong seal

maker.name: Taizan Yohei family (帯山與兵衛), Takahashi family

wares: Awata faience: hibachi, tea wares, incense burners
rows.where_on_object: base

rows.what_it_tells: Awata tea and display ware of the Taizan kiln; the family was among the largest Awata makers.
rows.cautions: Morse says the variety of Taizan marks cannot be sorted by family generation. Bowes shows common modern faience with the same impressed mark, so it also appears on commercial late wares. Bowes calls Taizan 'one of the most extensive manufacturers of faience in Awata'.

facts.text: Bowes nos. 263–269 (p. 136): impressed Taizan mark on fine old ware and on 'modern faience of common quality'; no. 269 reads 'Awata Taizan', the maker and the district.
facts.quote: one of the most extensive manufacturers

facts.text: Morse: the founding Takahashi Tokuro came from Omi and built a kiln in Awata in 1673; 'the mark Taizan was first used in 1760' (Ninagawa).
facts.quote: the mark Taizan was first used in 1760

facts.text: A Japanese dictionary says the first Taizan Yohei (高橋藤九郎) began in Awata Higashimachi, was active 1673–81, and took the name 帯山.

rows.meaning: Taizan Yohei – the Kyoto Satsuma export decorator (9th head, 1856–1922)

maker.name: Taizan Yohei IX (帯山與兵衛, 1856–1922), adopted 1878
maker.place: Awata, Kyoto (kiln moved to Yawata 1894, 南山焼)

wares: Kyoto Satsuma (京薩摩) vases, tea sets
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: English Wikipedia says exports began in 1872; the 9th Yohei (1878–1922) is the maker of the export Satsuma that carries the name, and Kodansha dates him 1856–1922.
rows.what_it_tells: Awata decorator who sold Satsuma-style wares to the West, working beside the 6th Kinkōzan.
rows.cautions: Eight earlier Taizan Yohei existed; the 8th (d.1878) also made wares for Europe and America.

facts.text: The 9th Taizan Yohei (b.1856, d.1922) was born in Kyoto, adopted into the Taizan family in 1878 and moved the kiln to Yawata in 1894; he promoted overseas sales with Kinkōzan VI, and his style was called 京薩摩.
facts.quote: その様式は京薩摩と呼ばれ

facts.text: English Wikipedia lists Taizan/Obi-ya as c.1673–1922, exporting from 1872.
The Kinkōzan family blog lists the Taizan Yohei family as one of the Awata houses.

Another source differs: Names the 8th Taizan Yohei (head from 1861), not the 9th, as the partner of Kinkōzan VI in starting overseas trade in 1872; the dictionary credits the 9th (adopted 1878) with promoting overseas sales with Kinkōzan VI. Not necessarily contradictory, but the generation should be checked.
facts.quote: 八代帯山與兵衛（生没年未詳，1861年家督を継ぐ）

facts.text: Taizan Yohei, Kinkōzan Sōbei, Yasuda Genshichi and Itō Tōzan were the Awata potters who won awards at the 1888 Barcelona exposition.
facts.quote: 1888年のバルセロナ万国博覧会で受賞した粟田焼の陶工たち

rows.meaning: Hōzan – kiln name of the Unrin'in (雲林院) Bunzō family of Awata

maker.name: Hōzan Bunzō family (宝山文蔵), 9th head took the name in 1723
maker.place: Awata, Kyoto (16th head moved to Gojōzaka)

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The 9th head (d. 1723) received the name from Hōzan-ji on Mt. Ikoma and the family used 宝山 as kiln mark ever since; the 16th head (1820–1889) moved to Gojōzaka.
rows.what_it_tells: Awata kiln; on Meiji gilt pieces it is a Kyoto Satsuma decorating house. The 2020 exhibition list shows 寳山 painted beside the company mark of the Kyoto Ceramics Co.
rows.cautions: Morse notes the Hōzan family also copied Ninsei, Iwakurayama and Awata marks. Gotheborg lists a Yasuda Hozan and a Hozan of Kyoto separate from the Awata family – the same kanji on different studios.

facts.text: The 9th Hōzan Bunzō (d.1723) received the name 宝山 from Hōzan-ji in Yamato and 'every generation used 宝山 as kiln mark'; the 16th (1820–1889) moved from Awataguchi to Gojōzaka.
Morse: Hōzan (Case 27): founder Bunzō came from Omi in the mid-seventeenth century; the family used marks Akashi, Asahimine and Taihei Hōzan and imitated Ninsei.
The 2020 display list transcribes 寳山 on a vase beside 京都陶磁器合資会社.
facts.quote: 京都陶磁器合資会社 寳山

rows.meaning: Taihei – honorific name and seal granted to the 16th Hōzan in 1857
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kodansha says the 16th head was given the 号 and seal 泰平 in Ansei 4 (1857).
rows.what_it_tells: A Hōzan-family piece of the second half of the 19th century.
rows.cautions: Morse writes the old mark as 'Taihei' and 'Taihei Hōzan' without dates, and does not clearly tie the reading to the 16th head.

facts.text: The 16th Hōzan Bunzō (1820–1889) was given the 号 and seal 泰平 in 1857.
facts.quote: 安政4年に「泰平」の号と印

facts.text: Morse lists Taihei and Taihei Hōzan among marks used by the Hōzan family.

rows.meaning: Seikōzan – a Kyoto decorating studio (name 'refined-skill mountain')

maker.name: Seikōzan (also Seikōzan Kichiroku in Bowes); later Yasuda Co. artists

wares: Kyoto Satsuma; porcelain in Eiraku-style kinrande (Bowes)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Bowes (1882) already shows 'Dai Nippon Seikōzan' in blue on a porcelain teapot in Eiraku kinrande style (no.291, p.143); the Satsuma gilt pieces are Meiji.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto house making export Satsuma and Eiraku copies.
rows.cautions: The name can read as an individual or a company. Gotheborg lists both 'Seikozan' and 'Seikozan, Yasuda Co.'. Bowes's Seikozan Kichiroku is a follower of the Yeiraku family.

facts.text: The 2020 display list records 精巧山 on paired vases with 100 poets and on teabowls, and 精巧山造 on one teabowl.
Bowes no. 291: painted in blue upon a porcelain teapot in kinrande 'in imitation of the ware made by the Yeiraku family'; Dai Nippon Seikōzan.
Bowes index: 'Seikozan Kichiroku, 143'.
Gotheborg and Cefiro pair Seikōzan with the Yasuda company.

rows.meaning: Ryōzan – Kyoto Satsuma painter associated with the Yasuda company

maker.name: Ryōzan (亮山, 1868–1912 per Cefiro); decorator of Yasuda Kyoto Tōjiki Gōshi Kaisha

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Cefiro gives 1868–1912 (the Meiji era) for the name.
rows.what_it_tells: Painter on Yasuda company wares.
rows.cautions: The kanji 亮山 and the 'Okamoto Ryozan' identification come only from collector sites, not from Japanese references; Cefiro also shows a 'KYOTO RYOZAN' vase under a Shimazu crest.

facts.text: Cefiro lists Ryōzan 亮山 (1868–1912) among the Kyoto makers, and shows a 'Kyoto Ryozan' vase under the Shimazu crest.
Gotheborg lists Ryozan, and 'Ryozan, Yasuda Co.'.

rows.kana: きょうととうじきごうしがいしゃ
rows.meaning: Kyoto Ceramics Limited Partnership (the Yasuda company)
rows.device: company name plus a trademark
wares: Kyoto Satsuma export wares (Seikōzan, Ryōzan, Hōzan decorators)
rows.technique: gilt or enamel painted company name with a trademark
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji (Cefiro, Wikipedia); no establishment date is confirmed, and Kyoto Tōjiki Gōshi Kaisha is a Japanese commercial form of the 1890s onward.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto exporter-decorator; individual artists (Seikōzan, Ryōzan, Hōzan) worked under it.
rows.cautions: The identification of Yasuda with 京都陶磁器合資会社 rests on comparing a display-list entry with collector pages, not on a company history. The firm's dates are not established.

facts.text: A 2020 exhibit vase is transcribed 京都陶磁器合資会社 together with 寳山.
Wikipedia (en) lists Yasuda as 'Yasuda Kyoto Tokiji Goshigaisha', Meiji period; Cefiro shows the full company name plus a trademark on a vase.

rows.meaning: Yabu Meizan – Osaka decorator of export Satsuma (born Yabu Masashichi 政七)
rows.device: gilt in a square seal or hand-written
wares: Satsuma blanks decorated in Osaka (Chin Jukan XII and Kyoto blanks)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kodansha: set up a Satsuma-painting studio at Nakanoshima in Meiji 13 (1880); died 1934.
rows.what_it_tells: An Osaka decorating house of the highest grade; blanks from Naeshirogawa and Kyoto; Meizan works won awards abroad.
rows.cautions: Gotheborg lists two entries, 'Meizan (1880–1920)' and 'Meizan, Yabu', so a bare 明山 may be another hand.

facts.text: Yabu Meizan (b. 1853 Osaka, d. 1934) learned painting in Tokyo and set up a Satsuma studio at Nakanoshima in Meiji 13; 'Meizan Satsuma' won international awards.
The 2020 display list records 藪明山 on teabowls and vases, and 大日本明山製 on a pair of vases.

rows.kana: だいにっぽんめいざんせい
rows.meaning: Made by Meizan, Great Japan

maker.name: Yabu Meizan or a studio hand

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji; the record is undated.
rows.what_it_tells: A signature without 藪; attribution to the Yabu workshop is likely but not proven.
rows.cautions: No source ties it to Yabu Meizan himself.

facts.text: The 2020 display list records 大日本明山製 on a pair of vases with cranes, flowers and figures, under the artist heading 'Dainihon Meizan'.

rows.meaning: Nakamura Baikei – decorator of Kyoto Satsuma
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji; no dates recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A named decorator.
rows.cautions: Single record; Gotheborg gives the kanji as 梅渓 / 中村梅渓 (plum valley), a different form of Baikei.

facts.text: Two exhibits are signed 中村楳渓造 and 中村楳渓 (feudal lord procession bowl; children shooting arrows teabowl).
Gotheborg lists Baikei and Nakamura Baikei (中村梅渓).

rows.meaning: Koshida – 'made by Koshida'; 祥山 Shōzan as decorator

maker.name: Koshida workshop (越田), c.1880–1927; resumed after 1945

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: English Wikipedia gives c.1880–1927, resumed after 1945.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto Satsuma studio.
rows.cautions: There was post-1945 production under the same name; the place comes from English Wikipedia only.

facts.text: Display list: 越田製造 with 祥山 on a pierced fan-shaped jar and 越田 / 祥山 on a box.

rows.meaning: Hankinzan – Osaka-style house name (阪 = Osaka)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji; no dates are recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A house signing 堂 (hall) or 造 (made).
rows.cautions: The Osaka reading of 阪 is an inference; the exhibition list gives no place. Gotheborg's Hankinzan entry is a reverse transliteration.

facts.text: Four exhibits are transcribed 阪錦山堂 or 阪錦山造.

rows.meaning: Bizan – decorator name; several people used it

maker.name: more than one Bizan (old Kyoto Bizan d.1862; later decorators)

rows.technique: painted in gold; Bowes: 'Painted by Bizan, Great Japan'
rows.where_on_object: inside bowl or base
rows.date_note: Morse's Bizan (born Kanazawa) died 1862 aged 58 and worked with Awata tea pots; Bowes shows Meiji 'Dai Nippon Bizan yegaku' on Taizan bowls.
rows.what_it_tells: A painter's name; the same signature belongs to multiple hands.
rows.cautions: Gotheborg: 'There were a number of Bizans working over the years'; this is not the Kutani Shimizu Bizan.

facts.text: Bowes nos.270–271: Taizan-made bowls 'probably decorated at Tokio' carry gold 'Dai Nippon, Bizan yegaku – painted by Bizan, Great Japan'.
Morse: Bizan, from Kanazawa, studied painting in Kyoto, decorated Awata teapots and died 1862 aged 58.
facts.quote: died in 1862 at the age of fifty-eight

facts.text: The 2020 list transcribes 美山 on an incense burner with landscape and figures.

rows.meaning: Hododa (Hotoda) – a Tokyo decorating house
rows.where_on_object: base under the crest
rows.date_note: Meiji; the sources give no dates.
rows.what_it_tells: A Tokyo painting house.
rows.cautions: Both readings (Hododa and Hotoda) circulate, and only Western collector sources cite the kanji.

facts.text: Gotheborg lists 薩广 保土田 ('Satsuma Hododa') and 保土田造 ('Hotoda zo') and shows pieces under the crest.

rows.meaning: Seifū Yohei, a Kyoto porcelain family (Gojōzaka); three-character form with 與平
rows.device: impressed or incised seal 清風, or blue-painted

maker.name: Seifū Yohei I (1801/03–1861), II (1845–1878), III (1851–1914), later heads

wares: Kyoto porcelain, sencha and tea wares
rows.technique: impressed seal (Bowes, Morse); incised 大日本清風造 on the base; blue underglaze signature (Bowes 307, Cleveland)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse says the first Seifū came to Kyoto from Kanazawa in 1844 and set up an oven in Gojōbashi; Cleveland catalogues Seifū III pieces of 1887–1914 and later Seifū wares to 1946.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto porcelain studio; the generation matters (III was an Imperial Household Artist and has Teishitsu gigei'in on box lids).
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on the first Seifū's years: Cleveland gives 1801–1861, Kodansha 1803–1861. Morse's third Seifū (pseudonym Baikai) does not match Kodansha's third-generation art name (号 清山 / 晁浦 / 晟山), so the generation numbering is unsettled. Box inscriptions (清風與平 seal; 帝室技芸員) are on the box, not the piece.

facts.text: Cleveland: 大日本清風造 incised on the base of a gu-shaped vase by Seifū Yohei III (1893–97); box lid inscribed 帝室技芸員 and seal 清風與平.
Cleveland: 清風 inscribed on the base of other Seifū III wares (1893–1914); an impressed 'Seifū' seal on a teapot base.
Bowes shows the impressed seal of Seifu and a blue painted 'Dai Nippon Seifu tsukuru' on modern porcelain (nos. 307–309).
Morse: Seifū Yohei, pseudonym Baihin, came from Kanazawa in 1844 and set up an oven in Gojōbashi; Seifū (imp.) on 1850 pieces.

rows.meaning: Kanzan Denshichi – Kiyomizu potter (1821–1890) who made Western-colour porcelain and later export wares
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kodansha says he moved to Kyoto in 1862, built a kiln at Kiyomizu, learned Wagener's Western pigments after the Restoration, exhibited at Vienna in 1873 and used 'Kanzan Denshichi' from 1872, while Morse says the Kanzan kiln began in 1805.
rows.what_it_tells: Kyoto export porcelain with European-type painting. Morse says that in 1872 successors of the family made large quantities of highly decorated pottery for the foreign market, commonly seen as Kanzan.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse 幹山 with 乾山 (Kenzan). The Kodansha page prints the name as 乾山伝七 after 1872, against 幹山 in other spellings, so confirm the character on the piece. Morse says the Kanzan kiln began in 1805 while Kodansha puts the potter's birth in 1821; the dates refer to different people or generations. Morse records a blue-written 'Rakutō kō Kanzan tsukuru' (洛東 = east of Kyoto).

facts.text: Kanzan Denshichi (1821–1890) of Owari moved to Kyoto in 1862 and later built a kiln at Kiyomizu; exhibited Western-style porcelain at Vienna 1873.
Morse: Denshichi Kanzan began baking in Kiyomizu in 1805; in 1872 successors made decorated export wares.
facts.quote: began the baking of pottery in Kiyomizu

rows.meaning: Eiraku – 'eternal pleasure': silver seal awarded to Eiraku Hozen in 1827
rows.device: square seal

maker.name: Eiraku Zengorō family (西村善五郎), from the 11th, Hōzen (保全, 1795–1854)

wares: Kyoto kinrande, aka-e porcelain and faience, tea wares
rows.technique: impressed seal on faience and porcelain; or painted 'Dai Nippon Eiraku tsukuru' in red/gold on porcelain
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Hōzen was invited to the Kishu Nishihama garden kiln in 1827 and given gold and silver seals 河濱支流 and 永樂, and the family took the name Eiraku formally only in Meiji (Japanese Wikipedia).
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto kiln of the Zengorō house; the Eiraku name begins with Hōzen. Wazen (和全, 1823–1896) moved to Kaga (Yamashiro) in 1866 and made Kutani-style wares.
rows.cautions: Bowes (1882) attributes the 永樂 seal to Ryōzen, the 10th head, as a reward from the Tokugawa. Morse, the Japanese encyclopedia and Japanese Wikipedia say it was Hōzen (1827, Kishu Tokugawa). Eiraku wares were widely imitated: Bowes's Seikōzan teapot is a copy in Eiraku style, and pieces reading 'Yeiraku made in Kutani' (Bowes) were made by a family member who settled in Kaga, not at the Kyoto kiln.

facts.text: Heibonsha: Hōzen was granted gold and silver seals 〈河浜支流〉〈永楽〉 by the Kishu Tokugawa house (garden kiln of Nishihama, 1827).
facts.quote: 〈河浜支流〉〈永楽〉の金･銀印を下賜

facts.text: Morse: the Daimyō of Kii gave Hōzen two seals, silver and gold, 'Kahin Shirin' and 'Yeiraku'.
Bowes pp.133–134: Yeiraku impressed on faience and porcelain (nos. 251–254), and 'Dai Nippon, Yeiraku tsukuru' painted in red/gold on kinrande porcelain.
Wazen (1823–1896) revived Ninsei's Omuro kiln in 1852, taught Kutani wares at Yamashiro, and made Okazaki Eiraku in Aichi after the Restoration.

rows.meaning: 'A branch of the river-bank': gold seal granted to Eiraku Hozen by the Kishu Tokugawa
rows.device: square gold seal
wares: Kyoto ceramics made for Kishu and tea wares
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Awarded in 1827; Hōzen died 1854.
rows.what_it_tells: Strongly associated with Hōzen's Kishu (Kairakuen) period wares.
rows.cautions: Morse spells it 'Kahin Shirin'. The seal is a gift mark; later Eiraku family members used other seals; imitation is plausible but not recorded in the sources.

facts.text: Heibonsha encyclopedia: gold seal 河浜支流 and silver seal 永楽, presented by the Kishu Tokugawa.
Morse reads the seals as 'Kahin Shirin' (gold) and 'Yeiraku' (silver).

rows.romaji: Sei in a hexagon (Kiyomizu Rokubei seal)
rows.meaning: 清 ('Kiyo') inside a hexagon – the seal of the Kiyomizu Rokubei family, passed down from the first Rokubei
rows.device: the character 清 in a six-sided (hexagonal) frame; the 2nd generation used a double hexagon frame
wares: Kyoto Kiyomizu ware, tea wares, porcelain
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The first Rokubei began in 1737 (Morse); the year the seal was given is not stated, so 1737 is the earliest possible, and Britannica says it came from the Tenryūji priest and was used by every generation.
rows.what_it_tells: Wares of the Kiyomizu Rokubei family. The generation has to be fixed from the piece itself: 1st 1738–1799, 2nd 1790–1860, 3rd 1822–1883, 4th 1848–1920, 5th 1875–1959.
rows.cautions: Britannica says the hexagon seal was received from the Tenryūji monk 桂州; another dictionary mentions a '六目の印' (six-eyes seal) from Myōhōin-no-miya, so the two accounts differ. Morse notes a bowl of Rokubei 'with mark erased' being passed off, and the 4th generation also used 清六 and 六居 seals.

facts.text: Britannica: the 1st Rokubei received a hexagonal 「清」 seal from the priest Keishū of Tenryūji, and every generation used it.
Morse: 1st Rokubei's later work bore 'the impressed mark Sei, in hexagon', also 'Seifu' in a double gourd; earlier work marked Roku (incised).
Kodansha: the 2nd Rokubei used a seal of 清 in a double-frame hexagon; the 4th used 清六 and 六居.
facts.quote: 二重枠の六角に清の字の印

rows.meaning: Rokubei – impressed name mark and incised 六 of the early Kiyomizu Rokubei family

maker.name: Kiyomizu Rokubei I (1738–1799), 號 愚斎

rows.technique: incised 'Roku' on early Shigaraki-clay pieces; impressed 'Rokubei' on later work
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse: Kiyomizu Rokubei acquired the potter's art in 1737, first used Shigaraki clay with incised 'Roku' (about 1740 in his Case 29), and continued until 1787.
rows.what_it_tells: Early work of the first Rokubei.
rows.cautions: Many later Rokubeis used the name; see the hexagon seal row.

facts.text: Morse: first Rokubei's pieces are 'usually signed with the incised mark Roku'; later the impressed mark Sei in hexagon, 'Rokubei', and rarely 'Kiyomizu Gusai' and 'Dai Michi'.
The Met Museum holds an 18th-century Kiyomizu Rokubei I teabowl.

rows.meaning: Dōhachi – Takahashi Dōhachi, Kyoto potter family (Awata → Gojōzaka)
rows.technique: impressed seal on faience; painted in black on raku; scratched with 'Dai Nippon Dohachi sei' (1875)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse dates his impressed Dohachi pieces to 1790; Bowes shows works of 1820 and 1875 by later generations.
rows.what_it_tells: One of the five chief impressed Kyoto marks (Bowes). The second generation, Nin'ami Dōhachi (1783–1855), is the most famous.
rows.cautions: Four or six generations share the mark. Pieces by Nin'ami and later copies in his style are numerous; for example, Makuzu Kōzan II made a bowl 'in the style of Nin'ami Dōhachi' signed Kōzan (Ashmolean EA2000.181). Sources disagree on the first generation's years (1739, 1742, 1749–1804).

facts.text: Bowes nos. 241–243: Dohachi impressed on a perfume box c.1820; painted in black on raku ware; and scratched 'Dai Nippon, Dohachi seisu' on a vase by a descendant in 1875.
Morse, Case 30: Dohachi (impressed) pieces of 1790; the name is 'justly celebrated in the annals of Kiyomizu potters'.
Japanese dictionaries list Dōhachi I (d.1804, Ise-born, kiln at Sanjō Awataguchi), II Nin'ami (1783–1855), III (1811–1879), IV (1845–1897).
facts.quote: 江戸後期に始まる清水焼陶工の代々の名

rows.meaning: Nin'ami: the name of Dōhachi II (1783–1855), made from the name 阿弥 and the character 仁 given by his patrons

maker.name: Takahashi Dōhachi II (高橋道八二代, 1783–1855)
maker.place: Kyoto (Awata, then Gojōzaka; late kiln at Fushimi Momoyama)

wares: tea wares, 雲錦手, Momoyama kiln wares
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Heibonsha: from 1825 (Bunsei 8) he called himself Hokkyō Nin'ami.
rows.what_it_tells: Dōhachi II's mature name; the pieces are among the most copied in Kyoto ware.
rows.cautions: Later potters work 'in the style of Nin'ami Dōhachi'; the Ashmolean bowl (c.1925, by Makuzu Hanzan) is signed 'Kōzan', not Nin'ami.

facts.text: Heibonsha: Dōhachi II received the name 阿弥 from the Daigo Sanbōin-no-miya and the 仁 character and the rank of hokkyō from Ninna-ji-no-miya; he called himself 法橋仁阿弥 from 1825.
The Ashmolean bowl EA2000.181 (c.1925) is 'in the style of Nin'ami Dōhachi' by Miyagawa Hanzan, signed Kōzan.

rows.meaning: Ninsei – seal of Nonomura Ninsei (Omuro kiln, Kyoto), taken from 仁 (Ninna-ji) + 清 (Seiemon)
rows.device: impressed seal 仁清 (large and small seals exist, according to Britannica)
wares: tea wares, incense burners, 色絵 overglaze enamel pottery
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The name 仁清 was given about 1657 by Ninna-ji (山川日本史小辞典), Ninsei died c.1694, and the seal appears on later copies.
rows.what_it_tells: At most 'in the Ninsei manner'. A 仁清 seal has been forged since the seventeenth century.
rows.cautions: Bowes (1882): the seal on decorated figure bowls is 'frequently forged upon ware made in the present day'; Morse: 'from that time to the present, imitations have been attempted bearing the forged mark Ninsei' and many pieces in his collection signed Ninsei are doubtful. Ninsei II (second Seiemon) is poorly separated from I. Wazen revived the Omuro kiln in 1852.

facts.text: Bowes nos.233–236: the Ninsei seal impressed on tea bowls; figure-decorated examples 'unquestionably of recent date'; 'The seal is frequently forged'.
facts.quote: frequently forged upon ware made in the

facts.text: Morse: forged 'Ninsei' marks on imitations since the time Ninsei taught other Kyoto kilns.
Heibonsha: Ninsei impressed a 〈仁清〉 seal on products; Britannica: 'large and small Ninsei seals are stamped on his works'.
facts.quote: 製品に〈仁清〉の銘印を捺した

facts.text: Nipponica: the 2nd Seiemon's work is far below the first, and 2nd-generation pieces are not separable.
facts.quote: その力量は初代にはるか及ばず

facts.text: Metropolitan Museum has a c.1660 tea jar and an Omuro water jar attributed to Ninsei.

rows.meaning: Kenzan – art name of Ogata Shinsei (1663–1743), brother of Kōrin; used later by successors and imitators

maker.name: Ogata Kenzan I (d.1743 aged 83, brother of Kōrin) and later users of the name

rows.technique: brush-painted signature, often in brown or black; also incised
rows.where_on_object: base or on the decorated face
rows.date_note: Morse dates Kenzan's work from the later seventeenth century to the earlier eighteenth; he died in 1743, so signatures after 1743 are by successors or imitators.
rows.what_it_tells: Do not treat as proof of a first-generation Kenzan. A Kenzan signature is among the most forged in Japanese ceramics.
rows.cautions: Morse writes: 'No signature has been so often forged as that of Kenzan; and spurious Kenzan may be found in every stock'. Bowes shows Kenzan painted in brown or black on teapots. Morse and later sources note a Kenzan III of the Bunsei era (1818-30), recorded in Dr Frank's catalogue (cited by Morse), and Morse also lists a piece signed Kenzan in writing together with an impressed Seifu mark.

facts.text: Morse: 'No signature has been so often forged as that of Kenzan'; also records a water-jar inscribed 'Kenzan Sandai Bunsei nensei' (Kenzan the third, Bunsei era).
facts.quote: No signature has been so often forged

facts.text: Bowes nos. 237-240 show Kenzan painted in brown or black on tea jars, bowls and a teapot; Bowes describes Kenzan as copying Ninsei and Makuzu ware.
A Japanese dictionary gives Kenzan's 号 as 乾山, 紫翠, 逃禅, 尚古斎, 陶隠.
facts.quote: 乾山，紫翠，逃禅，尚古斎，陶隠

rows.meaning: Mokubei – Aoki Mokubei (1767–1833), Kyoto potter and painter
rows.technique: signed with the name or one of his 号, usually with a seal
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Died 1833 (dictionaries); Morse says he visited Kaga in 1807 for three years.
rows.what_it_tells: Many later potters adopted his style.
rows.cautions: Morse cannot confirm that the impressed 'Kinju' Kaga pieces are Mokubei's, and notes that the name Sahei was also his but pieces bearing a Sahei mark are far older, with no record that he used it; he calls his specimen 'characteristic' only. The Japanese sources cited here give no mark facsimile.

facts.text: Heibonsha: 木米 from his childhood home 木屋; other names 聾米, 九々鱗, 百六散人, 古器観, 停雲楼.
Morse: Mokubei visited Kaga in 1807; the impressed mark 'Kinju' is 'said to be a mark used by Mokubei'.
facts.quote: said to be a mark used by Mokubei

facts.text: Met holds several Mokubei teapots and bowls (catalogued as Mokubei, 1800s).
Another source differs: Writes 百六山人 where Heibonsha has 百六散人 (variant spelling); lists 龍米 and 青來, which Heibonsha's list omits; 停雲楼 is absent.

rows.meaning: Raku: the seal given by Toyotomi Hideyoshi to Chōjirō / Jōkei and used by the Raku family of Kyoto
rows.device: the single character 樂, a different stamp for each generation

maker.name: Raku Kichizaemon family (樂吉左衛門), founder Chōjirō; 15th head today

rows.technique: impressed seal on the foot ring
rows.where_on_object: inside the foot ring (高台内)
rows.date_note: Hideyoshi gave the seal in the late 16th century (the sources give no year); Bowes puts the family's origin in Kyoto in 1550. Every head since has used it.
rows.what_it_tells: Raku family pieces; the head's name must be read from the stamp variety (Bowes: 'each succeeding generation has used a stamp of its own').
rows.cautions: Bowes says the seal went to Chōjirō himself (Japanese dictionaries say the 2nd head Jōkei), that the second Chōjirō lost it and that each later head cut his own. Raku-style wares were also made at branch kilns (大樋焼, 玉水焼) and by amateurs who write 'Raku' too (Japanese dictionaries), so the seal is not exclusive to the Raku family.

facts.text: Britannica: the 2nd head Jōkei received a 「楽」 seal from Hideyoshi and took Raku as house name; the seal is stamped inside the foot.
Bowes: the Taikō presented a gold seal 'Raku' to Chōjirō; eleven generations; each generation used its own stamp (nos. 224–232).
facts.quote: each succeeding generation has used a

facts.text: Nipponica: the main branch kilns are 玉水焼 and 大樋焼; the Raku head today is the 15th.
Another source differs: The 樂 seal was granted by Hideyoshi, in this account to Tanaka Sōkei (father of the 2nd head Jōkei), not to Jōkei; the author says it is presumed, not documented.
facts.quote: 「樂」の印を賜ったと考えられ

facts.text: Another source differs: Bowes has the Taikō presenting the gold seal to Chōjirō; this essay names Sōkei, after Chōjirō's death.

rows.meaning: Made by Makuzu Kōzan, the studio name of Miyagawa Kōzan at Yokohama (Makuzu from Makuzugahara, Kyoto)
rows.device: brush or seal-script characters

maker.name: Miyagawa Kōzan (宮川香山) – I (1842/43–1916), II Hannosuke (1859–1940/41), III Katsunosuke (d.1945), IV Tomonosuke

wares: Makuzu ware (Yokohama): high-relief, underglaze-painted porcelain, 'Satsuma'-type faience
rows.technique: impressed or inlaid white-clay signature on faience (Bowes); blue underglaze painted seal-style signature (Ashmolean, 1890s)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kōzan I moved to Yokohama in 1870-71, and the kiln lasted through Kōzan IV (after 1945; d.1959 according to the Makuzu archive).
rows.what_it_tells: A Makuzu piece. The mark alone does not tell the generation; look at the form: the blue seal-script 'Makuzu Kōzan sei' of the 1880s-90s, and the later (c.1925-40) 'Makuzu' double-gourd seal.
rows.cautions: The characters given here are reconstructed from romanised transcriptions; no catalogued object in the sources shows the full Japanese transcription of 大日本眞葛香山製. 'Makuzu' also appears with other potters on Kyoto Makuzugahara wares, since Makuzugahara is a Kyoto district whose name other potters also used (Bowes lists 'Makuzuhara' marks). Bowes says the Ōta factory is where 'most of the imitations of Satsuma faience have been made'.

facts.text: Bowes nos.495–497, 503 (pp.205–206): 'Makuzu Kōzan tsukuru' impressed on a vase; 'Miyakawa Kōzan tsukuru' inlaid in white clay; 'Makuzu Kōzan' on a flower pot.
facts.quote: Makuzu Kozan, the name of the maker

facts.text: Ashmolean EA1996.132 (1890s): underglaze blue seal-mark on the base reading 'Makusu gama Kōzan sei' (made at Makuzu kiln); the signatures are written, not stamped.
Japanese dictionaries: Miyagawa Kōzan I (1842–1916) moved from Kyoto's Makuzugahara to Yokohama's Ōta in 1871 and was Imperial Household Artist; the ware is 眞葛焼 / 太田焼.
Morse: the present Makuzu in Yokohama 'made for a time monstrous pieces of Satsuma', then high-fired porcelain.

rows.meaning: Miyagawa Kōzan – the potter's own name (宮川 family name)

maker.name: Miyagawa Kōzan (宮川香山) – I (1842/43–1916), II Hannosuke (1859–1940/41), III Katsunosuke (d.1945), IV Tomonosuke

rows.technique: inlaid in white clay on brown pottery (Bowes 497); also written
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.what_it_tells: Used on earlier wares at Yokohama; the studio name 眞葛 is the usual form later.
rows.cautions: Four heads (I–IV) used the name; Kōzan II was born Hannosuke and called himself Hanzan (半山) earlier.

facts.text: Bowes no.497 (p.205): 'Miyakawa Kōzan tsukuru' inlaid in white clay upon a flower pot.
Makuzu archive: Kōzan II c.1917–1940, III died May 1945, IV Tomonosuke revived after the war.
The official kiln site (Miyagawa Kōsai family) gives Kōzan I 1843–1916 and II 1859–1940, a year off the encyclopedias (1842).
facts.quote: 二代 宮川香山安政6年（1859）～昭和15年（1940）

facts.text: Kōzan I opened the Makuzu kiln at Ota village, Yokohama, in 1871 and was named an Imperial Household Artist (帝室技芸員).
facts.quote: 太田村（現在の横浜市南区）に眞葛窯を開き

rows.meaning: Makuzu – impressed seal inside a double-gourd frame, on later Makuzu wares
rows.device: characters inside a double-gourd outline
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Ashmolean dates a vase with this seal to 1925–1940, attributed to Miyagawa Hanzan (Kōzan II).
rows.what_it_tells: Later (Kōzan II) period Makuzu ware.
rows.cautions: The Ashmolean reads the seal as 'Makuza' in a double gourd, probably 'Makuzu'; the characters are not given. Only one museum record gives it.

facts.text: Ashmolean EA1990.1 (vase with shrimp, 1925–1940): impressed seal 'Makuza' in a double gourd on the base; original box inscribed 'Iga' (lost).

rows.meaning: Hanzan – early art name of Miyagawa Hannosuke (Kōzan II)

maker.name: Miyagawa Hannosuke (宮川半之助, 1859–1940), Kōzan II

rows.where_on_object: on the body or base
rows.date_note: Hanzan about age 20 (c.1879) signs early Makuzu works until he took the name Kōzan II (c.1917).
rows.what_it_tells: Dates a Makuzu piece to the period before he took the Kōzan name.
rows.cautions: The Ashmolean lists his pieces under Hanzan even after 1917.

facts.text: The Makuzu archive says early Meiji takauki-bori works carry inscriptions of Hannosuke's pseudonym 'Hanzan' when he was about 20.

rows.meaning: Kutani ('Nine Valleys'): the place name written as a mark, alone or beside a painter's or shop's name.
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red, black or gold (sometimes in a panel); sometimes impressed
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Written on Revived Kutani (Saikō-Kutani) wares from the early 1800s and on almost all later Kaga ware; the start date is approximate. Western books of 1875-1901 already treat it as the usual Kaga mark.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the district (Kaga, now Ishikawa), not a maker. A collector can say the piece is meant to read as Kaga/Kutani ware; the painter and date must come from the other characters, the style and the body.
rows.cautions: The mark is cheap to write and was written on wares decorated elsewhere or made long after: Audsley and Bowes (1875) say porcelain made in other districts was sent to Kaga to be painted and that 'on some pieces the Kutani mark is forged'; Morse (1901) says the product 'is still signed with the old mark Kutani' although the kilns moved, and that much modern Kutani is decorated in Tokyo. Plain 九谷 in a modern hand on a 20th-century tea set is an origin claim, not a date or a maker.

facts.text: The word Kutani, alone or with the potter's name, is seldom missing from painted Kaga marks (1882).
facts.quote: the word Kutani does not appear

facts.text: Kanazawa City Library's list of recorded Kutani base marks includes plain 九谷 among marks on Revived Kutani in the Ishikawa Kutani Museum's opening catalogue.
Porcelain from other districts was decorated in Kaga and marked Kutani; the Kutani mark was forged on some pieces by 1875.
Morse (1901): kilns moved to Yamashiro (1815) yet the product 'is still signed with the old mark Kutani'; much modern Kutani decorated in Tokyo.
facts.quote: still signed with the old mark Kutani

facts.text: Collector reference: pieces marked Kutani were mostly decorated in the Kutani district by many makers and trading shops, but decorators moved, and pieces marked Yokohama and Kobe carry Kutani-style painting.

rows.meaning: Made at Kutani (sei = made).
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red or black
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Dealer-collector dating of about 1870 to early 20th century; the form is already in Bowes 1882 and Morse 1901, so it is Meiji or earlier. Later copying continues to today.
rows.what_it_tells: Says only that the piece was made (or decorated) at Kutani; the maker is not named. Common on Meiji export wares.
rows.cautions: A form that anybody could write; it was used on Meiji export wares and on twentieth-century wares. The Kanazawa library list shows 九谷製 as one of the recorded forms but gives no date.

facts.text: Bowes (1882) prints 'Kutani sei' as one of the forms of the Kutani mark.
The Kanazawa City Library bibliography lists 九谷製 among the base marks shown in the Ishikawa Kutani Museum's catalogue and on Revived Kutani.
Collector reference dates examples of 'Kutani sei' to about 1880 and about 1910-20.

rows.meaning: Made at Kutani (zō = made); also read tsukuru.
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red or black
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: A collector reference dates examples to late Meiji (about 1880-1900); there are no firm limits.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the district, not the maker. A 'Kutani zo' with a shop name (e.g. Wataya, Kutani zo Wataya sei) points to an export firm.
rows.cautions: The dates come from a single collector source, and the reading of the character (zō or tsukuru) varies by book.

facts.text: Collector reference reads 九谷造 as 'Kutani tsukuru/zo', dating examples to late Meiji (1880-90) and to about 1900.

rows.kana: だいにほんくたにせい
rows.meaning: Made at Kutani, Great Japan.
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red or black (often in a panel or square)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Present on pieces catalogued by Bowes (1882) and Morse (1901), so before 1890. 'Dai Nippon' in characters is generally felt to be Meiji; collectors note it on mass export wares into the 1930s.
