rows.what_it_tells: Says made at Kutani and 'Great Japan'; mostly Meiji export ware. A broad period marker, not a maker.
rows.cautions: The rule that 大日本 means Meiji only is a collectors' rule of thumb; Gotheborg itself records Dai Nippon marks on export wares into the 1930s. Kanazawa's list also gives 大日本加賀九谷 and 大日本九谷 forms with other characters.

facts.text: Bowes (1882) prints 'Dai Nippon Kutani sei' (Made in Kutani, Great Japan).
Morse (1901, no. 1059) records 'Dai Nippon Kutani sei (written)', dated 1800 by the catalogue.
Kanazawa City Library lists 大日本九谷製 and related 大日本加賀国九谷 among recorded Kutani marks.

rows.meaning: Kutani in Kaga province.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The sources give no dates; collector examples are of the Meiji and Taishō periods.
rows.what_it_tells: Place name for the Kaga region; sometimes with the maker (鏑木) or 大日本.
rows.cautions: Place only. Several big Kanazawa firms put their own name before Kutani (see 鏑木).

facts.text: Kanazawa City Library records marks such as 大日本加賀国九谷 and 加賀九谷 with the maker or shop name.
Collector reference shows 'Kaga Kutani' read top to bottom, right to left.

rows.meaning: 'At Kutani' (the 於 prefix: made at Kutani by ...).
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Late Edo to Meiji; the 於九谷 form is recorded from Revived Kutani. The sources give no fixed years.
rows.what_it_tells: 'Made at Kutani' preceding a maker's or kiln's name. The Cleveland Museum's bowl has 'Kutani Dashoken ni oite Yagi Jinsaku seisu' (made by Yagi Jinsaku at the Dashoken kiln in Kutani).
rows.cautions: An address-style phrase, not a seal; check what follows 於九谷 for the maker.

facts.text: Cleveland catalogue reads a bowl's base inscription as 'made by Yagi Jinsaku at Dashoken factory in Kutani'.
Kanazawa City Library cites 定本九谷's list of marks including 於九谷.
A Tokyo National Museum bowl by Eiraku Wazen (1823-96) is marked 於九谷永楽造 in red enamel (Edo, 19th c.), so 於九谷 + maker name appears on Kyoto-made gold-brocade ware as well as Kaga pieces.

rows.meaning: Fuku: 'good fortune'; the commonest base mark of Old Kutani (Ko-Kutani) plates, written in a single or double square.
rows.device: the character 福 in a square or double square
rows.technique: painted in underglaze blue or in overglaze colour inside a square or double square (二重角福)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Ko-Kutani is usually dated 1655-1710 at the Kutani kiln (Kaga), which closed around 1710 (Kutani Guide). The 福 mark continues on Revived Kutani and later; see the entry for 福 on Saikō-Kutani.
rows.what_it_tells: A fortune character used as an auspicious mark; it is the most frequent mark on Old Kutani plates but most pieces carry none. It does not name a maker.
rows.cautions: Where Old Kutani was made is disputed: some scholars attribute the 17th-century overglaze-enamelled plates to Arita in Hizen, others to the Kutani kiln in Kaga; a Japanese encyclopedic entry (Kotobank) says an Arita origin has also been proposed. Dealers' double-square 福 also appears on twentieth-century copies, and a 福 does not prove Ko-Kutani; Art Institute of Chicago and Cleveland records show FUKU on later 'Ao-Kutani' and on 1700s pieces.

facts.text: Old Kutani carries 福 in a single or double square (including variant forms) more than any other mark; some have 五郎太夫, 祐, 大明, 太朋 or none.
The Ishikawa Prefectural Museum's catalogue sections on the backs of Old Kutani and on Revived Kutani are described as having mainly 福.
Encyclopedic entries say Old Kutani was made from the mid-17th century at Kutani, Kaga, but that an Arita origin has also been argued.
facts.quote: 有田産とする説もある

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues 'FUKU in square seal' on a Kutani plate of the mid-1600s.

rows.meaning: Fuku again, on Revived Kutani and later wares.
rows.device: the character 福 in a square
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red or black in a square or double square
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Recorded from Revived Kutani kilns (Wakasugi, Yoshidaya, Shōza's early work) and continues to modern mass-produced Kutani.
rows.what_it_tells: A reassuring, old-style mark. On Meiji and later pieces it can sit beside a painter's name (e.g. 角福 with 庄三).
rows.cautions: It does not show a Ko-Kutani or Edo date: many 19th- and 20th-century pieces carry it. A collector reference says Ko-Kutani-style dishes marked fuku are hard to prove genuine.

facts.text: Revived Kutani base marks are mainly 福 (Ishikawa Prefectural Museum's Kutani catalogue).
In Edo-period Kutani the base normally carried the kiln name or an auspicious square 福 and rarely the painter's name.
facts.quote: 窯元の名前か、吉祥を意味した角「福」

facts.text: A collector reference says fuku is common on Kutani porcelain, and a 'Ko-Kutani style' dish marked fuku is hard to prove genuine.

rows.meaning: 'Great Ming'-type mark recorded on Ko-Kutani, sometimes read as 太明 or 大明; other rare marks on Old Kutani: 五郎太夫, 祐, 太朋.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The years are the same Ko-Kutani years as for the 福 mark.
rows.what_it_tells: Rare Old Kutani base marks; a collector can use them to recognise Old Kutani groups rather than a maker.
rows.cautions: The two Japanese sources write the character differently (太明 vs 大明), and the reading is not agreed; these are Chinese-looking marks and should not be read as Ming reign dates.

facts.text: Kanazawa City Library, citing 九谷名品図録: Old Kutani backs have 福 and also 禄 and 太明.
The Kutani Guide lists 五郎太夫, 祐, 大明 and 太朋 beside 福 on Old Kutani, and notes that some pieces have no mark.

rows.meaning: Chinese Chenghua reign mark copied on early Kutani; Bowes says it is a forgery of the Chinese mark.
rows.kind: Chinese reign mark on a Japanese object
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Bowes figures it with a specimen dated about 1650; no firm limits.
rows.what_it_tells: Early Kutani sometimes copied Chinese reign marks as decoration; it does not date the piece to China.
rows.cautions: Bowes (1882) calls it a forgery of the Chinese Chenghua (1465-1487) mark. This is an imitation reign mark, not a Chinese object.

facts.text: Bowes 1882 prints 'Seika nen sei' beside Kutani wares of the earlier period and calls it a forgery of the Chenghua mark.
facts.quote: A forgery of the Chinese mark

rows.meaning: Kutani Shōza: the name of the Meiji export painter, written as a single line on the base.
rows.technique: painted in overglaze (one line of characters), sometimes small characters beside a square 九谷
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The one-line 九谷庄三 (with the Kutani family name) is a Meiji form; Shōza lived 1816-1883, and the 九谷 surname was adopted after the Restoration.
rows.what_it_tells: A sign of the 'Shōza style' (彩色金襴手) used for Meiji export ware from Terai/Nomi; usually a workshop product rather than his own hand.
rows.cautions: Many pieces were made by pupils or other craftsmen, and 'Shōza-style' (庄三風) imitations flooded export markets. Kutani Guide says the one-line mark was used as a brand, and a Kokugakuin University thesis says Audsley and Bowes already criticised the mass production. Do not read 九谷庄三 as proof of his own hand.

facts.text: Shōza (1816-1883) opened a decoration workshop at Terai in 1841 and perfected the 彩色金襴手 style; the one-line 九谷庄三 mark came in as a brand once his reputation made it so.
facts.quote: 一行書きの「九谷庄三」銘

facts.text: Shōza took the name 庄三 around Kaei (1848-54) and used the 九谷 surname only from the Meiji period.
facts.quote: 九谷姓を名のるようになったのは明治に入ってから

facts.text: Many works with the name were not made by his own hand; 'Shōza-style' imitations were exported, and Audsley (1875) and Bowes criticise the ware.
Kutani export in Meiji: Kutani overtook Seto and Mino in ceramic export value in 1887, with about 80% of Kutani output going abroad.

rows.meaning: Shōshichi: the childhood name of Kutani Shōza, written on his earlier works (from the Ono kiln period) before he became Shōza.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: He was at the Ono kiln from 1832 and had his own workshop from 1841; he took the name 庄三 about Kaei (1848-54). The Kutani Guide's mark page gives the independence year as 1850, where its own Shōza page gives 1841.
rows.what_it_tells: Early Shōza-circle work, mostly red-line (akae) painting on Hime-Kutani wares from the Ono kiln.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse it with the later brand marks; the Ono-kiln base mark itself was a square 小野, not his name.

facts.text: Shōza worked at the Ono kiln from 1832; some of the kiln's red-painted pieces carry the base mark 庄七.
Early on his name was not written (the base had the square 小野). After he went independent, only the childhood name 庄七 or a square 福 beside it was written.

rows.kana: おくたにえいらくぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Eiraku at Kutani: Eiraku Wazen's mark on gold-brocade (kinrande) wares made in Kaga.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Wazen (Eiraku Zengoro XII) came to Yamashiro in 1865 and taught about six years, then left Kaga.
rows.what_it_tells: Eiraku Wazen (1823-1896), the Kyoto potter invited to Kaga; red-ground kinrande with the 'Eiraku' style named after him.
rows.cautions: A mark that was often copied: the 'Eiraku' style (永楽) continued to be painted by Kutani potters, so 永楽 in Kutani is not necessarily Wazen; the Eiraku family (Kyoto) also used other marks (see the Dai Nihon Eiraku entry).

facts.text: Tokyo National Museum bowl by Eiraku Wazen is inscribed 於九谷永楽造 in red enamel.
Wazen settled at Yamashiro in 1865 and taught Kaga potters for about six years; the 'Eiraku' kinrande became one of Kutani's six styles.
Audsley and Bowes: pieces are met with marks 'made in Yeiraku fashion in Kutani'.
facts.quote: Made in Yeiraku fashion in Kutani

rows.kana: だいにほんえいらくぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Eiraku, Great Japan: Eiraku Tokuzen (Kyoto) mark.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Tokuzen (Eiraku Zengoro XIV, 1853-1909); the Tokyo National Museum dates its bowl to Meiji.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kyoto Eiraku-family mark used on gold-brocade export ware; sometimes met with Kutani-style decoration.
rows.cautions: Not a Kutani mark. The museum database lists the maker under two numberings (Eiraku Zengoro XIV / Hirata Haruyuki X), so check the generation. Marks of the same family differ: see 於九谷永楽造.

facts.text: Tokyo National Museum bowl G-211 'Phoenix design in overglaze enamel and gold' bears ｢大日本永楽造」 in underglaze blue.

rows.meaning: Made at Kinjō (= Kanazawa): marks of the Kasugayama kiln (金城製, 春日山, 金府造).
rows.technique: painted in overglaze red or black
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kasugayama (Kanazawa, Utatsuyama) opened in 1807 under Aoki Mokubei, who went home after about two years and the kiln declined; years are approximate.
rows.what_it_tells: Ware of the Kasugayama kiln (Mokubei and Honda Sadakichi), imitating Chinese Wu-su red-on-white ware.
rows.cautions: Rare; later painters of Kanazawa copied the Kinjō forms. Marks of the kiln (and Wakasugi) are recorded, but the 金城 form also appears on later Kanazawa wares.

facts.text: Kasugayama kiln wares often copy Chinese Gosu-akae and bear 金城製, 春日山 or 金府造.
The Kanazawa City Library's list names 金城製 among the recorded Kutani base marks.

rows.meaning: Mark of the Wakasugi kiln: 若 or 福.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kiln opened 1811 (Hayashi Hachibei at Wakasugi); the sources give no end year.
rows.what_it_tells: Revived Kutani kiln in Komatsu; it made blue-and-white ware and old-green-style colour ware. Shōza was apprenticed there at 11.
rows.cautions: Only one source gives its marks.

facts.text: Wakasugi kiln marks are given as 若 and 福.
Wakasugi was opened in 1811 by Hayashi Hachibei with Honda Sadakichi.
Shōza was sent as a boy of 11 to serve at the Wakasugi kiln (1826).
facts.quote: 若杉窯に奉公に出されました

rows.meaning: Made for Kaburagi (Kaburagi Shōho, Kanazawa export trader); brand marks 鏑木製, 鏑木造, 鏑木謹製, 加賀九谷鏑木製.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji (the guide places the brand in Meiji Kutani; no years given).
rows.what_it_tells: A big Meiji export dealer-brand; the pieces were painted by many different painters.
rows.cautions: A brand: do not read it as a single painter; quality varies.

facts.text: Kaburagi Shōho always put 鏑木 on the base, so that the name stood for a good product.
Kanazawa's list records marks such as 加賀九谷鏑木製之 and 加賀九谷鏑木製.

rows.kana: しょううんどうさへいぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Sahei at Shōundō (Matsumoto Sahei's studio); also 金陽堂左瓶造 after Shōundō failed.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji (no years given).
rows.what_it_tells: Matsumoto Sahei's marks; works with 松雲堂/左瓶造 and 金陽堂/左瓶造 are said to be the most trustworthy.
rows.cautions: Only the two named studio forms are described as the most reliable; other Sahei marks exist.

facts.text: Works marked 松雲堂 / 左瓶造 and 金陽堂 / 左瓶造 are the most reliable; the two differ in the studio used.
Kanazawa City Library's list cites 定本九谷's mark list including 大日本松雲堂.

rows.meaning: Made for Watano (Watano trading company); characters for 'no' varied by generation.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji (company lasted three generations).
rows.what_it_tells: An export house with offices in Kobe and Yokohama; the character for 'no' differs by generation.
rows.cautions: Only one source gives this; the characters 綿野 are reconstructed from the romanised reading and are not recorded on an object or in a Japanese-language source. The character for 'no' also changed by generation, so the exact form is unconfirmed.

facts.text: Watano Trading Company lasted three generations and was famous in Meiji with export offices in Kobe and Yokohama.

rows.meaning: Plain Kutani mark on mid-20th-century export tea sets, often with 'Made in Japan' or CPO.
rows.technique: impressed or painted; sometimes with a paper sticker 'Kutani, Made in Japan'
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Collector examples are dated to about the 1950s (Occupation-era PX trade, CPO).
rows.what_it_tells: Shows the style and trade, not a maker. 'CPO' with Kutani was a mark for goods sold at U.S. forces' exchanges in Japan.
rows.cautions: Only one collector source gives the CPO reading. Treat all plain 'Kutani' on mid-century 'geisha-girl' or dragonware tea sets as a generic style, not a Kutani-district product.

facts.text: Collector reference: Kutani marks over a diamond 'CPO' indicate sale at US Army and Navy bases, tentatively 1950s.
Geisha-girl lithophane cups marked Kutani are largely from the Nagoya area, many of the Occupied Japan period.

rows.meaning: Banko ('ten-thousand ages'): the impressed seal on Ise (Mie) wares.
rows.device: seal-script 萬古, sometimes in an oval

maker.name: Numanami Rōzan and later Ise potters

rows.technique: impressed seal, in varied seal-script forms with or without an oval border; rarely painted
rows.where_on_object: base or side of body
rows.date_note: Rōzan's kiln ran 1736-1777 and was revived in the 1830s; many potters of Kuwana, Yokkaichi and other places have used the mark up to today.
rows.what_it_tells: Mie (Ise) ware: either old Rōzan 'Ko-Banko', Mori Yūsetsu's revival, or later Yokkaichi mass-production. The oval-border form and the plain form differ; it does not identify a maker.
rows.cautions: Morse (1901) says Banko marks run over a hundred and fifty years and were used by many potters; there is 'no way of tracing the origin of the various pieces'. Western collectors' 'Banko' teapots exported after 1868 almost all carry the impressed mark. Audsley and Bowes (1881) tell a different founding story (Yu-usedzu, about 1845, copying Banko Kichibeye of Tokyo) which Japanese sources do not support.

facts.text: Rōzan impressed 萬古 or 萬古不易 on his wares, hence the name Banko ware.
facts.quote: 「萬古」あるいは「萬古不易」の印

facts.text: Many potters of Kuwana, Yokkaichi and other places used the common mark Banko, in many forms; the oldest carry it without the oval border.
Bowes (1882): the character is impressed upon nearly all wares of Ise, written in various styles, and is seldom used alone.
Morse (1901): the modern Ise ware is known as Banko and signed with the impressed mark; export work was not made until after 1868 (Ninagawa).

rows.meaning: 'Ten-thousand ages unchanging': Rōzan's wish that his ware last forever; stamped in his seal.
rows.device: seal-script 萬古不易
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: These are Rōzan's kiln years; later revivers used the seal.
rows.what_it_tells: The seal that gave Banko ware its name; on Ko-Banko from Rōzan's kiln and later seals of revival.
rows.cautions: Later makers used the same seal text 'to show the tradition' (Mie University), so a 萬古不易 seal does not show Rōzan's hand. Western books differ: Bowes (1882) prints 'Fuyeki' as 'unchanging' beside 萬古, while Morse (1901) lists 'Fueki Banko' as if it were a maker's name.

facts.text: Rōzan stamped 萬古不易 wishing his works to last; the wording is the origin of the name.
facts.quote: 「萬古不易」という印をおしたことによります

facts.text: Later Banko wares use the same seal text to show the tradition.
Dictionary: 製品に〈万古〉あるいは〈万古不易〉の印を捺したので万古焼と呼ばれる.
Mori Yusetsu, who revived Banko in 1832, was allowed to use the word 萬古 on his work but was not given Rozan's own seal; he stamped a separate 有節 seal beside 萬古.
facts.quote: 「萬古」の印のそばに「有節」の印

rows.meaning: Old Banko: the ware of Numanami Rōzan (1718-77), with Dutch-taste red-enamel patterns.
rows.technique: impressed 萬古 or 萬古不易, early forms without oval
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Opened in the Genbun era (1736-41) at Obuke; Rōzan died 1777, the kiln declined; a Tokyo branch at Kōume/Mukōjima from the Hōreki era (1751-64).
rows.what_it_tells: Ware of the founder; the mark is the seal. Pieces include cotton-print (更紗) patterns and Dutch-style painting.
rows.cautions: Western catalogues vary on his dates (Morse says he apprenticed with Kenzan and died 'in the latter years of the last century'). Japanese dictionaries give 1718/1719-1777. Many later 'Ko-Banko' style pieces exist.

facts.text: Rōzan (1718-77), a rich Kuwana merchant, opened the kiln at Obuke in 1736-41; the work is called Ko-Banko.
Rōzan's works are called Ko-Banko; in Edo he had a second kiln at Mukōjima (Koume) from 1751-64.

rows.meaning: Mori Yūsetsu (1808-82): his seal beside the 萬古 seal on Revived Banko.
rows.device: seal 有節 beside seal 萬古
rows.technique: impressed seals (萬古 seal with 有節)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The revival kiln at Obuke opened in 1831 or 1832 (a dictionary and a school source differ), and Yūsetsu died in 1882. Descendants (2nd to 4th) continued using similar marks.
rows.what_it_tells: Revived Banko (有節萬古) of Kuwana/Obuke: wood-mould teapots, a pink glaze (腥臙脂), tea wares. He got permission to use 萬古 from Rōzan's grandson.
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on the date: dictionaries give 1831 (Tenpō 2), while Mie Prefecture and Mie University give 1832 (Tenpō 3). Later Mori descendants and imitators use similar marks (Morse 1901).

facts.text: Yūsetsu stamped his own 有節 beside the 萬古 seal after obtaining permission from Rōzan's grandson.
facts.quote: 「萬古」の印のそばに「有節」の印

facts.text: The revival of 1831 (Tenpō 2) was by Mori Yūsetsu and his brother, who invented wooden-mould teapots and the pink glaze.
Morse (1901) records the marks Yusetsu, Yusetsu Banko and Banko Yusetsu, and a descendant at Obuke 'using similar marks'.

rows.meaning: Japan Yūsetsu: the export-era seal 日本有節.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse dates a piece 1840; the mark is a Yūsetsu export seal.
rows.what_it_tells: Shows Yūsetsu's aim at world markets. Morse lists Nihon Yūsetsu, with Fueki, as an exception: other names are not usually seen with the Banko mark.
rows.cautions: Described by a single Japanese source; do not read it as modern.

facts.text: Yūsetsu stamped 日本有節 on works, showing awareness of the world as other export kilns did.
Morse (1901): with the exception of Fueki and Nihon Yusetsu it is not usual to see other names with the Banko mark.

rows.meaning: Japan Banko: the Banko seal with 日本/Nippon, as on exported Ise teapots.
rows.where_on_object: body or base
rows.date_note: Bowes (1882) and Audsley (1881) record it; export Banko dates from after 1868 (Morse), and the end year is uncertain.
rows.what_it_tells: Export Banko of Yokkaichi, with Nippon beside Banko among up to fifteen impressed seals on a teapot.
rows.cautions: Collectors' 'Nippon' impressed on Banko is Meiji export; do not confuse it with the roman NIPPON of 1891-1921 under the US Tariff Act.

facts.text: Bowes prints BANKO, NIPPON (Banko ware, Japan) among the usual combinations of impressed seals.
A small Mori teapot of Yokkaichi shows fifteen impressed marks, among them four Banko, five sen-shu, one Mori uji and one Nippon.

rows.meaning: 'A thousand autumns': an auspicious seal stamped beside 萬古 on Ise teapots.
rows.where_on_object: body or base
rows.date_note: Bowes (1882) and Audsley (1881).
rows.what_it_tells: A paired lucky seal, beside 萬古; Mori Yūsetsu's brother was Chiaki (千秋).
rows.cautions: Audsley takes it as an auspicious phrase, while the Japanese sources name Yūsetsu's brother as 千秋 (Chiaki); the sources do not reconcile the two readings.

facts.text: Bowes prints SENSHU 'A Thousand Autumns' as one of the combined stamps.
Audsley and Bowes: five of 'sen-shu' (one thousand years) among the fifteen stamps on a Mori teapot.

rows.meaning: Yokkaichi Banko: red-clay and unglazed teapot ware of Yokkaichi from 1870.

maker.name: Yamanaka Chūzaemon and other Yokkaichi potters

rows.technique: impressed 萬古 with maker seals
rows.where_on_object: base or lid
rows.date_note: Yamanaka Chūzaemon succeeded in firing Yokkaichi Banko in 1870 (Meiji 3); the area became a regional industry.
rows.what_it_tells: Teapots and everyday wares of Yokkaichi (the 'Banko teapot' known to Western collectors).
rows.cautions: Modern Yokkaichi Banko of the 20th century uses the same 萬古 seal; look for the maker's seal beside it.

facts.text: Yamanaka Chūzaemon succeeded in firing Yokkaichi Banko in Meiji 3 (1870).
facts.quote: 明治3年（1870年）に四日市萬古の焼成に成功

facts.text: Since Meiji, centred at Yokkaichi, mostly red-clay unglazed teapots called Yokkaichi Banko.
facts.quote: 四日市萬古とよばれる

facts.text: Western collectors saw modern Ise ware of teapots and little vases signed with impressed Banko, made for export after 1868.
facts.quote: export was not made until after 1868

rows.meaning: Anto ware of Tsu, a branch of the Banko tradition.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Morse reports conflicting dates: Anto from the early 18th century (his view) or the first half (Ninagawa), revived about 1830; the years are approximate.
rows.what_it_tells: Tsu (Ise) ware made by a Banko-related potter.
rows.cautions: Authorities differ on when Anto begins; Morse reports conflicting testimony.

facts.text: Morse (1901): a brother of Numanami made pottery at Tsu using the mark Anto; other authorities date it a hundred years earlier.
An Anto kiln was founded from Ko-Banko at Tsu by Yoshisuke.

rows.meaning: Minpei: name of Kashū Minpei (1796-1871), founder of Awaji ware, stamped on his ware.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The Hyogo Museum of Ceramic Art dates the start of Minpei ware to the Bunsei era (1818-30); the sources give no end year.
rows.what_it_tells: Awaji faience of Minpei; later wares of the company 淡陶社 (founded 1883) and others.
rows.cautions: The marks are mainly known from Western catalogues of 1875-1901 ('Mimpei' is Morse's spelling). No Japanese-language description of the stamp is recorded, so its exact characters are not confirmed. Meiji export Awaji is often marked with the Sanpei flag or JAPAN (collector source).

facts.text: Hyogo museum: Minpei ware was started by Kashū Minpei in Bunsei (1818-30); after his death his nephew Sanpei and the Danto company continued, exporting.
Bowes (1882) prints a Minpei stamp on an Awaji figure.
Morse lists Awaji 'Mimpei' among Japanese pottery marks.

rows.meaning: Sanpei: Kashū Sanpei, Minpei's nephew; the 'Sanpei flag' is Awaji ware's commonest mark.
rows.device: flag
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Sanpei took over after Minpei died; the flag mark is said to begin in the 1880s.
rows.what_it_tells: Awaji faience from the Sanpei workshop.
rows.cautions: Collector sources say the Sanpei flag began in the 1880s; Bowes prints a painted 'Sanpei Gashu, Awaji' mark.

facts.text: Bowes (1882) prints 'Awaji, Gashu Sanpei' painted in gold on a faience vase.
After Minpei's death his nephew Sanpei and the Danto company continued the ware.
A collector reference says the most common Awaji mark is the Sanpei flag.

rows.meaning: Danto (Awaji ceramics company, Meiji): chidori (plover) mark with the company name.
rows.device: plover (chidori)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The company is later than Minpei (Meiji); a Hyogo prefectural museum text gives 1883 as the founding date (not confirmed), and a collector page says the Awaji kilns closed by 1939.
rows.what_it_tells: Awaji ware by the Danto company, later Danto joint-stock company.
rows.cautions: The chidori device comes from one collector source only, and the company's founding year is not confirmed.

facts.text: The Danto company (淡陶社) took over Minpei's pottery technique after his death and exported.
Collector reference: the Danto chidori bird mark began in the 1880s.
Another source differs: the 千鳥印 大日本商標淡陶會社 appears on Danto's dry-process tile backs of period III (Meiji 41-45, 1908-12), not the 1880s; applies to tiles, not necessarily to pottery.
facts.quote: 「千鳥印 大日本商標淡陶會社」が陽刻され

rows.meaning: Roman JAPAN or MADE IN JAPAN stamped on Awaji ware: 'JAPAN' about 1890-1922; 'MADE IN JAPAN' impressed 1922-1939.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: From the one collector source; 'JAPAN' before 1921 contradicts the usual 'Nippon' rule, so treat it with caution.
rows.what_it_tells: Dates only by the standard of that one source; see the JAPAN and MADE IN JAPAN entries.
rows.cautions: Only a single collector source gives this. The Western rule of thumb says 'Nippon' before 1921 for the US market; Awaji's 'JAPAN' may have been for other markets.

facts.text: Collector reference: Awaji pieces stamped JAPAN were produced 1890-1922; impressed MADE IN JAPAN 1922-1939.

rows.meaning: Inoue Ryōsai: a family workshop making export 'Sumida ware' (relief figures, stoneware) in Asakusa, Tokyo.
rows.technique: painted in blue or impressed; relief-figure wares with a cartouche (forms not confirmed)
rows.where_on_object: base or side cartouche
rows.date_note: Meiji onward. A Kanagawa Prefectural Museum bulletin says the first two generations worked in Asakusa for export and the third moved to Yokohama in 1914.
rows.what_it_tells: Export Sumida ware (relief figures); family workshop of three generations.
rows.cautions: 'Sumida ware' for export is Meiji Asakusa ware, unlike the Edo 'Sumidagawa-yaki' raku of Sahara Kikuu (1819). The exact signature forms for each generation are not established in open sources; dealers describe signed 'Ryōsai' cartouches.

facts.text: Inoue Ryōsai III (1888-1971) headed a family firm specialising in export Sumida ware and later made studio ceramics.
The Edo ware called Sumidagawa-yaki was a raku of about 1819 at Mukōjima; a different ware.

rows.meaning: Shimaoka Tatsuzō's katakana ta seal, sometimes absent on early pieces.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: He opened his Mashiko kiln in 1953 and died in 2007.
rows.what_it_tells: Mashiko mingei potter (b. 1919, d. 2007); most pieces carry the seal.
rows.cautions: This rests on a single blog source. A collector's expert says early pieces can be unmarked, so check box inscriptions as well.

facts.text: Shimaoka (1919-2007) studied with Hamada Shōji and opened his Mashiko kiln in 1953.
Most of his works carry the タ mark, but earlier pieces can be unmarked.
Another source differs: workshop built 1953 beside Hamada's kiln, first firing 1954 (Kotobank: opened kiln 1953).

rows.meaning: NIPPON in roman letters: the US country-of-origin mark on Japanese wares from 1891 to 1921.
rows.device: Roman letters beside a maker's device
wares: Japanese export porcelain for the US
rows.technique: printed, stamped or painted (green, blue, magenta, gold or red), often with Hand Painted
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The McKinley Tariff Act (1 October 1890) required English-word origin marking from 1 March 1891. The 1921 end date for 'Nippon' comes from a US Customs ruling reported only in collector sources; no primary Treasury Decision was found.
rows.what_it_tells: Made in Japan for the United States between 1891 and 1921. The mark does not name the maker; the maker's device (e.g. M in wreath, RC) beside it does.
rows.cautions: The date is not exact. Exports to other countries had no such rule, and 'Nippon' continued in company names such as Nippon Toki Kaisha after 1921. Paper labels were often used instead of base marks, so the absence of Nippon says nothing. Collector sources say faked 'Nippon' marks circulate on later pieces, especially from the 1960s; the sources do not name the 'maple leaf' or 'M in wreath' forgeries specifically.

facts.text: Section 6 of the 1890 Tariff Act required that from 1 March 1891 articles of foreign manufacture be marked 'in legible English words' to show country of origin, or be refused entry.
NIPPON began to appear on bases in 1891. In 1921 US Customs stopped accepting Nippon, so 'Japan' was required.
Nippon marks fetch higher prices than Japan, which created a market for fake marks.
Bowes (1882) transliterates a Japanese-character seal on Banko ware as 'Nippon'. The word in Japanese script is older than the roman marking rule and is not the same mark.

rows.meaning: JAPAN: the English country name that replaced Nippon after a 1921 US Customs ruling.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Collector sources state that after 1921 'Nippon' was no longer accepted and 'Japan' or 'Made in Japan' was used. They also say Awaji's JAPAN begins about 1890; the two statements are not reconciled.
rows.what_it_tells: Period marker only: made in Japan 1921 or later (earlier if exported elsewhere).
rows.cautions: This is not a hard limit: 'Japan' appears before 1921 on pieces for other markets, and one collector source dates Awaji JAPAN stamps 1890-1922. The 1921 ruling is cited only on collector pages.

facts.text: Marking changed from NIPPON to JAPAN or MADE IN JAPAN after 1921.
Noritake backstamps after 1921 state 'Japan' or 'Made in Japan'.

rows.kana: メイド・イン・ジャパン
rows.meaning: MADE IN JAPAN: the 1920s to present country mark; no maker named.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Collector sources give 1921 and later; one source dates the impressed 'MADE IN JAPAN' on Awaji ware to 1922-1939, and the mark continues after 1952.
rows.what_it_tells: Made in Japan after about 1921 (earlier for other markets); the maker comes from other marks.
rows.cautions: It does not date an item by itself after 1921; US Customs of the late 1940s also accepted plain 'Made in Japan' during the Occupation (Deseret and Kovels columnists), so it appears on Occupation-era wares. Some web pages claim a 'Made in' wording rule of 1914/1915, but none cites a primary source.

facts.text: Noritake used 'Made in Japan' after 1921 in place of Nippon.
Items produced after April 1952 reverted to 'Made in Japan'.
Another source differs: 'Made in Japan' was already permitted on exports from 5 Dec 1949, so the wording did not first 'revert' after April 1952.

rows.kana: オキュパイド・ジャパン
rows.meaning: Made in Occupied Japan: a country mark on export goods during the Allied Occupation (1947-1952).
rows.technique: stamped, printed, impressed, molded, or on a paper label
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Japanese sources say the mark was obligatory from 1947 to 1949 (Seto Cultural Foundation: March 1947-December 1949) and remained on some goods until the treaty took effect on 28 April 1952; the first post-war shipment arrived in New York on 10 August 1948 (New York Times, via Deseret News).
rows.what_it_tells: Dates a ceramic to the Occupation period; mostly ordinary export novelties from Nagoya and Seto.
rows.cautions: Not all exports carried it; a US Customs ruling of the late 1940s also accepted 'Made in Japan', 'Japan' or 'Occupied Japan'. Gotheborg says only every second piece had to be marked (so one of a pair may be unmarked), but no primary source confirms that rule. Collector sources say fakes occur, and sources disagree on the end date (18, 25 or 28 April 1952; 28 April is the treaty date).

facts.text: GHQ required the mark on exports: officially 1947-1949, on some goods until the 1952 treaty.
facts.quote: 公式には1947（昭和22）年から1949（昭和24）年まで

facts.text: According to the Seto Cultural Foundation the mark was obligatory from March 1947 to December 1949 and remained on some goods until April 1952.
facts.quote: 1947 年 3 月から 1949 年 12 月まで義務付け

facts.text: US Bureau of Customs ruling in the late 1940s allowed 'Made in Occupied Japan', 'Made in Japan', 'Japan' or 'Occupied Japan'; first shipment reached New York 10 Aug 1948.
Collector sources say half of exports had to be marked and that pieces of pairs may be unmarked; fakes occur.

Another source differs: SCAP directive of 5 Dec 1949 allows 'Made in Occupied Japan', 'Made in Japan' or 'Japan'; bare 'Occupied Japan' is not listed in the text read (Deseret credits a US Customs ruling and four forms).
facts.quote: Made in Occupied Japan,” “Made in Japan,” or “Japan

facts.text: Another source differs: directive covers export articles generally ('will be marked'), with no half-of-exports rule in the text read.
facts.quote: will be marked, stamped, branded or labeled

rows.chars: paper label (Made in Japan / Occupied Japan / Hand Painted)
rows.meaning: Paper, cloth or foil labels carrying the country of origin, used instead of a base mark.
rows.where_on_object: base or side
rows.date_note: From the McKinley era onward; many Occupied Japan pieces carried only labels.
rows.what_it_tells: A paper 'Made in Japan' label is the only mark on many pieces; its absence is not evidence.
rows.cautions: Labels fall off, so an unmarked piece may have been marked; collectors also report later stickers added to pieces.

facts.text: Collector reference: paper labels were used and may have fallen off, so the lack of NIPPON does not prove a later date.
Occupied Japan marking could be a paper label, cloth label, engraved, handwritten or stamped.

rows.meaning: 'HAND PAINTED': English wording used alongside Nippon, Japan and Occupied Japan marks.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Appears with Nippon (pre-1921), Japan (1920s-30s) and later.
rows.what_it_tells: Marketing wording; shows export taste. It dates only with the country word beside it.
rows.cautions: Marketing wording: the mark does not show whether the decoration is really hand-done, so do not treat it as a statement about technique.

facts.text: Early Noritake backstamps combine 'Hand Painted Nippon' with the wreath-circled M.
Collector page records 'Hand Painted - Nippon - Japan', 1920s, and 'Hand Painted - Japan', 1930s, among sundry marks.

rows.meaning: Great Japan in Chinese characters; a patriotic Meiji-period mark, not the US origin rule.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji is the usual period; collectors record it on mass-made export wares into the 1930s.
rows.what_it_tells: A period and nationalism marker; usually with Kutani, Satsuma-style or Nagoya wares.
rows.cautions: Not tied to the 1891-1921 'Nippon' rule; the Meiji-only rule has exceptions up to the 1930s.

facts.text: Marks with the characters 大日本 on the whole date to Meiji; Gotheborg notes they continue on Satsuma-style export porcelain into the 1930s.
Bowes (1882) and Morse (1901) record 'Dai Nippon' Kutani marks.

rows.meaning: Meito China: porcelain of the Nagoya Seito Sho company (founded 1908 by a former Noritake man), later Narumi.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meito marks continued after the Second World War, with crown variants.
rows.what_it_tells: A competitor of Noritake.
rows.cautions: This rests on one collector source; the founding and the name changes are not confirmed in a Japanese source.

facts.text: Nagoya Seito Sho was founded in 1908 by Asukai Kotero, a former Noritake employee; sold as Meito China; sold and renamed Narumi Seito Sho during WWII.

rows.meaning: Takito Company mark T and T in two rectangles, with a wreath-form T on some lusterware.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Company 1909-1948 per collector source; mark dates 1922-1944 or late 1920s-1930s.
rows.what_it_tells: Nagoya/Seto lusterware and moriage export decorator.
rows.cautions: The collector source describes T T in two rectangles, not 'T T in a wreath'; it describes 'T in a wreath' with Japan as another maker's lusterware mark. One source only.

facts.text: Takito Company 1909-1948, known for lusterware; mark TT in two rectangles dated about 1922-44.

rows.meaning: United China & Glass Company (US importer): the Ucagco mark on postwar Japanese china.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Collector dates 1947-1961 for most of the mark.
rows.what_it_tells: US importer/distributor; its patterns were made by many Japanese potteries.
rows.cautions: Importer, not maker; one collector source.

facts.text: Ucagco = United China and Glass Company, offices in New Orleans and New York; many Japanese patterns in the early 1950s.

rows.meaning: Gold Castle: trade brand of Tashiro Shoten (Nagoya) per a secondary reference.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Mid 20th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Postwar Nagoya export brand.
rows.cautions: Rests on a single source that relies on another book; treat with caution.

facts.text: Collector reference reports from Carol Bess White that Goldcastle and Chikusa belong to Tashiro Shoten, Nagoya.

rows.meaning: Lefton China: Chicago importer George Zoltan Lefton (founded 1940/41).
rows.technique: printed, stamped or on paper label
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Lefton imported from Japan after WWII; crown mark said to be 1948-1955.
rows.what_it_tells: An American importer; goods came from many Japanese factories.
rows.cautions: Importer's mark does not name the maker; later copyrighted marks exist.

facts.text: Lefton imported Japanese giftware; established 1940/41 in Chicago; Occupied Japan stamps.

rows.meaning: Ardalt (New York importer): double-A mark and Lenwile figure-mark.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Trademarks registered 1945.
rows.what_it_tells: US import brand for Japanese tableware and figurines.
rows.cautions: A single collector source relays the trademark records; the name is also seen on non-Japanese pieces.

facts.text: Ardalt Inc., 95 Madison Ave., New York; the AA mark first used 1945; Lenwile registered 1945.

rows.meaning: Chikaramachi (Noritake branch factory) marks 1928-1946; the factory later became Hinode Shokai.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: From a collector source.
rows.what_it_tells: A Noritake branch; UK-bound pieces say 'Foreign'.
rows.cautions: Single source.

facts.text: Chikaramachi Made in Japan used 1928-1946; renamed Hinode Shokai after the Noritake Morimura Gumi period.

rows.chars: (moriage, usually unmarked or Made in Japan)
rows.meaning: Raised slip 'moriage' (dragonware) wares are often unmarked or marked Made in Japan or Dai Nippon.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Dragonware from around the 1880s; mostly unmarked, made into the 1950s.
rows.what_it_tells: A technique and style, not a maker; marks, where present, give era.
rows.cautions: Do not date dragonware by decoration alone.

facts.text: Dragonware moriage dates from the 1880s and later; mostly unmarked and made into the 1950s.

rows.meaning: Tashiro Shoten Ltd: Nagoya/Yokohama porcelain shop; elephant mark; TA in cherry blossom.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Active before the Second World War to 1954 according to the source; the years are tentative.
rows.what_it_tells: Also traded as Trico China, Gold Castle and Chikusa.
rows.cautions: This rests on a single source.

facts.text: Tashiro Shoten active before WWII until 1954; marks include Elephant above MADE IN JAPAN and TA in cherry blossom.

rows.kana: にっぽんようこうぼうえき
rows.meaning: Nippon Yoko Boeki Co.: wreath with a bow and clover mark, JAPAN.
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: No dates are given.
rows.what_it_tells: A trading company whose factory still operates (per the collector page).
rows.cautions: This rests on a single source, and the mark could be mistaken for Noritake's.

facts.text: Mark of Nippon Yoko Boeki Co.: a wreath with a bow at the bottom and a clover, with JAPAN.

rows.meaning: G in a wreath: Noritake contract mark for Giftcraft (Toronto).
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Early to mid 1950s according to a collector.
rows.what_it_tells: Canadian importer's contract mark.
rows.cautions: This rests on a single source.

facts.text: 'G in a wreath' reported as a Noritake contract mark for Giftcraft Importers of Toronto, 1950s-60s.

rows.meaning: Round censor's seal reading 'approved / passed' (極), used on single-sheet prints after the Kansei reform
rows.device: Small round seal, about 1 cm, with the single character 極; the character is often white on a ground (the Totsuka seminar notes the white-out form requires a block)
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: Guild censorship was set up by the Kansei order of the 10th month of Kansei 2 (November 1790); the earliest known prints with the seal date from late 1790 or early 1791 (Fiorillo), and Totsuka concludes that every genuine kiwame impression is Kansei 3 (1791) or later. JAANUS gives 1842 as the end, since the seal was officially used 'without addition' until the nanushi seals replaced it in 1842-43.
rows.what_it_tells: The impression was made from a block carved between 1791 and 1842: after the Kansei reforms and before the Tenpō nanushi seals. It does not give a year or month by itself. Combined with a zodiac date seal it dates 1805-1814 prints exactly.
rows.cautions: Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints, and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四). Seals can be trimmed off, and a seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing: a kiwame impression of a design known earlier, such as Katsukawa Shunshō's 1783 'Edo hana mimasu Soga', is a post-1791 reprint, not a first edition (Totsuka). Basil Stewart (1922) calls 極 'the publisher's hallmark of quality', but JAANUS, the Art Research Center, Fiorillo, Cleveland and the Art Institute of Chicago treat it as the censor seal; Hokusai's 'aratame Iitsu' signature uses aratame as an artist's name change, not a censor seal.

facts.text: Kiwame is a small round censor seal reading 極 that was supposed to appear on all ukiyo-e issued 1791-1842, between the Kansei and Tenpō reforms; it was carved into the key block.

Totsuka (Art Research Center seminar, 2023): the form used in 1791-1842 is 'maru ni kiwame' (丸に極). The publishers' censorship group was formed by the order of Kansei 2, month 10, so every kiwame dates from Kansei 3 or later. The kiwame was added to the woodblock (追刻), not stamped on later.
facts.quote: 「丸に極」の極印が用いられた

facts.text: Earliest known prints with censor seals date from late 1790 or early 1791; guild censors were first called kiwame, later aratame.
Sakai divides the seal's use into 1790-1804 (極 with an animal-month seal), 1805-1810 (極 with an animal-month seal), 1811-1814 (極 with gyōji seals) and 1815-1842 (極 alone).
Cleveland and the Art Institute of Chicago catalogue kiwame on prints dated 1791 (Shunei), 1794 (Sharaku), 1808, 1811, 1814, c.1830 and 1835-36 (Hokusai's Hyakunin isshu), all inside the window.

rows.chars: 極 + 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥 + 月
rows.meaning: Small seal giving the zodiac animal of the year and the month number, struck beside 極
rows.device: Small rectangular (1806) or oval (1807 onward) seal with one zodiac branch character and one month numeral; 閏 before the numeral = intercalary month
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: The standard window is 1805-1810 (Schwan, Lane and Thompson via Seidel (2010); JAANUS lists 1805-10 and 1814; Sakai 1805-1810). Self's 'rectangular 5th-12th month 1806, oval 1807-1858' comes from Self alone, and no other source confirms the long run to 1858.
rows.what_it_tells: Year (to within the 12-year animal cycle, which the 1805-1814 window resolves) and month. Stewart reads a 'hare seven' seal as the 7th month of 1807.
rows.cautions: The same animals reappear 12 years later in 1817-1826, so a small oval animal-and-month seal with 極 and no 改 in the 1815-1842 window is not evidence for these years. Only Self records a one-off date seal c.1800 and a short-lived month-only seal used 8/1805-4/1806. Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes), and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四); seals can also be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: From 1805 a date seal with the animal of the year and the month number was often (not always) added to 極; it was used 1805-10 and 1814 'in particular'.
Month numeral plus zodiac sign is the seal form; 閏 ('uru' cypher) marks an intercalary month and fixes the year when present.
Sakai dates the animal-month seal 1805-1810 with kiwame, but marks the 1790-1804 and month entries as unconfirmed ('年月は不確定で検証が不十分').
facts.quote: 年月は、不確定で、検証が不十分

facts.text: Self reports a rectangular date seal for months 5-12 of 1806 and an oval date seal 1807-1858 'occasionally with kiwame'; no other source says this.

rows.meaning: Personal seal of the publisher-guild inspector (gyōji, a rotating guild officer) beside 極
rows.device: Round or square seal with one or two characters from the inspector's name
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: 1811-1814/15 (JAANUS: 'between 1811 and 1815'; Schwan and Lane as given by Seidel (2010), and Sakai, give 1811-1814); only Self gives a wider span, 1804 to c.1840.
rows.what_it_tells: A guild-censored print of 1811-1814/15 whose approving inspector can be named from the seal. The name seals are a minor dating tool because the lists are short and incomplete.
rows.cautions: Easily confused with publishers' marks and with the later nanushi seals. Lists of individual gyōji are in Schwan (2003); Sakai warns that his gyōji column is not confirmed. Seals were carved on the key block, so impressions from the original blocks keep them, later reprints included (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes); a recut or copy can reproduce them, and seals can be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: On some prints published between 1811 and 1815 the personal seals of individual gyōji appear with the kiwame seal; gyōji were guild members chosen in rotation, so publishers regulated themselves.
facts.quote: On some prints published between 1811 and 1815

facts.text: Sakai lists 1811-1814 as [極][行事] with the gyōji seal and cautions that the entries are not confirmed.
Self: individual gyōji seals from 1804 to c.1840; only Self gives this span.
Wetherall describes the process: the publisher submitted the draft to a gyōji of the picture-book dealers' guild; the seal was carved on the key block.

Totsuka (via ARC) identifies two publisher seals that appear beside the 極 seal before Kansei 3 as probably those of Mikawaya Rihei and Iwatoya Kisaburō, who belonged to the gyōji group in Bunka 4 (1807).
facts.quote: 三河屋利兵衛と岩戸屋喜三郎のもの

rows.chars: oval seal: animal above 改 below
rows.meaning: Rare early oval seal with a zodiac animal and the character 改, easily mistaken for the 1853-1871 aratame seals
rows.device: Oval seal: zodiac animal in the top part, 改 below
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: 1815-1832 according to Self; Seidel (2010) notes that Self is the only source for it.
rows.what_it_tells: Only that it is an uncommon type, probably from 1815-1832.
rows.cautions: Do not apply the 1853-1871 animal-to-year table to it. Only Self records it. Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes), and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四); seals can also be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: An uncommon type used 1815-1832 includes a zodiac date in the top of an oval seal with 'aratame' below, easy to confuse with later seals.
Self also records an oval seal with the aratame mark; Seidel (2010) says this is the only source known to claim it.

rows.chars_note: one round seal, 1-2 characters of the nanushi's surname
rows.meaning: Seal of the ward-headman (絵草紙掛り名主) who approved a print; one seal on each print
rows.device: One round seal (an inch or less) reading a short form of the nanushi's name, e.g. 村松, 衣笠, 濱
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: From 1842/43 to the 11th month of Kōka 3 (December 1846), after which the pair rule begins (Iwakiri as given by Seidel (2010)); Self dates the first seals (Taka and Take) to 1842, Iwakiri finds eight months of 1843-44 with no seal, Sakai gives 1843-1847, and Ukiyo-e Notes and Chiappa say 1842/43-1846/47.
rows.what_it_tells: A print approved by one of 11 nanushi between 1842 and 1846. The seal it carries narrows the date (see the 15 individual nanushi rows). Date seals are absent until about 1850-52 (Stewart; Seidel (2010)).
rows.cautions: The nanushi seal names the approving official, not the publisher. Prints of 1843-44 may carry no seal at all, which is not a sign of forgery. Self, Robinson and Illing disagree by a year or two on the span of individual seals (see the rows). Seals were carved on the key block, so impressions from the original blocks keep them, later reprints included (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes); a recut or copy can reproduce them, and seals can be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: In 1842 the guild's self-censorship ended and government censors, the e-nanushi (絵草紙掛り名主), were appointed; individual nanushi seals replaced kiwame and were used until about 1853.
facts.quote: Nanushi-in waren bis etwa 1853 in Benutzung

facts.text: Both nanushi examined the print, but only one put his name seal on it, from 1843 to Kōka 3/11 (1846).
facts.quote: nur einer von ihnen seinen Namensstempel

facts.text: Single seals ran 1842-1846 and paired seals 1847-1853 (Chiappa), or Kōka 4-Kaei 5 (Ukiyo-e Notes: 弘化4〜嘉永5ごろ(1847〜1852)); Sakai gives 1843-1847 [名主] and 1847-1852 [名主]+[名主].
Nanushi seal on a book: the preface of the 1844 book 『滑稽絵姿合』 has the 改印 of 改掛名主 村松源六.
facts.quote: 改掛名主である村松源六の改印

facts.text: Iwakiri (2002/2007) counts eleven nanushi with single seals, adds Mera, finds eight months (Tenpō 14/8-Tenpō 15/3) without a seal.

rows.meaning: Seals of two nanushi side by side, both approving the print
rows.device: Two round seals touching or adjacent, each with the nanushi's short name (e.g. 馬込 + 濱); usually next to each other
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: The period starts in the 12th month of Kōka 3 (January 1847 by the Gregorian calendar) according to Iwakiri, though most sources say 1847, and ends in the 11th month of 1853 (Seidel (2010), from Lane and Schwan) or at 'the very end of the 11th month or early in the twelfth' (Stewart, on Hiroshige's Yamadaya prints); three pairs rotated in 1847-48, then four to five pairs in 1849-53 (Robinson, Self).
rows.what_it_tells: A print approved between Dec 1846 and the end of 1853. The pair places the print within a window of one or two years; from the 2nd month of 1852 a date seal adds the exact month (see nanushi-pair-date-seal-1852).
rows.cautions: Two adjacent round seals whose characters you cannot read are almost always censor seals. Museum catalogues sometimes list the seals in a different order or date the print too early: Cleveland catalogues 'Mera, Watanabe' prints as c.1848-50, although the pair is recorded only for 1851-53. Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes), and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四); seals can also be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: From the 12th month of Kōka 3 both nanushi put their seals on the print; the three first pairs worked in monthly rotation, joined by five pairs from 1849.
facts.quote: Ab dem 12. Monat 1846 (Kōka III), setzten beide nanushi ihre Stempel

facts.text: From 1847 to 1853 the nanushi marked prints in pairs; the two seals are usually directly next to each other; an oval aratame seal is usually present 1848-1851 and a date seal 1852-53 (Self).
facts.quote: From 1847 to 1853, the Nanushi marked prints in pairs

facts.text: Stewart knows of 'twelve' censors' seals, found in pairs and less often single; prints dated Ox 11 (1853) carry two censors' seals.
The 双印 phase is dated 弘化4年から嘉永5年ごろ (1847-1852) in the Ukiyo-e Notes summary; Sakai gives 1847-1852 for [名主]+[名主] and 1852-1853 for [名主]+[名主]+[年月].

rows.chars: 名主 + 名主 + 年月
rows.chars_note: two nanushi seals and a small oval date seal
rows.kana: なぬしそういんとねんげついん
other_spellings: double nanushi seals with date seal
two censor seals and a date seal
rows.meaning: The last form of the nanushi period: two nanushi seals plus an animal-and-month seal
rows.device: Two round nanushi seals and one oval seal, e.g. 村田 + 衣笠 + 子十二
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: From the 2nd month of Kaei 5 (1852) until the 11th month of 1853 (Seidel (2010), from Lane, Schwan and the University of Vienna); Stewart's earliest is 'Rat 1852'; Sakai gives 1852-1853; the Art Institute of Chicago catalogues 'ox 2 (1853/II)' on Kuniyoshi's 'Snow on Benten Hill'.
rows.what_it_tells: Exact year and month: only two animals occur (子 1852, 丑 1853), the nanushi pair independently dates the month, and the pair rotated through four fixed combinations.
rows.cautions: The intercalary 2nd month of 1852 exists (子閏二). The animal cycle repeats only every 12 years, so a 寅/卯 seal with two nanushi is wrong. Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes), and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四); seals can also be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: From the 2nd month of 1852 to the 11th month of 1853 two nanushi seals and a date seal appear together; four pairs rotated monthly: Muramatsu/Fuku, Magome/Hama, Watanabe/Mera, Murata/Kinugasa.

Iwata and Koike read: 嘉永五年九月改め(子九) 馬込・濱; 嘉永五年十月改め(子十) 村松・福; 嘉永五年十二月改め(子十二) 村田・衣笠; 嘉永六年三月(丑三) 渡辺・米良. This matches a four-month rotation 馬込濱 -> 村松福 -> 渡辺米良 (11th month, inferred) -> 村田衣笠 -> 馬込濱 (1st month) -> 村松福 (2nd month) -> 渡辺米良 (3rd month).
facts.quote: 嘉永五年十二月改め(改印、「子十二」)

facts.text: Stewart: the oval date seal first occurs with censors' seals around 1850; the earliest noted is Rat year 1852.
Art Institute of Chicago records Kuniyoshi's 'Snow on Benten Hill at Kinryūzan' with 'Censorship seal: Fuku and Muramatsu, date seal: ox 2 (1853/II)'.
Murata and Mera were already paired as censoring nanushi in 1849 (Kaei 2), before the 1852 rotation, so pairings changed over time.
facts.quote: 名主村田左兵衛・米良太一郎の改割印

rows.meaning: Round seal 'examined', the censor seal that replaced the nanushi seals; sits beside a separate oval date seal
rows.device: Round seal with the single character 改 in seal script; beside it an oval seal with animal and month
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: From the last month or two of 1853 (the 11th month according to Seidel (2010), from Schwan and Self; 'the very end of the 11th month or early in the twelfth' according to Stewart; 'around 1854' on Ukiyo-e Notes; 嘉永六年十二月 on the Japanese site 浮世絵ぎゃらりぃ) to the 12th month of Ansei 4 (early 1858), when the 改 was dropped for a year; Sakai gives 1853-1857, and JAANUS says 'in 1853 the system was again changed'.
rows.what_it_tells: Print issued from Nov 1853 to 1857, month and year readable from the oval date seal beside it (寅 1854, 卯 1855, 辰 1856, 巳 1857; 丑 only for Nov-Dec 1853).
rows.cautions: Stewart says prints with 改 are 'sometimes wrongly described as being seal-dated for the Ansei period'; the seal is a censor mark, and the match of years is accidental. 改 reappears inside one round seal in 1859-1871 (see aratame-in-combined-1859). Cleveland catalogues 'aratame' on a Hotohoto Festival print dated 1853, which is possible only for the last month of that year. Seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes), and a recut or copy can reproduce them (the Edo-Tokyo Museum shows a later recut with a carelessly cut 改 and a missing 巳四); seals can also be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: At the end of 1853 the nanushi seals were replaced by a round seal with the character 改 and, beside it, an oval date seal; this lasted to 1857.
facts.quote: Ab dem 11. Monat des Jahres 1853 stempelten die nanushi nicht mehr

facts.text: Prints dated Ox 11 (1853) have two censors' seals, prints of 1854 and later have the aratame; the oval date seal accompanies it (Hiroshige's Yamadaya figure set).
Art Institute of Chicago records 'aratame; tatsu 7 (1856, 7th month)', 'aratame; mi 4 = 1857, 4th month', 'aratame; mi 8 (1857, 8th month)' on Hiroshige's Meisho Edo hyakkei.

rows.chars: oval date seal (animal + month), no 改
rows.meaning: The year in which the 改 seal was dropped and only the oval date seal remained
rows.device: Oval seal with one animal and one month numeral
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: From the 12th month of Ansei 4 (early 1858 Gregorian) to the 12th month of Ansei 5 (Lane and Self as given by Seidel (2010)), while Stewart and Chiappa give 1858 and Sakai gives 1857-1858.
rows.what_it_tells: A print issued in 1858 (午). Examples are Hiroshige's Fuji and 'Mountain and Sea as Wrestlers' series and the memorial portrait of Hiroshige.
rows.cautions: Cleveland catalogues 'aratame (trimmed)' on an 1858 Hiroshige print (Fireworks at Ryōgoku, 1940.986), but the rule predicts a date seal alone in 1858, so check whether the 'aratame' is a misread date seal. Seals were carved on the key block, so impressions from the original blocks keep them, later reprints included (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes); a recut or copy can reproduce them, and seals can be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: Between the 12th month of 1857 and the 12th month of 1858 only date seals without aratame were used.
Stewart: after 1857 the aratame seal disappears for a year; the Horse year 1858 prints show the date seal only; in the Ram year 1859 it reappears incorporated with the date in a single round seal.
In 1858 the aratame seal was dropped, and the oval date seal appears alone.
facts.quote: In 1858, the aratame seal was dropped

rows.chars: 改 + 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥 + 月 in one round seal
rows.meaning: One round seal holding 改, the year animal and the month
rows.device: Round seal, about 1 cm; arrangements vary: year on top and month at the bottom enclosing 改; or 改 bottom-left with month top-left and year right (most often 1859-63); or 改 on the left with year top-right and month bottom-right (most often 1864-71); other layouts occur
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: The seal runs from the 1st month of 1859 (Lane as given by Seidel (2010), Stewart, Sakai and the Japanese reference site Chiappa agree) to 1871 (Seidel (2010); a Kokugakuin paper reads 改+未十一 on a Meiji 4/11 print), though Sakai ends 改+year at 1867 and lists 1867-1875 as year-and-month only, and yoshitoshi.net and Chiappa end it in 1872; most sources say 1859-1871, and only Sakai has the 1867 break.
rows.what_it_tells: Gives the exact year and month: 改 and the date are in one seal. A leap-month character 閏 fixes the year (閏三 1860, 閏八 1862, 閏五 1865, 閏四 1868, 閏十 1870). The animal 未 occurs in both 1859 and 1871.
rows.cautions: 未 can be 1859 or 1871 and nothing in the seal separates them; use the artist (for example Yoshitoshi's 1868-71 works), era-name (nengō) inscriptions and layout. Do not confuse it with the 1853-57 type, where 改 and the date are two separate seals. Seals were carved on the key block, so impressions from the original blocks keep them, later reprints included (Wetherall; Ukiyo-e Notes); a recut or copy can reproduce them, and seals can be trimmed off. A seal dates the approval of the design, not the printing.

facts.text: In 1859 the seal changed so that the aratame (approval seal) and the zodiac date appear in a single round seal; the arrangement varied, early on 'year on top, month at the bottom enclosing aratame'.
facts.quote: both the aratame and zodiacal date appear in a single round seal

facts.text: A combined seal of aratame and date exists from the 1st month of 1859 to 1871.
facts.quote: Er ist vom 1. Monat des Jahres 1859 bis 1871 zu finden

facts.text: Stewart: from the Ram (Goat) year 1859 the aratame is incorporated with the date in a single round seal; if 'uru five' (leap fifth month) is incorporated with aratame in one round seal, the date is 1865.
In the 11th month of Meiji 4 (1871) a sugoroku (board-game print) bears 「改」・辛未・「未十一」.
Sakai gives 1859-1867 as [改]+[year animal and month] and 1867-1875 as [年月] alone, which conflicts with the 1871 sugoroku.

The Art Research Center (ARC) database reads a Bunkyū 1 (1861) combined seal '酉正九' as the 9th month of 1861 on a Toyokuni III actor print for the Ichimura-za play that opened on the 17th of the month.
facts.quote: 酉正九と彫られている

facts.text: Self, citing yoshitoshi.net, reads aratame + ox + 2 as 1865, 2nd month.

rows.meaning: Last pre-notice form: a small round seal with the zodiac year and month only
rows.device: Round seal; animal on the right, month numeral on the left; no 改
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: The seal was used from 1872 to 1875 or 1876 (Lane and Self; yoshitoshi.net: up to 1872 the seal has 改). JAANUS says censor seals were discontinued in 1875. Wetherall dates the revision of the publishing rules to September 1875 and the otodoke stamp to 'the fall of 1875'. Many prints lack any seal in these years because compliance was not enforced.
rows.what_it_tells: Year and month: 申 1872, 酉 1873, 戌 1874, 亥 1875. A seal in Sept 1874 reads 戌九 (Wetherall).
rows.cautions: Wetherall says the seal was changed 'several times a year' in Meiji 5-8 and that compliance varied. The seal gives the earliest date of approval, not of printing. From January 1873 the months are Gregorian (the calendar reform of 3 December 1872 made it 1 January 1873). The same animal signs recur in 1860-63, but with 改.

facts.text: From 1872 to 1875 a small round date seal with the zodiac sign at right and the month number at left was the only seal in use.
facts.quote: Von 1872-175 ist eine Phase zu beobachten

facts.text: Up to 1872 the seal included 改 and the year and month; 1872-1875 the seal includes only year and month.
facts.quote: Between 1872 and 1875, the seal includes only the year and month

facts.text: A Tokyo nichinichi shinbun nishikie issued about September 1874 carries a seal read as Meiji 7, 9th month.
facts.quote: the seal was used in the 9th month of Meiji 7, or September 1874

facts.text: Seals were changed several times a year in Meiji 5-8, and compliance varied.
JAANUS: censor seals were discontinued in 1875; from then publication date and publisher's name and address appeared in the margin.
facts.quote: In 1875 the use of censor seals was discontinued

rows.meaning: 'Notified' stamp giving the Meiji year, month and day on which the authorities accepted the publisher's notice
rows.device: Circle with 御届 in the centre; around it 明治 N 年 (right, clockwise) and N 月 N 日 (left)
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed seal (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: The stamp was required from the September 1875 revision of the 1869 publishing edict, in practice 'from the fall of 1875' (Wetherall). Fiorillo and others give the Home Ministry rules of 1876 as the start. The earliest example found is Kiyochika's 明治九年一月十三日 / 十五日 (1876).
rows.what_it_tells: Date of notification in Meiji years (Meiji N = 1867 + N). In the same period the margin names the real publisher (出版人) and artist (画工) with their addresses.
rows.cautions: The date is that of the notice, not the printing; Wetherall compares it to a postmark. Late reprints keep the notice, while recuts print their own. Prints with the month or day missing are probably later impressions, printed after the first edition sold out (yoshitoshi.net). Censor and date seals were carved on the key block, so every impression from the original blocks keeps them, including later reprints (Wetherall; the Art Research Center, Ritsumeikan University; Ukiyo-e Notes).

facts.text: In September 1875 the 1869 publishing edict was revised. Pre-publication inspection ended, and publishers had to print real names and addresses and give the year, month and day the notification was accepted, using an 御届 stamp.
facts.quote: In September 1875, the publishing edict of 1869 was heavily revised

facts.text: The stamp is circular, 御届 in the centre, 明治 and 年 on the right, 月 and 日 on the left.
Kiyochika's triptych 『東亰江戸橋之真景』 carries a 御届 stamp dated 1876 (Meiji 9) 1-15; 『東亰五大橋之一 両国真景』 carries 明治九年一月十三日.
From 1876 prints had to carry the exact day, month and year of publication; a print missing the date or month is probably a later printing.
In 1876 publishers had to submit designs to the Home Ministry and include their name, address and date.

Another source differs: For books, the duty to print publisher and printer names and addresses in the colophon was first written into the 1887 ordinance (Meiji 20), not 1875. This is about books and the 奥付; Wetherall's statement is about nishikie.
facts.quote: 明治 20 年「出版条例」ではじめて規定

rows.meaning: Printed margin notice of the Meiji registration system: date of notification, publisher's name and address, artist's name and address
rows.device: Text line (often in a cartouche or the margin) beside the otodoke stamp
wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed text (carved on the key block)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: From autumn 1875 or 1876, after the censor seals ended; from 1887 copyright wording also appears.
rows.what_it_tells: Exact registration date, the registered publisher and artist (with addresses), often the carver (彫) too. Compare the artist with the signature.
rows.cautions: The notice date is not a printing date. Recuts replace it with new text: Hiroshige's 'Edo hyakkei' recut 1891-92 prints margin inscriptions with block-cutting dates 'in place of what would have been the Edo-period publisher, date and censor seals' (Fiorillo). The notice names may be those of the registrant, not the maker.

facts.text: From September 1875 woodblock prints had to show the legal names and street addresses of the creator and the publisher, plus the otodoke date.
Kiyochika's 1876 block bears, at lower left, the 御届 stamp, 画工 and 版元 address and names, and the carver's 彫銀.
facts.quote: 御届印、画工、版元の住所・氏名、彫師の「彫銀」

facts.text: Recut Hiroshige editions of 1891-92 give 'the dates of the block cutting' in the margin instead of the Edo publisher, date and censor seals.

rows.meaning: 'Carved by (name)' signature of the block carver, printed with the key block

wares: Japanese woodblock prints (nishiki-e and printed books)
rows.where_on_object: margin of the print, usually near a lower corner, beside the publisher's mark
rows.date_note: Appears throughout the 19th century; useful for a workshop's working years, not for a date.
rows.what_it_tells: The carver (彫師). Iwata and Koike identify 彫竹 as Yokokawa Takejirō, 彫庄治 as 津下庄治郎 and 彫千之助 as Sugawa Sennosuke, in 1852; the Kiyochika block has 彫銀. The Art Research Center reads the inscription 彫十才子兼 as a ten-year-old Kobayashi (小林彫兼) carving part of the block.
rows.cautions: Carvers are often unidentified, and research on them is thin. The reading of 津下 is not confirmed; only the characters are given. A 彫 name is not a censor seal and says nothing about the approval date.

facts.text: The carver's 彫 signature is carved with the block; the Art Research Center notes that carvers and publishers are poorly researched and many are unknown.

rows.device: A small trademark of ivy leaf(s) set in a mountain (Mount Fuji) outline, printed in the book/print as the house's publisher's mark; NDL describes the family crest as 山形に蔦の葉 (ivy leaves in a mountain shape). maker.name: Tsutaya Jūzaburō (耕書堂)
maker.place: Edo: near the Yoshiwara great gate (c.1772-83), then Nihonbashi Tōri-abura-chō (from 1783)

rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Jūzaburō himself (1750-1797) began as a bookseller at the Yoshiwara gate c.1772/73 and published until his death in 1797 (National Diet Library), and the house and its successors used the same ivy-and-mountain seal; Marks lists the firm as late as 1847-52, from a seal on a Toyokuni III triptych in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston Boston, as quoted by Prints of Japan.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the publisher. On a print of 1774-1797 it is Tsutaya Jūzaburō's house; on a 19th-century print it is a later Tsutaya (the seal is not a date).
rows.cautions: Two houses used almost the same seal: Tsutaya Jūzaburō and Tsutaya Kichizō (Marks #556, active c.1820-1890). Prints of Japan, quoting Marks, says they are 'not easily distinguishable'. A seal alone therefore does not show that a print is of the 1780s-90s: check the artist, subject, censor seals (kiwame / aratame) and the Edo date. Later impressions and re-cuts of Utamaro and Sharaku are common.

facts.text: The National Diet Library describes Tsutaya's family crest as an ivy leaf in a mountain shape (蔦屋の紋〈山形に蔦の葉〉); the shop later called 耕書堂 began near the Yoshiwara gate c.1772 and moved to Nihonbashi Tōri-abura-chō in 1783; he was born in 1750 and died in 寛政9 (1797).

facts.text: Marks, as quoted by Prints of Japan, gives the publisher as entry #555, shop name Tsutaya, house name Kōshodō 耕書堂, family name Kitagawa Jūzaburō 喜多川重三郎; he opened a bookshop at the Yoshiwara gate in 1773 and began publishing in 1774; the closest Marks seal is #03-001.

rows.device: Seals recorded in a square frame and in a rectangular cartouche (Prints of Japan classes both under Marks #391); the short-name seal reads 西与 and the house-name seal 永寿堂 (Eijudō). maker.name: Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudō)
maker.place: Edo (Nihonbashi Bakurochō is given by secondary web pages; not verified in Marks)

rows.date_note: Marks gives ca. 1751 to 1869. Little was published 1841-1860, and in 1860 the firm was taken over by Maruya Tokuzō (Marks, via Prints of Japan).
rows.what_it_tells: Names one of the largest print publishers of Edo. Within 1751-1869 the artist and censor seals narrow the date; Eijudō appears on Hokusai's Fuji series (1830s) as well as Kiyonaga (1780s).

Marks says production stopped in early 1841 'apparently because of a change in leadership from Yohachi II to the adopted Yohachi III', and a 1799 memorial print for Toyokuni I names the founder. Do not confuse the house name Eijudō 永寿堂 with Iseya Sanjirō's Eijudō 栄樹堂, which reads the same but is written with different characters. Seals with 西与 also appear beside other publishers' seals on jointly issued sets, for example with Tsutaya in 1776, Moriya Jihei in 1836, and Tsuruya Kiemon and Jōshūya Jūzō in the 1820s (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston Boston, as quoted by Prints of Japan).

facts.text: Marks entry #391: seal name Nishiyo 西与, firm name Eijudō 永寿堂, family name Hibino 日比野; dates ca. 1751-1869. Marks (2010, p. 194) calls it 'among the most important publishers in the history of prints and may be the publisher with the biggest output over time'.
Nishimuraya stopped publishing in early 1841 when the head changed from Yohachi II to Yohachi III. Little appeared in 1841-1860, and the firm was taken over in the 3rd month of 1860 by Maruya Tokuzō.

rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Prints of Japan (Marks #525) gives 'as early as ca. 1832 or earlier to as late as 1838 or later'; the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) Museum records the publisher Takenouchi Magohachi as c.1833-1850; and a Japanese study says the Tōkaidō set was published 天保5 (1834) 正月 from Hōeidō.

rows.cautions: The set was heavily printed and reprinted, and quality varies widely from print to print (according to a Japanese source). The blocks passed to Senkakudō (Tsuruya), so a print can carry both seals or only the later publisher's. A Hōeidō seal alone is not proof of an early state.

facts.text: Small round seal first appeared in 1915 (Capelari's Swan in Pomegranate Tree); large and small overlapped 1915-16; continues today in black and red.

Prints of the 1920s-40s usually carry seals of about 6.5 mm, with outliers of 5.5-7.1 mm; the rule that an earlier print has a seal 1 mm smaller rests on a misunderstanding of hand-carved hanko (Moku-Hanga citing Watanabe Shōichirō and Shimizu Hisao).

After the war the oblong copyright seal was dropped and the round seal returned; a prewar design with the round seal but no oblong seal is a postwar reprint (Egenolf, Shimizu). Pachter's design A = the postwar 6 mm round seal; design I = the present 7 mm seal.
Dealer guidance (Scholten): seal variations cannot be relied on alone to date an impression.

rows.meaning: Publisher Daikokuya Heikichi, an inherited name (family name Matsuki Heikichi 松木平吉); seal short name Daihei 大平; house name Shōjudō 松寿堂
rows.device: Seal group read 大平 (Daihei) with house name 松寿堂; Marks seals of this house include a rectangular type (#209 in the Prints of Japan rectangle group).
rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Marks gives ca. 1764-1931 for the line of heads, plus a separate set of dates ca. 1820s-1910s (Prints of Japan). The 5th head, Matsuki Heikichi (1871-1931), ran the firm until his retirement in 1930.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the leading Meiji Tokyo publisher (Kiyochika landscapes, political cartoons); the house runs from the 18th century to 1931.
rows.cautions: The name Heikichi passed down the generations, so the same seal can come from different heads. After 1876 Meiji law required the publisher's full name and address in the margin: read that inscription, not only the seal.

facts.text: Daikokuya was directed by a succession of men who took the name Matsuki Heikichi; it flourished in Meiji, especially the last two decades of the 19th century; 5th head (1871-1931); an 1890 advertisement dates the firm back to 1764.
Marks entry #029: seal name Daihei 大平, house name Shōjudō 松寿堂, family name Matsuki Heikichi 松木平吉.
From 1876 prints had to carry the publisher's full name and street address, usually in a margin inscription; earlier a small seal gave a short form of the name.

variants: 版権所有 土井貞一
rows.meaning: Publisher Doi Sadaichi 土井貞一 (also read Teiichi); firm Doi Hangaten 土井版画店; seals DS1-DS17 list printer and carver names
rows.device: Margin seal reading 版権所有 土井貞一 ('copyright Doi Sadaichi'), usually with the printer's and carver's names in katakana/kanji (e.g. Matsushita/Katsumura DS1 1932-35; Yokoi/Ikeda DS15-17 1936-44); DS17 reads 版元土井. A watermark of 土 in a circle is also recorded on some papers.
rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Moku-Hanga (Walker and Doi catalogue) gives the Doi Sadaichi seals as 1931-1944, with exports suspended in 1941 and the print shop closed in 1944; other sources give the firm's start as 1924 or a year later.
rows.what_it_tells: Prewar Doi seals are collectable and early. A Doi Sadaichi seal on a Hasui or Koitsu print points to first printing in 1931-44, but see the cautions.
rows.cautions: Newly carved reproductions made since about 2020 have been sealed with the prewar Doi Sadaichi seal (DS15c, c.2020, applied by Doi's granddaughter to a new Hasui reproduction; see Egenolf's 2023 warning). Seals do not prove an impression is genuine. After Doi's death the firm sealed 版権所有 土井版画店 (1948-63).

facts.text: Doi Sadaichi seals DS1-DS17 span 1931-1944; DS1 reads 版権所有 土井貞一, printer Matsushita Tamotsu 松下葆, carver Katsumura Shozo 勝村鐘造 (1932-35); DS17 reads 版元土井 (1936-44, Noël Nouët prints).
