facts.text: Doi Teiichi (Sadaichi) founded Doi Hangaten in 1924, or a year later according to an Amsterdam catalogue; a dealer lists the active period as 1930-1945; one dealer dates Doi's death to 1944.
Reproductions made recently (apparently in 2023) are newly carved but bear the prewar 'Doi Sadaichi' seal.

rows.meaning: Postwar publisher Doi Hangaten 土井版画店; seals DH1-DH10 (1948-1963)
rows.device: Seal reading 版権所有 土井版画店 ('copyright Doi Hangaten') with printer (Itō, Onohiko, Gotō, Yokoi) and carver (Katsumura, Fujikawa, Yamada, Ikeda, Harada) names.
rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Moku-Hanga: DH1-DH10, 1948-1963.
rows.what_it_tells: Postwar printing: a print with a Doi Hangaten seal was printed 1948-63. Prints with the carver Harada Kametarō's name are roughly one third recarved prewar blocks, one third new reproductions of prewar designs and one third posthumous Koitsu designs that never existed prewar.
rows.cautions: Posthumous Koitsu prints dated prewar exist (Half-Moon Bridge at Kameido, per the Walker and Doi catalogue as quoted).

facts.text: DH1 1948-50 版権所有 土井版画店; DH10 1950-63; Harada Kametarō's role is described as a third recarved, a third new reproductions and a third posthumous Koitsu.

rows.cautions: Not to be mistaken for prewar Doi Sadaichi seals; the 2017 Asakusa Mokuhankan seals identify modern impressions.

rows.meaning: Kyoto publisher Unsōdō 芸艸堂, founded 1891 by Yamada Naosaburō 山田直三郎; seals read Unsōdō han (publisher Unsōdō), Tokyo Unsōdō han, Yūgen-gaisha Unsōdō han (Limited company Unsōdō publisher)
rows.device: Seals reading '… 芸艸堂版' (Unsōdō han) in several forms: Yūgen gaisha Unsōdō han; Unsōdō han; Tokyo Unsōdō han; plus stickers on the back of shikishiban prints.
rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Established 1891 and still in business; Kasamatsu's Unsōdō prints date from 1952 to 1960 (over 100 designs).
rows.what_it_tells: Names a Kyoto art-book and shin-hanga publisher; its prints carry original margin date characters carved into the key block.
rows.cautions: About 1960 Unsōdō had the margin dates carved off the key blocks of Kasamatsu, Asano and Okada, so later reprints lack the date, and a missing margin date suggests a printing after 1960 (Crossland and Grund, quoted by the University of Oregon). Reprints from the original blocks, such as Sekka's Momoyogusa, continue.

facts.text: Founded 1891 by Yamada Naosaburō; known for books of textile patterns, ceramics and papers; Kamisaka Sekka's Momoyogusa (1909-10), Takeuchi Seihō's Masterworks (1937-42); over 100 Kasamatsu Shirō designs 1952-1960 (Hotei Encyclopedia, Newland 2005, p.501).
Margin dates were carved off the key blocks c.1960; later reprints show no margin date (Crossland and Grund).

rows.chars_note: characters of the name not confirmed in a source
rows.meaning: Tokyo publisher of the Japanese Fairy Tale Series (crepe-paper books, chirimen-bon); imprints Kōbunsha (from c.1884), later 'T. Hasegawa' / 'Hasegawa & Co.' (from c.1889)
rows.device: An imprint on the colophon or title page ('Published by T. Hasegawa, Tokyo'), not a woodblock seal in the print area.
rows.where_on_object: colophon / title page of the crepe-paper book
rows.date_note: He traded as Kōbunsha from 1884; the first five tales were copyrighted on 17 August 1885, colour crepe-paper dates from c.1888, and he died on 17 July 1938, when his son Nishinomiya Yosaku took over.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies the Meiji publisher of crepe-paper fairy-tale books for foreign readers; the imprint dates a book to 1885-1930s.
rows.cautions: Later editions of the series were reissued for decades, so the imprint alone does not give the edition date; compare cover and paper (St. Olaf's 'old vs new' comparisons).

facts.text: As early as 1884 Hasegawa traded as Kōbunsha; copyrighted the first five tales 17 Aug 1885; colour crepe-paper likely began with 1888 titles; son Nishinomiya Yosaku joined 1914 and took over after Hasegawa's death 17 July 1938.
Early books used the Kōbunsha imprint; from c.1889 the names 'T. Hasegawa' and 'Hasegawa & Co.' appear.

rows.meaning: Seal 自摺 ('self-printed') in the margin of Yoshida Hiroshi's own-workshop prints (from 1925)
rows.device: Small seal 自摺 (jizuri) usually in the upper-left margin, above the Japanese title and date; its form and the date characters change over the years.
rows.where_on_object: in the picture area or margin of the print (position varies; check the margin)
rows.date_note: Self-published prints date from 1925 (dealer and Fiorillo-site entries); Yoshida died in 1950, and posthumous prints lack the jizuri seal.
rows.what_it_tells: Marks prints issued by Yoshida's own workshop, not by Watanabe or another publisher. The form of the jizuri seal can be matched to the issue year.
rows.cautions: Dealers say the seal signalled Yoshida's approval, not proof that he printed the impression himself. Posthumous prints do not carry it and are usually weaker. Several prints before 1923 were published by Watanabe.

facts.text: 1925 oban prints 'self-published by Yoshida Hiroshi (with jizuri 自摺 seal top left margin)'.
Hanga.com says Yoshida did not use a publisher apart from several prints published by Watanabe Shozaburo before 1923; posthumous prints lack the jizuri seal.

rows.meaning: Name given by Katsukawa Shunshō; used in the Katsukawa studio (actor prints, yellow-backs)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: beside or below the design, often with 画 ga
rows.date_note: Fiorillo and the National Gallery of Victoria give his studio years as 1779-93 or 1794; he left the Katsukawa school c.1793-95.
rows.what_it_tells: Early Katsukawa-style actor prints and book illustration by Hokusai; dates the sheet to the 1780s-early 1790s.
rows.cautions: Pupils and imitators of Shunshō also used 春 names; a Shunrō signature is not Hokusai's if the style is not his. Some Shunrō-signed sheets were signed by other artists later called Shunrō.

facts.text: Hokusai joined Shunshō's Katsukawa studio in 1779 and was given the name Shunrō.
He left the Katsukawa school after Shunshō's death in 1792/93 and took the name Sōri in late 1794.

rows.meaning: Art name taken over from the Tawaraya Sōri line; 'Hokusai Sōri ga' c.1798
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin or beside the image, with 画 or 筆
rows.date_note: Fiorillo (after Hiller): Sōri period late 1794 to early 1799; NGV quotes an 1798 painting signed 'Hokusai Sōri ga'.
rows.what_it_tells: Surimono, kyōka books and fine prints of the late 1790s; elegant, thin-line style.
rows.cautions: The name Sōri belonged to a Rinpa-school lineage; later Sōri names (Sōri II etc.) are other artists.

facts.text: Late 1794 to early 1799 is the 'Sōri period'.
An early painting of 1798 is signed 'Hokusai Sōri ga'.

rows.kana: がきょうじんほくさいが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Hokusai, the man mad about painting
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: upper left or lower left
rows.date_note: Cleveland dates the sheets 'c. 1800'; the plain 北斎 name (adopted c.1798-99) continues in the 1800s.
rows.what_it_tells: Early Hokusai (c.1798-1810): surimono and fine prints in his first independent manner.
rows.cautions: 'Hokusai' is the principal name until 1810, then reappears in later forms; the plain name alone does not narrow beyond c.1798-1820.

facts.text: Cleveland records c.1800 prints signed Gakyōjin Hokusai ga and Tōyō Gakyōjin Hokusai ga.
A kana signature 'Hokusai egaku' (ほくさゐゑかく) occurs on an early Great-Wave composition of c.1800-05.

rows.kana: ほくさいあらためたいと
rows.meaning: Hokusai, changing his name to Taitō
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: with 画賛 or 筆 after
rows.date_note: Fiorillo (after Hiller) gives the Taito period as 1810-1820; Cleveland dates a Taitō 'aratame' surimono to 1810 or 1814.
rows.what_it_tells: The Taitō name marks the Manga-era decade (Hokusai Manga from 1814).
rows.cautions: Taitō was later passed to a pupil (Taitō II); sheets of the 1830s-40s signed Taitō are not Hokusai.

facts.text: The 'Taito period' runs 1810-1820.
A Cleveland surimono is signed 'Katsushika Hokusai aratame Taito gasan'.

AIC records an 1818 sheet (The Famous Places on the Tokaido in One View) signed 'Katsushika sakino Hokusai Taito hitsu' ('formerly Hokusai'), with a Taito seal. This is a different formula from 'aratame Taito'.
facts.quote: Katsushika sakino Hokusai Taito hitsu // seal: Taito

rows.kana: ほくさいあらためいいつひつ
rows.meaning: From the brush of Iitsu, formerly Hokusai
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: upper left beside the title cartouche (Fuji series)
rows.date_note: The name Iitsu dates from c.1820/21 and was used on the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (c.1830-32), the Great Wave and the Red Fuji. The word 'aratame' marks the change of name.
rows.what_it_tells: Signature of the Fuji series and other prints of c.1830-34, the peak Hokusai period.
rows.cautions: Reproductions of the Great Wave and Red Fuji were made in the 20th century by Japanese firms such as Adachi, Uchida and Takamizawa, and they copy this signature and the publisher's seal. Judge paper, colour, blocks and printer's marks, not the signature.

facts.text: The Great Wave is signed 'Hokusai aratame Iitsu hitsu' (北斎改爲一筆), 'Drawn by Iitsu, formerly known as Hokusai'.
Cleveland: Red Fuji signed 'Hokusai aratame Iitsu hitsu' beside the title cartouche.
Facsimile editions of Hokusai and Hiroshige by modern Japanese publishers copy signatures and seals.

rows.kana: ぜんほくさいいいつひつ
rows.meaning: From the brush of Iitsu, formerly Hokusai
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: upper left beside title
rows.date_note: Cleveland records it on Lake Misaka (Fuji series c.1830-32) and on the 1835-36 One Hundred Poems with a Manji (卍) seal.
rows.what_it_tells: Late-Fuji-series and One Hundred Poems signature.
rows.cautions: Distinguish from 'Hokusai aratame Iitsu' (same period); both occur within one series.

facts.text: Lake Misaka is signed 'Zen Hokusai Iitsu hitsu'; One Hundred Poems prints (1835-36) 'Zen Hokusai' with a Manji seal.

rows.kana: がきょうろうじんまんじ
rows.meaning: Old man mad about painting, Manji
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin or beside the image
rows.date_note: Used from the 1834 Fugaku hyakkei (One Hundred Views of Fuji) to his death in 1849.
rows.what_it_tells: Late works: paintings and prints of his last 15 years (the swallow-tail hanging scrolls).
rows.cautions: Forged or studio-made versions are common on late paintings; Manji (卍) as a seal also appears on Hokusai-school work.

facts.text: Hokusai signed 'Gakyō Rōjin Manji' (卍) in his old age; Cleveland records Manji seal on 1835-36 prints.

rows.kana: いちゆうさいひろしげが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Hiroshige of the Ichiyūsai studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: beside the title, right
rows.date_note: Fiorillo dates 一幽齋 to c.1830-31 (a different gō in kanji from the 一立齋 of 1832-42).
rows.what_it_tells: Early landscapes and bird-and-flower prints (c.1830-31), for example Famous Places in the Eastern Capital.
rows.cautions: Look-alike gō: Ichiyūsai 一雄齋 (Kunisada, 1811-17) and Kuniyoshi's 一勇斎; check the characters.

facts.text: The 1830-31 gō is written 一幽齋.
Cleveland: Full Moon over Takanawa signed Ichiyūsai Hiroshige ga.

rows.kana: いちりゅうさいひろしげが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Hiroshige of the Ichiryūsai studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: beside the title or lower left
rows.date_note: Fiorillo gives Ichiryūsai c.1832-42; the seal 'Ichiryūsai' continues on prints into the 1850s (Cleveland).
rows.what_it_tells: Tōkaidō (Hōeidō) and Kisokaidō-era prints (1830s) and early 1840s; signature is the one on the Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō.
rows.cautions: The Ichiryūsai seal persists to 1858, so a seal alone does not date a print before 1842.

facts.text: Ichiryūsai is dated c.1832-42; Ryūsai c.1842-58.
Cleveland records Light Rain on the Embankment of the Sumida as 'Ichiryūsai Hiroshige ga' and an 1854 sheet with an Ichiryūsai seal.

Caution: Ichiryusai is not exclusive to Hiroshige I. 日本人名大辞典 gives 一立斎 as a gō of Hiroshige II and III as well, and AIC records an Ichiryusai seal on an 1865 print by Hiroshige II (Canary and wisteria, signed Rissho fude).
facts.quote: 別号に重宣,一幽斎,一立斎 / Seal: Ichiryusai (AIC 26000, 1865)

rows.meaning: Drawn by Hiroshige
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: in a lower box or cartouche, often with the publisher's seal below
rows.date_note: Plain 'Hiroshige ga' appears from the 1830s; in the 1850s the signature is typically enclosed in a red cartouche (Edo hyakkei, 1856-58).
rows.what_it_tells: The signature alone does not date the print; use the series, censor and date seals.
rows.cautions: Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) signed 'Hiroshige' after 1858, and Hiroshige III also signed 'Hiroshige'. Later Edo hyakkei and Tōkyō titles signed 'Hiroshige' are not by the master.

facts.text: On Edo hyakkei prints the signature 'Hiroshige ga' sits in a lower box with publisher and censor seals.
Hiroshige II signed Shigenobu, then Hiroshige after 1858; prints with 'Tōkyō' titles signed Hiroshige are usually III.

rows.meaning: From the brush of Hiroshige
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower left, often in a cartouche in the 1850s
rows.date_note: Cleveland records 'Hiroshige hitsu' in 1832-35 and in 1853. Fiorillo says the choice of ga or hitsu has no special significance, though a change can help date a print.
rows.what_it_tells: Slightly more formal wording; common on bird-and-flower and on the 1850s Sixty-odd Provinces series.
rows.cautions: It is not a different hand from 'ga'; do not read the choice of word as a sign that the print is genuine.

facts.text: The suffix hitsu (fude) versus ga has no special significance but a shift can help date a print.

rows.meaning: By Hiroshige, drawn at request
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: centre or beside the design
rows.date_note: Cleveland records 'sekkei ōju Hiroshige hitsu' on an 1854 collaborative triptych.
rows.what_it_tells: Commission or collaboration sheets (with Toyokuni, e.g. The Snowy Garden, 1854).
rows.cautions: Hiroshige III also signed 'ōju Hiroshige ga' (collector page); check the sheet's date.

facts.text: ōju means 'by special request', placed before a signature.

Caution: Oju (by request) is a formula, not a Hiroshige I marker. AIC records 'Oju Toyokuni ga' on a c.1848 Kunisada print, 'Oju Hiroshige ga' on 1860 prints by Hiroshige II and 'Oju Hiroshige hitsu' on a c.1875 print by Hiroshige III. A signature reading Oju Hiroshige can therefore be Hiroshige I, II or III; the date or the title series decides.
facts.quote: Signed: Oju Hiroshige ga (AIC 32498, 1860, Hiroshige II); Signed: Oju Hiroshige hitsu (AIC 32446, c.1875, Hiroshige III)

rows.meaning: Hiroshige of the Ryūsai studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: with Hiroshige seal on paintings
rows.date_note: Fiorillo: Ryūsai c.1842-58.
rows.what_it_tells: Late-period gō; common on paintings (Cleveland's Lake Suwa scroll signed Ryūsai).
rows.cautions: Fiorillo dates the Ryūsai signature to c.1842–58, not 1832–58, which affects the Lake Suwa scroll.

facts.text: Ryūsai (立齋) is dated c.1842-58.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Shigenobu (later Hiroshige II)

maker.name: Utagawa Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) (二代歌川廣重)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Hiroshige II signed Shigenobu while his master lived; three Edo hyakkei designs are attributed to Shigenobu.
rows.what_it_tells: A pupil's work from the master's studio, c.1850-58.
rows.cautions: Shigenobu is also a name of other artists (Kunisada pupils); check series.

facts.text: Three Meisho Edo hyakkei prints are attributed to Utagawa Shigenobu, 'later Hiroshige II'.
Shigenobu took the name Hiroshige after his master's death in 1858.
AIC records Shigenobu signatures in the forms 'Shigenobu fude' and 'Shigenobu hitsu' (1857; c.1843-52 flower-and-bird sheets), not 'ga'.

rows.meaning: Signature 'Hiroshige' after 1858, used by the second Hiroshige

maker.name: Utagawa Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) (二代歌川廣重)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Shigenobu took Hiroshige after 1858 and used it until he left the master's household c.1865/67.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Hiroshige' print dated 1859-65 with later-style colour is probably II.
rows.cautions: It is hard to tell from Hiroshige I on the signature alone; Marks and Fiorillo advise relying on style and date seals. Hiroshige III later also signed 'Hiroshige'.

facts.text: Hiroshige II adopted the name after 1858 and 'his works are often confused with his master's'.

rows.meaning: Art name used after he stopped using 'Hiroshige'

maker.name: Utagawa Hiroshige II (Shigenobu) (二代歌川廣重)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Hiroshige II used Risshō/Kisai Risshō after losing the Hiroshige name when he left the household (c.1865-69).
rows.what_it_tells: Late works of Hiroshige II.
rows.cautions: Sources differ on the date of the switch (1865, 1867).

facts.text: Hiroshige II also used Risshō (立祥) and Kisai.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Shigemasa (later Hiroshige III)

maker.name: Utagawa Hiroshige III (Shigemasa) (三代歌川廣重)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Gotō Torakichi's early name before 1867/1869.
rows.what_it_tells: Pupil-period work of Hiroshige III.
rows.cautions: Shigemasa is a very common name (Kitao Shigemasa 18th c.).

facts.text: Shigemasa (重政) is Hiroshige III, according to Fiorillo.

rows.meaning: Signature 'Hiroshige' on Meiji-era prints

maker.name: Utagawa Hiroshige III (Shigemasa) (三代歌川廣重)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Hiroshige III signed Hiroshige from c.1867-69 on Meiji views (Tōkyō titles).
rows.what_it_tells: Meiji-era (1870s-1890s) 'Hiroshige' prints with aniline red and Western-influenced scenes are III's.
rows.cautions: Often catalogued as II or as the master. Titles with 東京 (Tōkyō) are Meiji.

facts.text: Prints with 'Tōkyō' in the title signed Hiroshige are almost certainly III.

rows.kana: ごとてい くにさだが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Kunisada of the Gototei studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Fiorillo: Gototei c.1809-45; Cleveland records it on prints from 1814 to the mid 1820s.
rows.what_it_tells: Actor prints and beauties of the Bunka-Bunsei years (1810s-20s).
rows.cautions: Kunisada II and later pupils signed 'Kunisada'; the Gototei art name ties the sheet to the first.

facts.text: Gototei is used c.1809-1845.
Cleveland: 'Gototei Kunisada ga' on an 1814 actor print and a c.1820 beauty.

rows.kana: こうちょうろう くにさだが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Kunisada of the Kōchōrō studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin or in a cartouche
rows.date_note: Fiorillo gives Kōchōrō as 1824-61, used with 国貞 before 1844 and with 豊国 afterwards.
rows.what_it_tells: With 國貞 it dates a sheet to 1824-44, with 豊國 to 1844 or later.
rows.cautions: Kunisada II also used Kōchōrō.

facts.text: Kōchōrō is used 1824-61.
Cleveland: Abalone Divers signed 香蝶楼国貞画.

rows.kana: こうちょうろう とよくにが
rows.meaning: Kunisada signing as Toyokuni (from 1844)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: in a toshidama cartouche from c.1850
rows.date_note: Kunisada took Toyokuni in 1844 (Fiorillo); from c.1850 nearly all signatures sit in a toshidama (年玉) cartouche.
rows.what_it_tells: Dates a Kunisada sheet to 1844 or later.
rows.cautions: Numbering differs: Western sources say Toyokuni III, Japanese sources often Toyokuni II, and Cleveland records 'second generation'. Kunisada II later signed Toyokuni IV.

facts.text: Kunisada used Toyokuni from 1844; toshidama cartouche from c.1850.
Cleveland: 'Kunisada - second generation Toyokuni' for 1844-48.

Another source differs: Counts him as 2代(実は3代) 'second, actually third' Toyokuni; AIC files him as 'Utagawa Kunisada I (Toyokuni III)'. Cleveland's 'second generation' follows the self-styled numbering.

rows.kana: いちゆうさいくによしが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Kuniyoshi of the Ichiyūsai studio
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin or cartouche
rows.date_note: Kuniyoshi Project chart: Ichiyūsai c.1828-1850s.
rows.what_it_tells: The standard Kuniyoshi signature; seals beside it narrow the date.
rows.cautions: Pupils sign their own names; Kuniyoshi II exists.

facts.text: The chart lists Ichiyūsai Kuniyoshi from c.1828-30 into the early 1850s.
Cleveland: 'Ichiyusai Kuniyoshi ga' on early 1830s sheets and 1854.
Another source differs: AIC dates one sheet signed Ichiyusai Kuniyoshi ga (Roben Waterfall at Mount Oyama, 25617) to c.1818/20, earlier than c.1828-30.
facts.quote: Signature: Ichiyusai Kuniyoshi ga // kiwame seal (c. 1818/20)

rows.meaning: Heraldic seal of the Utagawa school
rows.where_on_object: beside the signature
rows.date_note: Kuniyoshi Project: c.1830-1847; he dropped it c.1844.
rows.what_it_tells: Marks Kuniyoshi sheets of the 1830s-early 1840s.
rows.cautions: Utagawa pupils/Kunisada used it until the 1860s; do not date those from it.

facts.text: Toshidama appears on Kuniyoshi sheets c.1830-47; abandoned after he left the Utagawa line c.1844.

rows.meaning: Kuniyoshi's paulownia-flower seal
rows.where_on_object: beside the signature
rows.date_note: Kuniyoshi Project: c.1844-1861; Cleveland records 'Artist's seal: Paulownia' on an 1854 print.
rows.what_it_tells: Dates a Kuniyoshi print to 1844 or later.
rows.cautions: Restrikes keep the seal.

facts.text: Paulownia seal c.1844-1861.
Cleveland: Futamigaura Bay, 'Artist's seal: Paulownia'.

rows.meaning: From the brush of Utamaro
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: beside the title cartouche
rows.date_note: Cleveland records 'Utamaro hitsu' on prints of c.1796-1802 and 歌麿画 on the 1793 Ten Types.
rows.what_it_tells: Standard 1790s signature.
rows.cautions: Utamaro II continued the name after 1806. Some designs add 'shōmei' (正名, 'genuine name').

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues 'Utamaro hitsu' on c.1796-97 and late-1790s sheets.
Some Utamaro designs add 'shōmei', 'genuine name'.

rows.meaning: The Utamaro signature as used by the second Utamaro, a pupil

maker.name: Kitagawa Utamaro II (二代喜多川歌麿)

rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.date_note: A print signed by Utamaro II is dated 1807, the year after Utamaro's death; he is said to have died about 1831 (uncertain).
rows.what_it_tells: An Utamaro signature on a print made after 1806 may be the pupil's.
rows.cautions: The pupil signed with the same name, so the signature alone does not tell master from pupil.

facts.text: Utamaro II was a pupil of Utamaro (the dictionary lists him among Utamaro's 門人 with Tsukimaro and Fujimaro).
facts.quote: 門人に、2代歌麿、月麿（菊麿）、藤麿らがいる

facts.text: A print signed by Utamaro II is dated 1807, the year after Utamaro's death in 1806.
facts.quote: 1807 Shizuka of the Tamaya ... Kitagawa Utamaro II

facts.text: Utamaro II died c.1831, uncertain.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Harunobu
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: in the picture, lower margin
rows.date_note: Polychrome printing began 1765; Harunobu died 1770.
rows.what_it_tells: An original dates to 1765-70.
rows.cautions: Widely forged and reprinted: Cleveland catalogues a 'Harunobu ga' sheet as 1868-1912, a later reprint.

facts.text: Cleveland: 鈴木春信画 on the 1767 Five Virtues.
Cleveland catalogues 'Passing the Bamboo Grove', 'Harunobu ga', as 1868-1912.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Kiyonaga
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Cleveland: Kiyonaga ga on 1783-86 prints.
rows.what_it_tells: Dates 1780s sheets.
rows.cautions: Later reprints exist.

facts.text: Cleveland: 'Kiyonaga ga' on 1783-86 sheets.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Shunshō
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin; kakihan sometimes
rows.date_note: Cleveland: 1778-85 sheets; Shunshō d.1792.
rows.what_it_tells: Actor portraits of the 1770s-80s.
rows.cautions: Pupils sign their own names.

facts.text: Cleveland: 'Shunshō ga' and a kakihan on Seven Wise Women.

rows.kana: とうしゅうさいしゃらくが
rows.meaning: Drawn by Tōshūsai Sharaku
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower right corner
rows.date_note: All c.1794-95; Tsutaya Jūzaburō emblem and kiwame seal.
rows.what_it_tells: A print signed Sharaku is from his ten-month career.
rows.cautions: 20th-century facsimile editions copy it.

facts.text: Cleveland: 'Toshusai Sharaku ga' lower right with Tsutaya emblem and kiwame.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Torii Kiyonobu
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.date_note: Torii Kiyonobu I lived 1664–1729.

facts.text: Torii Kiyonobu I (1664-1729) was the founder of the Torii school.
Kiyonobu's artist seal reads 清信 (Kiyonobu); AIC also records the signature 'Yamato hitsu zugashi Torii Kiyonobu' with seal Kiyonobu.

rows.kana: おくむらまさのぶひつ
rows.meaning: From the brush of Okumura Masanobu
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.date_note: Okumura Masanobu lived 1686–1764.
rows.what_it_tells: He also ran his own publishing house, Okumuraya.

facts.text: Okumura Masanobu lived 1686-1764.
He also ran the publishing house Okumuraya (絵草紙問屋奥村屋 / 版元奥村屋).
AIC records the signature form 'Okumura Masanobu Hitsu'.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Isoda Koryūsai (Masakatsu)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.date_note: Active as a print designer from about 1769 until about 1780, when he turned to painting.

facts.text: Isoda Koryusai (1735-1790) was active as a print designer from c.1769 and gave up printmaking c.1780 for painting; the signature 'Koryusai ga' is recorded on AIC sheets of c.1780.
He was awarded the honorary rank hokkyo (法橋) in 1782; Fiorillo says the rank was given to priests and later to artists.
facts.quote: 法橋の位をあたえられた晩年

rows.kana: ちょうぶんさいえいし
rows.meaning: Chōbunsai Eishi
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.date_note: Chōbunsai Eishi lived 1756–1829.

facts.text: Chobunsai Eishi lived 1756-1829.
He was a former hatamoto (bannerman samurai) who studied under the Kano painter Kano Eisen'in (狩野栄川) and Bunryusai.
Signature forms in AIC include 'Chobunsai Eishi zu' with artist seal CHOBUNSAI (1798); Cleveland has 栄之筆 with a seal c.1801-4.
facts.quote: Signature: Chobunsai Eishi zu // Artist seal: CHOBUNSAI

rows.meaning: Drawn by Toyokuni (I)
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin; sealed 一陽斎
rows.date_note: Toyokuni I (1769-1825); Cleveland shows 'Toyokuni ga' on 1790s sheets and a painting sealed Ichiyōsai.
rows.what_it_tells: Actor and beauty prints of 1790s-1810s.
rows.cautions: Toyokuni II (Toyoshige) and Kunisada (Toyokuni III in the West) also signed Toyokuni; check the date.

facts.text: Cleveland: 'Toyokuni ga' on c.1793-97 and late 1790s prints; painting signed 歌川豊国画 and sealed 一陽斎.

rows.meaning: Drawn by Keisai Eisen
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Cleveland dates sheets from early 1820s to 1830s; Eisen d.1848.
rows.what_it_tells: Bijin-ga and Kisokaidō prints.
rows.cautions: Pupils signed Eisen names.

facts.text: Cleveland: 'Keisai Eisen ga' with kiwame, early 1820s; 'Keisai hitsu' with Eisen seal early 1830s.

rows.meaning: From the brush of Eizan
rows.technique: woodblock-printed signature (the key-block carved from the artist's brush draft)
rows.where_on_object: lower margin
rows.date_note: Cleveland dates 1810s-1830s.

Another source differs: AIC transcribes the publisher's mark 'hanken shoyu Watanabe Shozaburo' on Hasui sheets whose designs are dated 1924, 1926 and 1928 (e.g. 7399, 2641, 2601) and on Shoson sheets of 1926-28. AIC's dates are for the design; a later impression carries the later seal, and AIC may be abbreviating the legend, so this may not be a true conflict. Flag for a seal-by-seal check.

facts.text: Another source differs: AIC records 'circular 6mm Watanabe seal' on Hasui sheets with design dates 1920 to 1925 (197455, 2567, 2590), earlier than c.1924-25. Again the museum date is for the design.

AIC records block-printed 'Signed: Yoshida // Artist's seal: Hiroshi' on lifetime prints of 1926-28 and 'Signed: Yoshida (in block)' on a 1932 India print, so a Japanese-style block signature and seal occur on lifetime impressions as well as the English pencil signature.

facts.text: Torii Kotondo (real name Saito Shin) lived 1900-1976 and later became the fifth Torii Kiyotada, eighth head of the Torii school.
He took the name Kotondo (言人) in 1915 as a theatre signboard painter; in 1929 he inherited the headship and changed it to Kiyonobu (清言), and in 1962 became 5th Kiyotada.
AIC records the print signatures 'Kotondo saku' on sheets dated Showa 4 (1929).

rows.meaning: Namikawa (Yasuyuki) of Kyoto
rows.device: none; four characters

maker.name: Namikawa Yasuyuki 並河靖之 (1845-1927), Kyoto

wares: wire cloisonné vases, boxes, incense burners
rows.technique: engraved on an applied silver plaque, tablet or cartouche set into the base (silver plate on the base); on the 1912 Tokyo National Museum censer recorded as 刻銘 (engraved)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The earliest piece carrying the plaque in the V&A is dated ca. 1875-80; Namikawa retired in 1915 and his firm closed soon after (Sotheby's), and the 1912 censer shows the mark in use to the end. The dates are the museums' dating of pieces, not of the mark.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies the Kyoto workshop of Namikawa Yasuyuki, the leading Kyoto maker of fine wire cloisonné; Baur dates marked pieces to the Meiji period.
rows.cautions: The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) says signed copies of his work were made after his success, and notes one vase whose plaque is poorly made, with badly engraved characters (the first character 京 especially) and decoration that is stiff for Yasuyuki, though it is still likely original. A plaque alone does not prove a piece genuine: judge the plaque's engraving, the wirework and the enamel ground together. Auction houses also call pieces 'workshop of Namikawa', and some dealer listings give the signature as 'Namikawa Yasuyuki'.

facts.text: The Tokyo National Museum censer made by Namikawa Yasuyuki in 1912 (Taishō 1) is recorded with the engraved mark 京都 並河.
V&A records describe the mark as four characters engraved on a silver plate, plaque or cartouche applied to the base.
facts.quote: applied silver plaque with the engraved four-character mark

facts.text: The Musée Baur lists 京都並河 as Namikawa Yasuyuki's seal on four Meiji pieces.
The V&A warns that signed copies of his work were made and flags a poorly engraved plaque.
facts.quote: signed copies were made of his work

facts.text: Namikawa retired in 1915 and his company closed soon after; he became an Imperial Household Artist in 1896.

Another source differs: No retirement in 1915: Namikawa went into retirement at his Yamashina villa from about 1918; the Kyoto workshop closed in 1923 (the Tokyo medal works in 1929); he died in 1927.
facts.quote: 京都の工場は1923（大正12）年に閉鎖

facts.text: Namikawa's early cloisonné is often unsigned; marks appear mainly on later work (so absence of 京都並河 on early pieces is normal).
facts.quote: 前期の製作では銘を入れていないものが多く

facts.text: Namikawa took up cloisonné as a side business at home and made it his full-time work in 1878 (Meiji 11).

rows.meaning: Pioneer or leader: seal of Namikawa Sōsuke
rows.device: The single character 魁, in silver wire

maker.name: Namikawa Sōsuke 濤川惣助 (1847-1910), Tokyo

wares: musen and yusen cloisonné vases, trays, plates, plaques
rows.technique: worked in silver wire (yusen) and set into the base enamel; also recorded as a 印 (seal) on the base
rows.where_on_object: base (inside the base on vases)
rows.date_note: Dated from the pieces: V&A c.1900, Baur 1900-1910. Earlier use is not established; the lower bound is the earliest dated example, not a proven start.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies Namikawa Sōsuke's Tokyo workshop. The mark is the single character 魁, not 濤川 or a 'Sō' cartouche. Musen (wireless) enamelling and soft colour gradation are typical of his work.
rows.cautions: The V&A and Tokyo University of the Arts both record it; a dish at Geidai also has an ink box inscription naming him, which is how such pieces are normally confirmed. Many pieces are only attributed to his workshop. He was an Imperial Household Artist from 1896; nothing shows that others used the mark, but the sources do not say either way.

facts.text: The mark is recorded as 底面「魁」印 on a Namikawa Sōsuke fan-shaped dish, with a box-lid ink inscription naming him.
The V&A describes a silver yusen Sakigake seal inside the bases of a pair of Sōsuke vases, Tokyo, c.1900.
The Musée Baur lists 魁 as Namikawa Sōsuke's seal on c.1900-1910 pieces.

rows.chars: (Andō Company mark; character form not confirmed)

rows.meaning: Mark of the Andō cloisonné company, Nagoya
rows.device: Company mark made of silver wire, in several V&A pieces filled with white enamel

maker.name: Andō Cloisonné Company 安藤七宝店, Nagoya

wares: cloisonné vases and bowls, many with moriage (raised) decoration
rows.technique: silver wire (yusen) applied to the base enamel, sometimes filled with white enamel
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: V&A pieces carrying it date from c.1900 to c.1950-60, so the mark runs into the mid-twentieth century. The firm dates from 1880.
rows.what_it_tells: Nagoya firm; its dark matt brown counter-enamel and moriage work are typical. Pieces with the firm's mark are generally Meiji to Showa.
rows.cautions: The sources do not describe the shape of the mark. The same mark continues after the Meiji period, so it does not date a piece to Meiji. The firm still trades, so modern Andō pieces exist; check the base plate and enamel quality.

facts.text: The V&A records a base enamelled matt brown with the silver yusen mark of the Ando Company (c.1912-26).

facts.text: The firm was founded in 1880 (Meiji 13) at Tamaya-chō, Nagoya, with a grandson of Kaji Tsunekichi as works manager.
