rows.date_note: V&A dates the piece c.1900-10 and calls the mark 'early'.
rows.what_it_tells: A stamped mark inside a gilt base plate is a different form from the later silver-wire mark on enamel.
rows.cautions: Single Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) entry; the form of the stamp is not described. The box carries the ink signature of Andō Jūbei and a company label showing Nagoya Castle and the 1900 Paris gold medal.

facts.text: V&A: 'The early stamped mark of the Ando Company has been applied inside the gilt base plate.'
facts.quote: early stamped mark of the Ando Company

rows.kana: あんどうしっぽうてん
rows.meaning: Andō Cloisonné Shop (made by / respectfully made by)
rows.device: written characters
rows.where_on_object: varies (a collectors' site lists them; position not given)
rows.date_note: The source gives no dates.
rows.what_it_tells: Written forms of the firm's name; 謹製 means made with care, a retail-style phrase.
rows.cautions: Known only from one collectors' tag list, which is a weak source, and the source does not say where on the object these appear. Treat as a lead, not as established marks.

facts.text: A collectors' site lists 安藤七宝店, 安藤七宝店製 and 安藤七寳店謹製 as inscriptions on Andō items.

rows.meaning: Andō Jūbei, the company's head
rows.device: ink signature on the box
rows.where_on_object: box (not the object)
rows.date_note: V&A dates the box with the vase c.1900-10.
rows.what_it_tells: Shows the box was issued by the firm.
rows.cautions: The box signature is not a mark on the enamel itself. Sources differ on the founder: Nagoya city names Muradaya Jūbei as founder in 1880, while overseas sources name Andō Jūbei (1876-1953 in one source, so he cannot have founded it in 1880). The difference is unresolved.

facts.text: The box of a c.1900-10 Andō vase carries the signature of Ando Jubei.
Nagoya city names 村田屋重兵衛 as founder in 1880.
facts.quote: 村田屋重兵衛が玉屋町にて創業

facts.text: Andō Jūbei (1876-1953) was born Andō Jūzaburō and took his late father's name Jūbei; he studied in Britain after winning a gold medal at Glasgow in 1901, so a box signed by him c.1900-10 is the work of a man in his twenties-thirties.
facts.quote: 安藤重兵衛原名安藤重三郎

rows.kana: あいちはやしこでんじ
rows.meaning: Hayashi Kodenji of Aichi
rows.device: none

maker.name: Hayashi Kodenji 林小傳治 (also 林小伝治, 林小伝次), Nagoya

rows.technique: engraved, in a rectangular cartouche or circle
rows.where_on_object: interior of the silver-gilt inner base plate
rows.date_note: V&A dates the two pieces c.1880-90.
rows.what_it_tells: Nagoya maker; his dark blue ground is characteristic.
rows.cautions: The V&A gives these marks only in English (six-character 'Aichi Hayashi Kodenji' in a rectangle; four-character 'Aichi Hayashi Ko[denji]' in a circle); the characters shown here are a reconstruction. The names Kodenji and Kodenzi vary. Treat the characters as unconfirmed until read from an image.

facts.text: V&A: silver-gilt inner base plate with the engraved six-character mark 'Aichi Hayashi Kodenji' within a rectangular cartouche.
V&A: a second vase has the four-character mark 'Aichi Hayashi Ko[denji]' within a circular area.
Hayashi Kodenji won a bronze medal at the 13th Tokyo Chōkōkai exhibition in 1898.

Scholars write the name 林小伝治 (Muto) or 林小伝次 (Miyajima 1988; Tobunken 1899); dates 1831-1915; a pupil of Tsukamoto Kaisuke, he opened the sales route to foreigners in 1863. So pieces c.1910 are in his lifetime but a 1915 death ends the signature's personal use.
facts.quote: 貝助に学んだ林小伝治（1831-1915）

rows.kana: なごやはやしこでんじ
rows.meaning: Hayashi Kodenji of Nagoya
rows.device: none
rows.technique: engraved on the inner base plate (with the mark)
rows.where_on_object: inner base plate
rows.date_note: V&A dates the piece c.1890.
rows.what_it_tells: Same maker as the Aichi form, using the city name.
rows.cautions: The V&A describes five characters; the form shown here is reconstructed from its transliteration.

facts.text: V&A: the inner base plate carries the mark and an engraved five-character signature 'Nagoya Hayashi Ko[denji]'.

rows.kana: だいにほんあいちはやしさく
other_spellings: Made by Hayashi of Aichi Prefecture, Great Japan
rows.meaning: Made by Hayashi of Aichi Prefecture, Great Japan
rows.device: concentric circles
rows.technique: engraved inscription in concentric circles, with the maker's mark
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: V&A dates the pair c.1910.
rows.what_it_tells: Place-and-maker inscription in the 'Dai Nihon (Great Japan)' export style.
rows.cautions: The characters are inferred from the Victoria and Albert Museum's (V&A) romanisation. The 'Dai Nihon' form is a country marker common on Meiji exports and is not unique to him.

facts.text: V&A: both vases have the engraved inscription 'Dai Nihon Aichi Hayashi saku' within concentric circles, with the mark of Hayashi Kodenji.

rows.meaning: Stamped mark of Hayashi Kodenji
rows.device: none
wares: cloisonné vases on dark blue ground
rows.where_on_object: gilt interior of the base
rows.date_note: V&A dates the vase c.1880-85.
rows.what_it_tells: Another recorded form of his mark.
rows.cautions: The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) describes it only as a stamped mark and does not give the text.

facts.text: V&A: the very dark blue ground is typical of Hayashi Kodenji, whose stamped mark is on the gilt interior of the base.
facts.quote: stamped mark is carried on the gilt interior

rows.meaning: Kawade (Shibatarō)
rows.device: two characters in a red enamel double gourd

maker.name: Kawade Shibatarō 川出柴太郎 (1856-1921), Nagoya; chief technician at Andō 1902-10 per one source

rows.technique: gold wire seal with red enamel gourd
rows.where_on_object: lid
rows.date_note: V&A dates the box c.1900-12.
rows.what_it_tells: Nagoya maker, also credited with Andō's moriage pieces.
rows.cautions: The V&A gives the two characters only as 'Kawade [Shibatarō]', not as 川出, and the characters 川出 do not appear in the V&A text. Sannenzaka also lists works by him credited to Andō, so a Kawade piece can be made for Andō.

facts.text: V&A: the lid has a gold yusen seal with the two characters Kawade in a red enamel double gourd.
facts.quote: gold yusen seal with the two characters Kawade

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists pieces as 川出柴太郎（安藤七宝店）, showing he worked within Andō.
facts.quote: 川出柴太郎（安藤七宝店）

rows.meaning: Hattori (Tadasaburō)
rows.device: none

maker.name: Hattori Tadasaburō 服部唯三郎, Nagoya

rows.technique: engraved directly into the silver-gilt base interior
rows.where_on_object: base interior
rows.date_note: V&A dates the pair c.1900-10.
rows.what_it_tells: Often credited with inventing moriage (raised) enamel.
rows.cautions: The V&A calls the mark 'two-character Hattori'; Sannenzaka lists the signed work as 服部唯三郎.

facts.text: V&A: the two-character mark Hattori is engraved directly into the silver-gilt interior of the base.
Sannenzaka lists 孔雀羽根に牡丹図花瓶 by 服部唯三郎 as signed.

rows.meaning: Mark of Gonda Hirosuke's Hakuryūen (White Dragon Garden)
rows.device: derived from 白, first part of 白龍園

maker.name: Gonda Hirosuke 権田廣助 (I, 1865-1937), Nagoya

rows.technique: silver yusen on dark brown enamel inside the base; box with red seal 権田謹製
rows.where_on_object: inner base
rows.date_note: V&A dates the tazza c.1912-26; the maker's dates are 1865-1937.
rows.what_it_tells: Nagoya studio mark; box seal and lid label name the Hakuryūen.
rows.cautions: The character is described, not shown. Another Gonda mark may exist: the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) lists two other vases of c.1900-10 without describing a mark.

facts.text: V&A: the inner base carries the silver yusen mark of Gonda Hirosuke, based on the character 白 for his Hakuryūen company.
facts.quote: based on the character for Haku (white)

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists 花蝶に兵隊図鉢 as signed 権田廣助.

rows.meaning: Kumeno Teitarō (signed)
rows.device: none
rows.where_on_object: not stated
rows.date_note: No dates for the mark.
rows.what_it_tells: His style: hammered body, silver foil under translucent turquoise, polychrome silver wire.
rows.cautions: Known only from exhibition lists that mark pieces as 在銘 (signed); the form and position of the mark are not recorded. Unsigned pieces in his style exist (Victoria and Albert Museum, V&A, c.1920-40).

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists several pieces as signed 粂野締太郎.
The V&A calls this style 'often associated with Kumeno Teitarō' and cites signed examples.

rows.meaning: Inaba of the Kinunken studio, Kyoto
rows.device: none

maker.name: Inaba Nanaho 稲葉七穂 (the first), Kyoto 錦雲軒稲葉七宝

rows.where_on_object: not stated
rows.date_note: Active from the Meiji period to early Showa, according to a Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum record.
rows.what_it_tells: Kyoto rival to Namikawa.
rows.cautions: The form and position of the signature are not described; the name in the Sannenzaka list is Kinunken Inaba. The 稲葉 mark is not confirmed.

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists 花鳥図花瓶 as by 錦雲軒稲葉.

錦雲軒 was the studio name of Ozaki Kyūbei, a potter who learned cloisonné in 1870 and set up a Kyoto cloisonné company the next year; in 1889 the first Inaba Shichiho (Isshin, 1849-1931) took the name and founded 錦雲軒稲葉.
facts.quote: 錦雲軒稲葉を創業する

rows.meaning: Ōta Tamejirō (signed)
rows.device: none
rows.where_on_object: not stated
rows.date_note: No dates.
rows.what_it_tells: Maker exhibited in the Sannenzaka Owari show.
rows.cautions: The name is 太田為治郎; the English list romanises it 'Tamashiro', and Tamejirō is the reading of the characters used here. 'Ōta Tamezō' and 'Hikokichi' are not confirmed.

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists several vases as 太田為治郎.

rows.chars: 大日本愛知縣原藤雄造
variants: 大日本愛知県原藤雄造
rows.kana: だいにほんあいちけんはらふじおぞう
rows.romaji: Dai Nihon Aichi ken Hara Fujio zō
rows.romaji_plain: Dai Nihon Aichi ken Hara Fujio zo
rows.meaning: Made by Hara Fujio of Aichi prefecture in Great Japan
rows.device: none
rows.where_on_object: interior foot
rows.date_note: V&A dates the piece ca. 1870-80.
rows.what_it_tells: Early Owari maker whose signature is brush-written, not in metal.
rows.cautions: The characters are a reconstruction from the V&A romanisation.

facts.text: V&A: the interior foot has the artist's signature written in gold lacquer; mark 'Dai Nihon Aichi ken Hara Fujio Zo'.

rows.meaning: Pure silver
rows.device: none
rows.where_on_object: silver rim or base plate
rows.date_note: Seen on V&A pieces c.1900-1920s.
rows.what_it_tells: The rim or base plate is silver; says nothing about the maker.
rows.cautions: On cloisonné this is a metal-purity stamp only; the silver topic covers it fully. The V&A found it on Andō, Hayashi and unmarked Nagoya pieces alike.

facts.text: V&A: silver rim and base plate with the jungin (pure silver) mark on pieces by or near Andō and Hayashi.

rows.meaning: Mark of Yoshi (attributed to Hayakawa Yoshitarō)
rows.device: none
rows.where_on_object: not stated
rows.date_note: No dates.
rows.what_it_tells: Listed as a seal named Yoshi.
rows.cautions: The attribution is the exhibition's and is not proven; there is a single source.

facts.text: Sannenzaka lists a vase with cherry blossoms as 芳印 (attributed to Hayakawa Yoshitarō).

rows.kana: きりゅうこうしょうがいしゃせい
other_spellings: First Japanese Manufacturing and Trading Company
rows.meaning: Made by the Kiryu (Kiritsu) Kosho Kaisha, the semi-official export company
rows.device: stamped beneath the company's 'double mountain' emblem

maker.name: 起立工商会社 (Kiryu Kosho Kaisha)
maker.place: Tokyo (works at Tsukiji and Kobikicho); shops abroad incl. New York

rows.where_on_object: recessed base, beneath the double-mountain emblem
rows.date_note: The company was founded in the wake of the 1873 Vienna exposition (a Kobe paper dates the founding documents to Meiji 7 = 1874; cefiro gives 1873) and closed in 1891 (Meiji 24); the stamp cannot be later than the company.
rows.what_it_tells: A piece made to the company's order and designs (1,969 designs of 1877-1890 survive at Tokyo University of the Arts). The company, not a named craftsman, is the maker; the metalworker may be named separately on the side (e.g. Sugiura Yukimune).
rows.cautions: The Japanese characters are reconstructed from the Christie's/Khalili transliteration 'Kiryu Kosho Kaisha sei'; no source shows them on an object, so check the form on the piece (會/会). Only one auction source reports the stamp, and no museum record does. The reading 'Kiryu' (not 'Kiritsu') is Earle's, 'established from early engravings and photographs'.

facts.text: Stamped on the base 'Kiryu Kosho Kaisha sei' beneath the 'double-mountain' mark of the company, on a bronze and mixed-metal vase signed on the side by Sugiura Yukimune (Christie's, 18 Sep 2007).
facts.quote: Kiryu Kosho Kaisha sei beneath the "double-mountain" mark

facts.text: The company was founded after the 1873 Vienna exposition with Matsuo Gisuke as president and Wakai Kenzaburo as vice-president, made mainly porcelain and bronzes, had a bronze works at Tsukiji, and was wound up in 1891 (Meiji 24).
facts.quote: 明治二十四年に起立工商会社は廃業

rows.meaning: Emblem of the Kiryu Kosho Kaisha: two mountains
rows.device: two peaks side by side (as described in Christie's; shape not seen by me)

maker.name: 起立工商会社 (Kiryu Kosho Kaisha)

rows.where_on_object: recessed base
rows.date_note: The span is the same as the company's.
rows.what_it_tells: With 'Kako' stamped above or beside it, it marks a Suzuki Chokichi vase of c.1877-1891. Earle says that with few exceptions these vases are signed Kako or, more rarely, 'Kiritsu Kiryu Kaisha', in either case under the double mountain.
rows.cautions: The source describes the mark in words only, so its exact shape is not confirmed. Look-alike Chinese 'mountain' stamps are reported but not confirmed.

facts.text: Vases of 10-12 inches are 'either signed Kako (Suzuki Chokichi's art name) or, more rarely, Kiritsu Kiryu Kaisha, in either case under a double mountain mark'.

rows.meaning: Kakō, art name of the bronze-caster Suzuki Chōkichi (1848-1919)
wares: cast bronze vases and okimono (Kiritsu Kosho Kaisha period)
rows.technique: stamped (cast-stamp characters on the recessed base)
rows.where_on_object: recessed base, beside the double-mountain emblem
rows.date_note: The years in which Chokichi worked with the Kiritsu Kosho Kaisha; the sources do not state exact years for the stamped form.
rows.what_it_tells: A bronze cast under Suzuki Chokichi's supervision for the Kiritsu Kosho Kaisha; the inlay may be by other hands.
rows.cautions: Different form from the incised 嘉幸 on his hawks (see kako-incised). Christie's says Chokichi 'apparently supervised the casting' and others did the soft-metal decoration. 'Kako' may be confused with other art names reading Kako/Yoshiyuki.

facts.text: Art name 嘉幸 (read かこう / よしゆき); 1848-1919, born Iruma District, Musashi.
Bronze jar c. 1881-83 'signed on the recessed base in stamped characters Kako beneath the double mountain mark of the Kiryu Kosho Kaisha' (Christie's, 20 June 2001).
facts.quote: stamped characters Kako beneath the double mountain mark

rows.meaning: Kakō (Suzuki Chōkichi), incised signature
rows.technique: incised with a broad chisel (太鏨による線刻)
rows.where_on_object: back of the tail feathers of each of the Twelve Hawks
rows.date_note: The Twelve Hawks were made for the 1893 Chicago exposition; this is the only dated example of the incised form recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: Chokichi's own hand-signed work, as opposed to the company-stamped Kako of the Kiritsu years.
rows.cautions: Only the Twelve Hawks (National Crafts Museum, Important Cultural Property) are confirmed as carrying this form. The 銅鷲置物 in the Tokyo National Museum is attributed to him by name (鈴木長吉作); the records do not show its mark.

facts.text: Each hawk has the signature 「嘉幸」 incised with a broad chisel on the back of the tail; the feet are numbered 一 to 十二.
facts.quote: 太鏨による線刻で「嘉幸」の銘が記される

facts.text: The Tokyo National Museum eagle (1893) is by Chokichi, who was appointed 帝室技芸員 in 1896.
facts.quote: 明治二十九年(一八九六)宮内省より帝室技芸員に任命

rows.meaning: Jōun (Ōshima Jōun 大島如雲), cast-in seal
rows.where_on_object: on the casting itself
rows.date_note: The range runs from a work dated 1890 (濡れ獅子図丸額, per the museum record) to a vase of 1907, for which no mark is recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A work cast by or in the workshop of Ōshima Jōun.
rows.cautions: Jōun's life dates (1858-1940) come from a search summary and are not confirmed by a full page. The 'Joun' cast seal is a shop seal, and posthumous or workshop use is not documented.

facts.text: Peony inkstone ME1399, bronze cast, Tokyo University of the Arts: 鋳印「如雲」.

rows.meaning: Ichijōken, studio or art name engraved beside Jōun's cast seal
wares: cast bronze plaques with gold inlay
rows.technique: engraved (刻銘), with cast seal 如雲
rows.where_on_object: front or back of the plaque
rows.what_it_tells: On two Geidai plaques the engraved 一乗軒 appears together with the cast seal 如雲.
rows.cautions: Whose studio name 一乗軒 is (Jōun's or a decorator's) is not stated in the records; the Geidai catalogue pairs it with 如雲 only.

facts.text: Dragon plaque ME691 and 'Tanuki in the rain' ME680: 刻銘「一乗軒」 鋳印「如雲」.
facts.quote: 刻銘「一乗軒」 鋳印「如雲」

rows.chars: 帝室技藝員 従五位海野勝珉
variants: 帝室技芸員 従五位海野勝珉
rows.kana: ていしつぎげいいん じゅごいのげ うんのしょうみん
rows.meaning: Imperial Household Artist, Junior Fifth Rank, Unno Shōmin
rows.where_on_object: on the piece
rows.date_note: The court title and rank wording mean the piece is after his appointment as Imperial Household Artist (1890, according to cefiro's page).
rows.what_it_tells: Signed with his court title: a work of his later career, not a pre-appointment one.
rows.cautions: This is the form on a teaching sample (手板) at Geidai (Tokyo University of the Arts); export pieces may carry only a short name. Forged titled signatures are not documented in the sources. The museum record shows one character as 〓 (unencodable), likely 珉.

facts.text: Peony hand-board ME395: 刻銘「帝室技藝員 従五位海野勝(〓)」.
facts.quote: 帝室技藝員　従五位海野勝

facts.text: Another source differs: Unno was appointed 帝室技芸員 in Meiji 29 (1896), not 1890 as the record's date_note (from cefiro) says; in the same paper 1890 is the year of his Kano Natsuo apprenticeship, Third National Exposition judging and Tokyo School of Fine Arts post.

rows.chars: 東京美術学校所蔵品模造
variants: 東京美術学校所藏品模造
rows.kana: とうきょうびじゅつがっこうしょぞうひんもぞう
other_spellings: Tokyo School of Fine Arts replica
rows.meaning: Copy of an object in the collection of the Tokyo School of Fine Arts

maker.name: 東京美術学校 (Tokyo School of Fine Arts)

rows.technique: stamped on a stamping plate (刻印板)
rows.where_on_object: back of each copy
rows.date_note: No year is given; the school existed from 1887, before the 1949 merger into Tokyo University of the Arts.
rows.what_it_tells: An official school replica (electroformed copper) of a model by Kano Natsuo, Unno Shomin or Kagawa Katsuhiro, not a work by them.
rows.cautions: Do not read the master's name on such a copy as authorship. Teaching copies later circulate as 'Natsuo' or 'Shomin' pieces.

facts.text: 30 electrotype copies after Natsuo (1-12), Shomin (13-29) and Katsuhiro (30), each stamped on the back 刻印板「東京美術学校所蔵品模造」.
facts.quote: 刻印板「東京美術学校所蔵品模造」

rows.kana: だいにほんぶんせいねんせいみんちゅう
rows.meaning: Cast by Seimin of Great Japan in the Bunsei era (1818-30)
rows.where_on_object: reverse of one leg
rows.date_note: Wording claims Bunsei (1818-30), yet the piece is dated late 19th century by Christie's.
rows.what_it_tells: Seimin was a famed lost-wax caster; the era name in the inscription is an assertion, not evidence of date.
rows.cautions: Christie's: 'His sign Seimin is routinely found on pieces of somewhat later date.' A Seimin name with a Bunsei date on a Meiji-style bronze is therefore a retrospective signature. The characters here are reconstructed from a transliteration and may differ from the object.

facts.text: Incense burner, late 19th c., signed on a leg 'Dainihon Bunsei-nen Seimin chu'; Seimin (1761-1837) the famous bronze-caster; his sign is routinely found on later pieces (Christie's, 20 June 2001).
facts.quote: His sign Seimin is routinely found on pieces of somewhat later date

rows.meaning: Great Japan: prefix to a maker's signature
rows.where_on_object: beginning of the signature on the base
rows.date_note: Meiji-era imperial style; used before and after 1912.
rows.what_it_tells: Says 'Japan' in the formal style of the empire; says nothing about the maker or date by itself.
rows.cautions: Not a maker. Komai pieces use the longer 日本國京都住 (see the Komai rows); the same prefix appears on later reproductions.

facts.text: Used as a signature prefix: 'Dainihon Bunsei-nen Seimin chu' on a Seimin bronze, and 'Dai Nihon Kyoto shi Okuno sei' on a Kyoto piece.
facts.quote: Dai Nihon Kyoto shi Okuno sei

rows.kana: にほんこくきょうとじゅうこまいせい
other_spellings: Nihon koku Kyoto ju Komai sei
rows.meaning: Made by Komai, resident of Kyoto, Japan

maker.name: 駒井 Komai (Komai Otojirō 駒井音次郎, 1842-1917, and the Komai workshop)

wares: nunome-zogan (damascene) iron and shakudo boxes, vases, plates, cigarette cases
rows.technique: inlaid in gold (signature in gold overlay) or engraved
rows.where_on_object: on the object, often within a border near the foot or inside the lid
rows.date_note: The workshop was founded in 1841 by Komai Seibei (cefiro); Otojiro's period was c.1870s-1906, and Otojiro II continued to the 1910s; the signature form alone does not date the item.
rows.what_it_tells: Kyoto damascene of the Komai workshop; exported widely and sold abroad as 'Komai Work'.
rows.cautions: Many Kyoto shops made 'Komai-style' damascene (a 'Murakami of Kyoto' box is sold as such). Dealers report a dragonfly emblem, but no museum record shows it. The signature without further evidence does not separate Otojiro from his son or workshop hands.

facts.text: Komai pieces are signed 'Nihon koku Kyoto ju Komai sei' and 'Kyoto no ju Komai sei [made by Komai of Kyoto]', the latter in gold overlay within a border just above the foot (Christie's, 20 June 2001).
facts.quote: Kyoto no ju Komai sei [made by Komai of Kyoto]

facts.text: Otojiro learned nunome-zogan from a Higo craftsman, made much export work, and his pieces were sold abroad as 'Komai Work' and later 'Damascene Work'.
facts.quote: 「Komai Work」、のちに「Damascene Work」と称されました

rows.kana: にほんこくさいきょうじゅうこまいせい
other_spellings: Nihon koku Saikyo jyu Komai sei
rows.meaning: Made by Komai, resident of Saikyō (Kyoto), Japan
rows.where_on_object: on the object
rows.date_note: Saikyō (西京, 'western capital') was a name used for Kyoto after the capital moved to Tokyo, so the form is likely early Meiji, but no source dates it.
rows.what_it_tells: Same workshop; uses the older 'Saikyō' name for Kyoto.
rows.cautions: The characters are taken from the transliteration 'Saikyo Jyu Komai Sei' in a Christie's text; 西京 is a reading of that, so check it on the object.

facts.text: A temple-shaped box with nunome-zogan is 'signed Nihon koku Saikyo Jyu Komai Sei, late 19th century'.
facts.quote: Nihon koku Saikyo Jyu Komai Sei

rows.meaning: Komai (short signature)
rows.where_on_object: on the object
rows.date_note: Pieces so signed in Christie's lots date c. 1880-1900.
rows.what_it_tells: Short signature of the same workshop.
rows.cautions: 'S. Komai' / エス駒井商会 (a box at the Sannenzaka Museum) is a different shop name from Otojiro's; do not merge them.

facts.text: Vases 'signed Komai, circa 1880-1900'.
The Sannenzaka Museum holds an 'エス駒井商会' octagonal jewel box alongside Otojiro's work.
facts.quote: エス駒井商会《八角厨子形宝石箪笥》

rows.meaning: Made by Miyao (the Miyao company of Eisuke Miyao)

maker.name: 宮尾栄助 Miyao Eisuke (Miyao company)

wares: bronze okimono (samurai), vases, shibayama panels, ivory
rows.technique: cast or incised on the base, sometimes with a seal
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: First recorded at the second National Industrial Exposition (1881) with the caster Momose Sozaemon (Earle, as reported by Christie's); marked work is 'late 19th century'.
rows.what_it_tells: A trading firm, not a single smith: Miyao commissioned the pieces; the caster may differ.
rows.cautions: 'Yokohama' as the base is Earle's ('apparently based first in Yokohama'); a Japanese dealer sells a 宮尾栄助 figure as Kyoto. Later fake signatures on modern bronzes are to be expected, but none are documented in the sources. The characters 宮尾製 are taken from the transliteration 'Miyao Sei'.

facts.text: Bronze vase and cover 'signed Miyao Sei, late 19th century'; also a vase 'signed on the base Miyao with a seal'; company made large samurai bronzes, shibayama panels and ivories, apparently based in Yokohama then Nihonbashi after about 1890.
A television appraiser says Miyao Eisuke was not a metalworker but a producer-trader who had craftsmen make export crafts.
facts.quote: 金工家ではなく、プロデューサーのような人

facts.text: Japanese dealers sell figures with the inscription 銘:宮尾栄助.

rows.kana: げんりゅうさいせいやぞう
rows.meaning: Made by Genryūsai Seiya
wares: patinated bronze okimono (tigers, elephants), vases, koro
rows.where_on_object: base, with a seal
rows.date_note: Meiji period (dealer and auction wording).
rows.what_it_tells: Name of an export-bronze maker much sold in the West.
rows.cautions: No scholarly biography, museum record or Japanese-language source for Seiya is recorded, so the maker's dates and place are unknown, and reproductions are not documented. The Bonhams text gives only the romanization, so the characters 玄龍斎精哉 are not confirmed from the source, and 造 is reconstructed from 'zo'.

facts.text: Monumental inlaid vase: 'the base signed with seal Genryusai Seiya zo'; typical of Seiya in subject and patination, size suggests made for exhibition in the West.

rows.meaning: Made by Seiya
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Meiji.
rows.what_it_tells: Short form of the Seiya signature.
rows.cautions: Seen only in dealer and auction listing wording ('Seiya sei', 'Seiya saku'); the characters are assumed. Treat as unconfirmed.

facts.text: Auction and dealer listings read the signature as 'Seiya sei' on tiger and elephant okimono.

rows.meaning: Ryōun (Takahashi Ryōun 高橋凌雲)
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Exhibited at Paris in 1900 (Earle via Christie's).
rows.what_it_tells: Signature of a Meiji bronze-caster who exhibited at Paris, 1900.
rows.cautions: The carp vase is identified with the Paris 1900 piece by subject only.

facts.text: Carp vase 'signed on the base in cast characters Ryoun'; Takahashi Ryoun exhibited a vase of this subject at Paris 1900.
facts.quote: signed on the base in cast characters Ryoun

facts.text: Another source differs: The Japanese periodical writes the maker 高橋龍雲, not 高橋凌雲.
Another source gives the chars as 龍雲.

rows.meaning: Carved by Kashima Ippu
rows.where_on_object: near the foot
rows.date_note: Late Meiji.
rows.what_it_tells: Tokyo (Edo-school) nunome inlay, distinct from Kyoto Komai.
rows.cautions: 'Ippu Koku' means 'carved by Ippu'; the casting could be someone else's. The characters 鹿島一布刻 are reconstructed from 'Ippu Koku'; the long form 鹿島一布齊楽則 comes from the Cefiro text.

facts.text: Vase 'signed near the foot in incised characters Ippu Koku with a seal Mitsu'; the long signature 鹿島一布齊楽則 and a kaō appear on a box.

rows.chars: 打物 彫刻 象嵌
rows.romaji: inset-tablet signature naming hammerer, sculptor and inlayer
rows.romaji_plain: inset tablet signature uchimono choko zogan
rows.meaning: Several craftsmen named by trade on one inset plate

maker.name: Kurokawa Eisho, Kamijo Kazutoshi, Kashima Ippu (plus 'Sawada sei' seal)

rows.where_on_object: inset tablet
rows.date_note: Late Meiji (Christie's 2012).
rows.what_it_tells: Big exhibition vases name each trade: hammer worker, sculptor, inlayer; the seal names the firm.
rows.cautions: Single example; the source does not give the Japanese wording of the tablet.

facts.text: Signed on an inset tablet: uchimono Kurokawa Eisho, choko Kamijo Kazutoshi, zogan Kashima Ippu, and sealed 'Sawada sei' (Christie's, May 2012).

rows.meaning: Pure silver (a maker's claim of quality)
rows.device: two characters, often in a small cartouche beside the maker's name
wares: Meiji and Taisho export silver (tea sets, bowls, cigarette cases)
rows.where_on_object: base or rim, beside the maker's mark
rows.date_note: Dealers and 925-1000 sources say mainly Meiji and shortly after; no official source dates it.
rows.what_it_tells: The workshop's own statement that the silver is high grade. It is not a government assay.
rows.cautions: Not a hallmark: it is a trade claim, and the actual fineness is often 950 (a dealer's assertion) but varies; test the metal. The Mint hallmark began only in 1929 and is voluntary.

facts.text: Konoike's standard silver marks are 鴻池造 / 純銀 and 鴻池 / 純銀 (made by Konoike; pure silver).
A 1936 Miyamoto Shoko silver centrepiece carries a 'four-character maker's mark' and a 'two-character Jungin mark'.
Today's industry guideline allows 純銀 only for 999‰ or more; the Meiji and Taisho 純銀 on Konoike or Miyamoto silver is the maker's claim and should not be read against that rule.

rows.meaning: Made by Konoike
rows.where_on_object: beside 純銀
rows.date_note: The forum gives 1890 as the workshop's founding; mark years are not stated.
rows.what_it_tells: A Yokohama silver workshop; with 純銀 beneath.
rows.cautions: The characters and the founding year come only from a forum. No source supports a 'K' initial. Dealers write 'Y. Konoike, Yokohama'.

facts.text: Yokohama workshop founded 1890, specialised in silverware; standard marks 鴻池造 / 純銀 and 鴻池 / 純銀; three label variants.

rows.meaning: Made by Miyamoto
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: The firm was founded in 1880 (forum); the years of the mark are not stated.
rows.what_it_tells: A Tokyo silversmith-retailer still trading; marked 宮本製 plus 純銀 on export-era pieces.
rows.cautions: Liang Yi describes a 'four-character maker's mark' on the 1936 piece, which suggests a longer form (perhaps 宮本商行) than 宮本製; the characters are not transcribed.

facts.text: Founded 1880 by Miyamoto Masaru; moved to Ginza 1899; mark variations include 宮本製 (made by Miyamoto).
A 1936 Miyamoto Shoko centrepiece has a four-character maker's mark and a two-character jungin mark.

rows.meaning: Retailer's name, place and the word 'sterling'

maker.name: Arthur & Bond
maker.place: Yokohama (38 Water Street; branches Kobe, London)

wares: silver tea services, punch bowls, the Liscum Bowl
rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: An English firm of the Meiji period; Bonhams dates the service late Meiji/Taisho; one source says the firm did not survive the 1923 earthquake (no second source confirms this).
rows.what_it_tells: English-owned retailer that designed silver executed by Japanese silversmiths. The English words are for Western buyers.
rows.cautions: 'Sterling' here is the retailer's own claim, and Japanese-made silver from the firm can also lack any mark. The McMullen bowl is dated c. 1890; the Liscum Bowl is 1900 or 1902 depending on the page.

facts.text: A dragon tea and coffee set 'marked Arthur and Bond, Yokohama, sterling' (Bonhams).
facts.quote: marked Arthur and Bond, Yokohama, sterling

facts.text: English purveyors in Yokohama; silver designed by them and executed by Japanese artists; Liscum Bowl.
facts.quote: designed and had executed by Japanese artists

facts.text: Arthur & Bond opened in Yokohama in 1889 and became a partnership in 1890; their shop stood next to Kuhn & Komor on Water Street.
facts.quote: opened his art dealer's shop in Yokohama in 1889

rows.meaning: Retailer's name and 'sterling'

maker.name: Kuhn & Komor
maker.place: Yokohama; branches Kobe, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore

rows.where_on_object: base
rows.date_note: Kuhn & Komor was founded in 1894 (Wikipedia, as a cross-check only). The Wikipedia article gives the Kuhn business in Yokohama from 1869 and a closure around 1936; these dates are not independently confirmed.
rows.what_it_tells: Another foreign Yokohama retailer; with Japanese marks on some pieces.
rows.cautions: The sources for the stamp are sales listings. The founding year differs between 1869 (Kuhn & Co.) and 1894 (Kuhn & Komor).

facts.text: Listings describe Japanese marks and 'Kuhn & Komor / Sterling' on Meiji silver.

Another source differs: Date range: the Yokohama company traded until 1923 under Julius Kuhn and the shop was probably destroyed in the 1923 earthquake; Komor & Komor was the Hong Kong successor name from 1916. The record's 1936 end (from Wikipedia) is not supported here.
The Yokohama shop Kuhn & Komor was founded in 1894 at 37 Water Street by Siegfried Komor and Arthur Kuhn; the earlier Kuhn & Co dated from about 1869 (M. M. Kuhn).
facts.quote: The original shop in Yokohama was founded in 1894

rows.meaning: Samurai Shokai (curio dealer), Yokohama

maker.name: 侍商会 Samurai Shōkai (Nomura Yōzō 野村洋三)

rows.where_on_object: object or box
rows.date_note: Founded 1894 or 1895 (Japan Today, 1910, says 'fifteen years ago'); burned in 1923.
rows.what_it_tells: A leading Japanese-owned Yokohama curio dealer that financed craftsmen.
rows.cautions: The mark's form is known only from the phrase 'signed Samurai Shokai, Yokohama' on dragon cups and a box; no characters or silver standard are recorded. The characters 野村洋三 for Nomura are reconstructed from the romanised 'Yozo Nomura'.

facts.text: Dragon cups and a box 'signed Samurai Shokai, Yokohama'; the dealer supported silversmiths and lacquer artists.

rows.chars: 日の丸 + ひし形に品位 (例 925)
rows.romaji: Hinomaru and lozenge with fineness number
rows.romaji_plain: Hinomaru and lozenge with fineness number
rows.meaning: Assayed by the Japan Mint (造幣局): flag device plus a lozenge holding the fineness in thousandths
rows.device: the Japanese flag (日の丸) with a lozenge (ひし形) containing the fineness figure, for silver e.g. 925
rows.where_on_object: on the article
rows.date_note: Hallmarking began in 昭和4 (1929) with the Mint's Tokyo branch; the Mint describes the current flag-and-lozenge design, but the 1929 design is not recorded.
rows.what_it_tells: A 1929-or-later article assayed by the Mint to the stated fineness. The hallmark is voluntary: most Japanese silver carries only the maker's mark.
rows.cautions: The early (1929) mark may have looked different; this is not established. Absence of the hallmark means nothing. Silver has five grades, but the Mint's page gives the numbers as images, so the full list is not given here.

facts.text: The Mint hallmark is the Japanese flag plus a lozenge with the fineness number, 925 for sterling.
Mint began 品位証明 (hallmarking) of precious-metal products in 昭和4 (1929).
facts.quote: 昭和4年 ... 貴金属製品の品位証明

rows.meaning: Pure metal marked 999 instead of 1000
rows.where_on_object: on the article
rows.date_note: From April 2012 (平成24年4月) 999 replaced 1000; older marks stay valid.
rows.what_it_tells: Marked 999 (or older 1000) means pure metal; the mark appears with the flag and lozenge. A piece marked 999 is from 2012 or later.
rows.cautions: Gold 917 became 916 and 417 became 416; grades 835, 625 and 500 were withdrawn from April 2012.

facts.text: From April 2012 new marks follow ISO 9202 / JIS H6309; pure metal is marked 999; this is the same fineness as the earlier 1000.
facts.quote: 純金属の表示を「９９９」と表示する

rows.kana: じゅうろくやえおもてぎく
rows.meaning: The sixteen-petal double-layer front-facing chrysanthemum: the Imperial House's crest (菊花紋章, 菊の御紋)
rows.device: A chrysanthemum seen from the front with sixteen petals in a front row and a second row of sixteen petal tips showing between them (thirty-two petal edges in all), around a small central disc
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: front, lid, centre of a plate or cup, box lid or cartouche; on gifts, often on the object and its box
rows.date_note: The sixteen-petal form was barred to princely houses in 1869 (Meiji 2), so in practice it was reserved for the emperor; by custom it dates to the Kamakura period (Go-Toba, 1180-1239), a 1926 ordinance fixed it in law, it was abolished in 1947, and it is still used by custom.
rows.what_it_tells: On an object it says only that someone wanted to evoke, or was authorised to carry, the Imperial House's crest. Genuine imperial use means gifts, commissions and furnishings of the Imperial Household, or military and state items bearing the official form. The crest is then a clue to an official channel (a gift, a household order, a government commission), never proof by itself.
rows.cautions: Do not read 'chrysanthemum' as 'imperial'. Count the petals and the rows: sixteen front petals plus a second row is the emperor's, while a single row, a 14-petal flower or a reverse (calyx) chrysanthemum is a different crest (princes, branch houses, temples, or just decoration). Before 1868 the chrysanthemum was unrestricted and spread to commoners, confectionery and Buddhist fittings. Variant chrysanthemums also occur on court (kinri) porcelain made for the court and nobility. Meiji-era export pieces and gifts to foreign visitors carry the crest, so a chrysanthemum on an export-style piece may be an official gift or only decoration. Imperial gifts are documented by an Imperial Household or donor record, not by the crest.

facts.text: By custom the thirty-two-petal double-layer chrysanthemum (十六葉八重表菊) became the imperial crest in the Kamakura period; Retired Emperor Go-Toba (1180-1239) favoured the flower and used it as a personal emblem.

The Imperial Household Ordinance of 1926 (皇室儀制令, Taishō 15, Imperial Household Ordinance No. 7), Art. 12, made the sixteen-petal double-layer front chrysanthemum the crest of the emperor, empress, dowagers, crown prince and crown princess and their grandchildren and spouses; it was abolished in 1947.

Objects bearing the imperial crest were presented to foreign dignitaries: the Met's cloisonne presentation vases (about 1906) carry a gold-wire chrysanthemum of thirty-two petals, and the 1918 silver vase at Philadelphia was commissioned by the imperial household for the crown prince to give to guests before his trip to England.

rows.kana: じゅうよんようひとえうらぎく
rows.meaning: The fourteen-petal single-row reverse chrysanthemum: model crest of imperial princes and princesses
rows.device: A chrysanthemum seen from the back (the calyx side, with the sepal points showing between the petals): fourteen petals in a single row; sixteen-petal single-row reverse forms (十六葉一重裏菊) also occur in princely houses
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: as for the imperial crest
rows.date_note: The crest was set as the model princely crest by Meiji 4 Dajōkan No. 286 (1871) and written into the 1926 ordinance, Article 13. The ordinance was abolished in 1947.
rows.what_it_tells: A 14-petal or single-row chrysanthemum points at a prince's household or a branch house, a political or corporate emblem, or a decorative flower, not at the emperor. Objects of a princely household (gifts, trousseau, tableware) can carry it.
rows.cautions: This is the form most often confused with the imperial crest. Different princely houses altered it: Arisugawa and Fushimi used reverse forms with additions, and Chichibu, Mikasa and Kuni used a reduced double-row front chrysanthemum, which is the easiest to mistake for the emperor's. The Liberal Democratic Party's emblem also sits inside a 14-petal shadow chrysanthemum. Do not attribute a chrysanthemum to a prince without the household's record.

facts.text: Individual houses differed: Arisugawa and Fushimi houses used 14- or 16-petal single reverse forms with additions; Chichibu, Mikasa and Kuni houses used a smaller fourteen-petal double-row front form.

The Reikanji survey of court porcelain included three-layered chrysanthemum crests said to be used by some monzeki (imperial-descended abbots). Of 62 porcelains with imperial crests surveyed, 29 carried variant chrysanthemums.
Another source differs: Nipponica (菊模様) dates the setting of 十六弁八重表菊 for the imperial house and 十四弁一重裏菊 for princes to 1869 (Meiji 2), not 1871.
facts.quote: 1869年（明治2）、「十六弁八重表菊」は皇室

facts.text: Another source differs: Heibonsha (キク) says the chrysanthemum was fixed as the imperial crest by a Dajōkan notice of January 1868 (Meiji 1), and that use outside the imperial house was clearly prohibited in 1871 (Meiji 4).
facts.quote: 明確に禁止したのは1871年（明治4）

facts.text: Heibonsha dates the explicit ban on chrysanthemum crests outside the imperial house to 1871 (Meiji 4), agreeing with the Meiji 4 decrees; Nipponica instead gives 1869 for the crest designation.

rows.meaning: The five-seven-five paulownia: the Japanese government's crest (prime minister, cabinet) and the Imperial House's old private crest
rows.device: Paulownia leaves below with a three-spike flower head above; the blossoms are counted five, seven and five (the centre spike carries seven)
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: lid, centre of a plate, cup, box, coin
rows.date_note: The Imperial House used it from the 16th century or earlier and gave it as a gift to the Ashikaga, Oda and Toyotomi; it was taken as the government emblem from the Meiji period (the 1872 court dress rules put it on the coats of senior officials).
rows.what_it_tells: The government form points to an official or state link (prime minister's cabinet, ministries, presentation cups, coins) or to a Toyotomi-style 'power' crest. On a Momoyama piece it may mean a family granted the crest by Toyotomi, or one imitating Toyotomi.
rows.cautions: Paulownia was also the personal crest of dozens of families and was free to all from 1884 (public notice). The five-three form is by far the commonest family version. Count the flower spikes before reading 'government'.

facts.text: The paulownia is also a crest of Japan's imperial family, less known than the chrysanthemum (Redfern, citing Nukada 1996).
Meiji-era tableware for the emperor was made with a gilt paulownia crest by Seiji Kaisha (Fukagawa), so the paulownia is also found on Meiji imperial-household porcelain.
Nukada Iwao's book 『桐と菊』 (1996) is the standard Japanese study of the two imperial crests.

rows.meaning: The three-five-three paulownia: the commonest paulownia crest
rows.device: Paulownia leaves below with a three-spike flower head above; the blossoms are counted three, five and three (the centre spike carries five)
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: as for other crests
rows.date_note: Commoners and daimyo widely used it from the Edo period, and it was free for all after the 1884 notice.
rows.what_it_tells: A family crest of one of thousands of families, or a stock decorative paulownia. Without a named family and a pedigree it tells nothing of ownership.
rows.cautions: It is often described as the Toyotomi crest, but Hideyoshi's own variants (太閤桐) are the five-three and five-seven forms with specific leaf and spike drawing. Plain 五三桐 on a modern piece is usually decoration.

facts.text: Nipponica names the paulownia first among plant crests in actual use.

rows.meaning: Taikō (Toyotomi Hideyoshi) paulownia: the paulownia crest as drawn for Hideyoshi
rows.device: A paulownia whose leaves and flower spikes are drawn with Hideyoshi's particular forms (several five-three and five-seven variants); on the Toyotomi mon paired with the chrysanthemum on his robes
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: robe, lacquer, metalwork
rows.date_note: Tied to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's era (Momoyama); use of the design continued afterwards on Toyotomi-related shrines, objects and copies.
rows.what_it_tells: A Momoyama-style paulownia on lacquer (Kōdaiji maki-e), robes or metalwork points to Toyotomi circles or later homage, such as Toyotomi shrines (Toyokuni).
rows.cautions: 'Hideyoshi paulownia' is a name for a group of designs, not one fixed drawing. The Met's portable chest with paulownia crests is tied by its catalogue to the family crest of Hideyoshi, but a paulownia on a chest does not by itself date it to the 1590s. Later Edo and Meiji pieces copy the motif.

facts.text: Taikō-giri is the collective name for the five-seven and five-three paulownia variants used by Toyotomi Hideyoshi; the crest passed from the throne to Ashikaga, Oda and Hideyoshi.
An Osaka city education-board document says the paulownia and the chrysanthemum were given to Hideyoshi by the emperor and that he limited their use to loyal daimyo.
A Hideyoshi-era robe at Hōkoku Shrine (ICP) shows one paulownia and two chrysanthemums in a triple arrangement, received by Katagiri Sadataka from Hideyoshi.
facts.quote: 桐一つと菊花二つを三つ盛りふうに刺繍し

rows.meaning: A combined chrysanthemum-and-paulownia crest (two chrysanthemums and one paulownia) of Toyotomi robes
rows.device: Three crests placed as a triple cluster: one paulownia blossom group and two chrysanthemum blossoms
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: robe chest and back
rows.date_note: The one dated record says only that the robe is Momoyama, with a 1775 box inscription.
rows.what_it_tells: Marks a robe or object that came to a house from Hideyoshi himself (as with the Katagiri family); it records a gift, not the maker.
rows.cautions: Chrysanthemum plus paulownia also appears on later gifts, on Meiji state porcelain and on decorative export pieces; the combination alone does not prove Toyotomi origin. The Met's ca. 1596 ewer with chrysanthemum and paulownia crests in alternating fields is a Momoyama example.

facts.text: A sayagata-pattern jacket (dōfuku) at Hōkoku Shrine has five crests, each one paulownia and two chrysanthemum blossoms in a three-blossom cluster, embroidered; a 1775 box inscription says Katagiri Sadataka (1560-1627) received it from Hideyoshi. Designated Important Cultural Property 1989.
facts.quote: 桐一つと菊花二つを三つ盛りふうに刺繍し

facts.text: The Met's ca. 1596 wine ewer is decorated with chrysanthemum and paulownia crests in alternating fields.

rows.meaning: The red sun disc on white: Japan's national flag (日章旗); used as a flag mark
rows.device: A plain red disc on a white ground, disc at the centre (7:10 flag, disc nearer the hoist in the 1870 rule; 2:3, centred, from 1999)
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: flags, cloth
rows.date_note: The 1854 shogunate ship mark (日本総船印); 1870 Dajōkan Proclamation No. 57 made it the 御国旗 for ships; the 1999 act fixed the flag in law.
rows.what_it_tells: On a printed cloth, flag, patriotic souvenir or medal it points to national or military sentiment; it is a state emblem, not a maker's or owner's mark.
rows.cautions: Common on Meiji-Shōwa souvenirs (kimono lining, scrolls, lacquer, prints). A Hinomaru on a yosegaki flag or blanket is personal and military, not official, and does not date the piece by itself.

facts.text: The 1854 shogunate notice made a white banner with a red disc the 'Japan general ship mark' (日本総船印); Meiji 3 (1870) Dajōkan Proclamation No. 57 called it the national flag (御国旗) for merchant ships (ratio 7:10); the 1999 flag-and-anthem law fixed 2:3 with the disc three-fifths of the height.
facts.quote: 日本国総船印は白地日の丸幟相用い候

facts.text: Another source differs: Nipponica says the 1854 decision followed the opinion of Shimazu Nariakira; Heibonsha (旧版, 日本総船印) says the shogunate was pushed into it in July by Tokugawa Nariaki.
facts.quote: 島津斉彬(なりあきら)らの意見をいれ

rows.meaning: The rising-sun flag: sun disc with sixteen rays; the Army's flag from 1870 and the Navy's from 1889
rows.device: A red sun disc (off-centre in the Navy ensign) with sixteen red rays on a white field
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: flags, medals, cloth
rows.date_note: Army 16-ray flag 1870 (Meiji 3, Dajōkan 6/13); Army regimental colour 1879; Navy ensign 1889; SDF versions from 1954.
rows.what_it_tells: On a military object (Army/Navy medal, sake cup, cloth, badge) it marks the armed forces of the period; with a chrysanthemum finial it belongs to a regimental colour.
rows.cautions: The sixteen rays echo the sixteen petals of the chrysanthemum crest; it is a flag design, not an imperial crest. Postwar and tourist items use it freely.

facts.text: The Army adopted a sixteen-ray rising-sun flag in 1870 (first use at a review on 17 April, formalised by proclamation on 13 June); the sixteen rays match the sixteen petals of the imperial crest; the Navy's ensign followed in 1889.

rows.meaning: A gift sake cup with the paulownia crest, given by the throne or government
rows.device: A shallow cup (sakazuki) with a paulownia crest
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: inside or outside the cup
rows.date_note: The Edo-Tokyo Museum holds one catalogued as 19th-20th century. A summary of another record dates a paulownia cup to Meiji 28 (1895), given in the Sino-Japanese War.
rows.what_it_tells: A crested cup of this kind was received from the imperial house or a ministry as a reward (military service, exhibition, public work); the paperwork or its box would say for what. The paulownia or chrysanthemum shows the channel, not the occasion.
rows.cautions: Commemorative cups are mass produced for veterans' groups and can bear the crest too, so look for an inscription, a box and a record of the award. The Met's imperial-gift items were presented to foreign visitors, while the Edo-Tokyo cup is domestic.

facts.text: The Edo-Tokyo Museum holds a 'gift sake cup with paulownia crest' (桐紋賜盃), 9.2 x 3.3 cm, catalogued as 19th-20th century; the record gives no further description.
A summary of another Edo-Tokyo Museum record describes a paulownia-crest cup given in the Sino-Japanese War, Meiji 28 (1895); only the summary was seen, not the full record.

rows.meaning: Three hollyhock (aoi) leaves: the crest of the Tokugawa shoguns, usually in a ring (丸に三つ葉葵)
rows.device: Three heart-shaped aoi leaves meeting at the centre, their stalks radiating, usually inside a circle
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: lacquer, armour, vessels, banners, palanquins
rows.date_note: The Tokugawa crest of the Edo period; the haori at the Tokugawa Art Museum is catalogued as Momoyama (dated 1601-1700 in the museum record). The Tokugawa houses and linked shrines have used it ever since.
rows.what_it_tells: On lacquer, armour or porcelain it names the Tokugawa house or a branch (see Kishū, Owari, Aizu rows); a real Tokugawa object has a documented provenance.
rows.cautions: Heavily copied on tourist goods since the Meiji period and used by shrines and temples. A hollyhock on an export piece is not a Tokugawa commission. Three-leaf hollyhock was also borne by many Matsudaira families and by shrines and temples with Tokugawa links.

facts.text: A Tokugawa Art Museum haori (Important Cultural Property) has five three-leaf hollyhock crests (両胸、両後袖、背中の五か所) in tsujigahana, said to have been Tokugawa Ieyasu's and passed to Yoshinao of Owari.
facts.quote: 両胸、両後袖、背中の五か所に三つ葉葵紋を置く

facts.text: 丸に三つ葵 is the crest of the Tokugawa shogun house and the Matsudaira clan, and of shrines and temples with Tokugawa links.
facts.quote: 丸に三つ葵：徳川将軍家、松平氏

facts.text: In the Edo period the shogunate strictly restricted the use of the three-leaf hollyhock, unlike the chrysanthemum.
A Walters Art Museum incense burner is catalogued as having the Tokugawa family crest (aoi mon).

rows.meaning: A cross in a circle: the Shimazu (Satsuma) crest
rows.device: A plain upright cross (arms of equal length) inside a ring
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: base or reserve panel; also lacquer lids
rows.date_note: The Shimazu house crest; the sources do not say when it was adopted.
rows.what_it_tells: On Satsuma ware, lacquer or armour it can show Shimazu patronage or merely 'Satsuma'. A genuine Shimazu object comes with a provenance and a high-quality body.
rows.cautions: The circled cross is the single most common mark on export 'Satsuma' of the Meiji period and later, a decoration or a brand cue rather than a commission by the Shimazu. A collector's reference notes it is on many but far from all Satsuma wares, and that it proves neither date nor kiln. It is not a Christian cross.

facts.text: A black-lacquer letter box with a maru ni jūji crest in maki-e on the lid is recorded among the Miyakonojō Shimazu family papers (National Diet Library record).
Collector sources say the circled cross is a widely used Satsuma signifier on export wares and that the mon alone does not prove a piece genuine or date it.

rows.meaning: The Nabeshima house crest (a harness-ornament leaf, 杏葉)
rows.device: A leaf-like harness ornament with a ribbed (筋) leaf for the main house's 筋杏葉 and a flower-form 花杏葉 with a half-round stamen at the centre for women's furnishings and branch houses; often 'held' (抱き) in pairs
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: lid or body of lacquer; in relief on a porcelain body
rows.date_note: Saga (Nabeshima) domain lacquer is Edo-period (a 19th-century example), and the family still used the crest in 1923 (tea set).
rows.what_it_tells: On Saga-domain lacquer or porcelain, it shows Nabeshima family ownership. The rib type helps: 筋杏葉 is used only by the main house; 花杏葉 by branch houses and on women's furnishings.
rows.cautions: Nabeshima ware as a class is a domain kiln for gifts to the shogunate and daimyo. The family crest appears on special commissions (Fukagawa 1923 tea set), but the sources do not say that export-era Nabeshima wares bear one. Modern 'Nabeshima style' copies add crests. The lacquer example is Edo-period.

facts.text: A black lacquer rice container with 花杏葉紋 (Nabeshima Hōkōkai, 19th c.): the 花杏葉 has a half-round stamen at the centre and was used on women's furnishings and as branch houses' regular crest; the 筋杏葉 with dense vertical lines was used only by the main house as its fixed crest.
facts.quote: 本家のみが定紋として用いた

facts.text: A Fukagawa Seiji tea set of 1923 for the 12th Marquis Nabeshima carries the 杏葉 crest in relief.
A crest list gives 鍋島筋杏葉 (抱き筋杏葉) as the main Nabeshima house's crest.
facts.quote: 鍋島筋杏葉（抱き筋杏葉）：鍋島宗家

rows.meaning: Nine stars: one centre circle with eight around it; the Hosokawa 'separated' form is 細川九曜
rows.device: Nine round discs: a larger central disc ringed by eight; in the Hosokawa form the nine discs are separate and not touching
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: armour, norimono panels, lacquer, flags
rows.date_note: Hosokawa tradition says Tadaoki received it from Oda Nobunaga; the Hosokawa changed to the separated form after 1747.
rows.what_it_tells: On armour, palanquins or textiles, it points to Hosokawa (Kumamoto) or to one of the other houses using nine stars. It is the star-worship crest of many families.
rows.cautions: A circled nine-star crest is borne by dozens of families, including the Date, Sōma, Toda, Aoyama and others; the separated drawing is the Hosokawa form. Do not attribute on the drawing alone.

facts.text: The nine-star crest has one central star ringed by eight; it comes from the nine luminaries (sun, moon, five planets, two nodes). Users include Hosokawa, Date, Sōma, Toda, Aoyama, Chiba and Kiso. The Hosokawa changed their design to the separated 離れ九曜 after the 1747 killing of Hosokawa Munetaka.
facts.quote: 中央の星を八星が囲む九曜紋

facts.text: Eisei Bunko (the Hosokawa museum) held a 2024 exhibition on the nine-star crest on armour, textiles and furnishings; the Hosokawa tradition says Tadaoki received it from Oda Nobunaga.

rows.meaning: Bamboo and sparrows: the Date crest (仙台笹), derived from the Uesugi crest
rows.device: Bamboo-grass leaves arranged around a ring (竹輪) with a pair of facing sparrows in the centre
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: lacquer, armour, palanquins
rows.date_note: The crest was given by Uesugi Sadazane to Date Sanemoto (the source gives no date); the Date main house later used it.
rows.what_it_tells: On Sendai- or Uwajima-domain objects it names the Date family. Uwajima Date used a different bundle form (宇和島笹).
rows.cautions: The sparrow-and-bamboo design is also a Uesugi, Kajūji-court and many other families' crest; it is an ordinary decorative motif too. The sparrow count and arrangement matter.

facts.text: Takahashi Akemi, 「伊達家の家紋に関する一考察」 (Sendai City Museum research report 19, 1999), is a study of the Date crests.

rows.kana: いちもんじにみつぼし
rows.meaning: A horizontal bar over three discs: the Mōri crest (with 沢瀉 as the other)
rows.device: A short horizontal bar over three round discs (stars)
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: armour, lacquer, architecture
rows.date_note: Mōri house crest; adoption date not established.
rows.what_it_tells: On Mōri objects (Chōshū, Hagi) it names the Mōri house; often paired with the 沢瀉 crest.
rows.cautions: Ichimonji-mitsuboshi is a family crest also borne by other families; check with the maker's mark or documents.

facts.text: The old Mōri main residence displays two crests throughout (一文字三星紋 and 澤瀉紋), e.g. on lamps and sliding-door pulls.
facts.quote: 一文字三星紋と澤瀉紋

rows.meaning: The Oda family's quince-blossom crest (織田木瓜), a five-section quince
rows.device: A quince-blossom (cucumber-cross-section) of five lobes in a ring; Oda's has five lobes (五つ木瓜), within a thick border
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: armour, banners
rows.date_note: Oda Nobunaga's era (16th c.) and after.
rows.what_it_tells: On armour, banners or later Oda family objects it names the Oda; the Oda also used the Eiraku coin crest (永楽銭).
rows.cautions: Mokkō is one of the ten most common family crests (Hotta, Itō, Arima and many more). A quince crest does not mean Oda.

facts.text: Oda Nobunaga, Hotta and Itō families used the mokkō crest.

rows.meaning: The Ii family's mandarin-orange (tachibana) crest, Hikone domain
rows.device: A tachibana (citrus) bough: three leaves and a fruit set in a ring in the 'Ii tachibana' drawing (井伊橘)
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: armour, banners
rows.date_note: Ii family; Hikone domain 1600-1871.
rows.what_it_tells: On Hikone-castle objects or Ii armour it names the Ii house. Tachibana is also a major family crest.
rows.cautions: Tachibana is one of the ten common crests; the Ii drawing (丸に変わり橘) differs from the plain one.

facts.text: 丸に変わり橘 (井伊橘) is the crest of the Count Ii family; 彦根橘 is a Shiga-prefecture derivative.
facts.quote: 丸に変わり橘（井伊橘）：伯爵井伊家

facts.text: The Hikone Castle Museum holds 25 armours made for Ii lords and kin; according to a tourism-board text, those bearing the family crest are finished in red lacquer.

rows.meaning: Tachibana (wild mandarin) crest (one of the ten commonest family crests)
rows.device: A citrus bough with leaves and a fruit, usually in a ring
rows.technique: crest (mon) as painted, lacquered, cast, woven or embroidered
rows.where_on_object: lacquer lid, kimono, ceramics, metalwork, banners
rows.date_note: Used as carriage crests in the Heian period, as family crests widely from the Kamakura period, and by commoners in the Edo period; still used today.
rows.what_it_tells: A Tachibana crest tells you only the motif, which thousands of families share. Find the family from the object's own papers, not from the crest. It is linked with the Tachibana clan and was popular with warrior families; the Ii used it.
rows.cautions: Very many families, shrines and temples share it, and it is also used as plain decoration, so it never establishes provenance. Variants (ring, number, drawing) separate branches in crest books but are not reliable on an object with no record.

facts.text: Tachibana is linked to the Tachibana clan and popular among warrior families; the Ii used it.
Records list 241 general categories and 5,116 individual crests; types include 通紋 (crests shared by many families), 定紋 (the main crest), 替紋 (alternates) and 女紋 (women's lineage crests).

cloisonne: Japan vs China, as the sources I read present them (weak: mostly dealer or collector material; the V&A texts are better): Japanese Meiji pieces use fine silver or brass wire and a silver or shakudō rim, neck ring and base plate, often applied; Meiji grounds are smooth, fine and glassy, with mirror-black and shaded translucent colours; V&A calls dark matt brown counter-enamel typical of Andō. Collector discussion says Chinese pieces more often show a ruyi border and uniform wire; this is a tendency, not a rule.
Meiji to later: V&A cites Namikawa's best period as c.1880-1910 ('golden age' also in Sotheby's); Andō's mark continues to c.1950-60; do not date by the mark alone.
Sōsuke's mark is 魁 (Sakigake), not 濤 or 濤川; Namikawa Yasuyuki's is the four characters 京都並河.
Founder: Kaji Tsunekichi 梶常吉 (born May 1803, died Sep 1883; began research 1833 per Nagoya city). Aichi prefecture dates the start to the Tenpō era.

kamon.topic: Owner's crests on lacquer: trousseau sets (婚礼調度)
kamon.text: Daimyo wedding furnishings were made in maki-e with the family crest scattered over a unified design ('大名婚礼調度'), and lacquer grades were fixed by ground, maki-e technique and design, including 'crest scattered' (家紋散らし) and 'with crest' (家紋付き) classes. The bride's and groom's crests can appear together or alone: the Owari Tokugawa doll furnishings of Sachigimi (11th Owari head's second wife) carry both her natal Konoe 抱牡丹 (embracing peony) crest and the Tokugawa 葵 (aoi) crest, while another Owari bride's set (Noriko-hime, of the Niwa family) was made with her own Niwa 直違 crest, and a set without crests also exists. So the crest on a trousseau piece tells which family commissioned or owned that set, not who made it; check whether it is the bride's house, the groom's, or both. Chiyohime's 1639 set (National Treasure, Tokugawa Reimeikai) is the oldest surviving wedding set in one lot; the national-heritage record does not itself mention a crest.

kamon.topic: Crests on made-to-order porcelain and lacquer (Nabeshima, Arita)
kamon.text: Nabeshima ware was a domain kiln making gifts for the shogunate and daimyo; its clearest marker in the sources read is the comb-pattern foot (櫛目高台) and the three-footed plates, not a crest. The Nabeshima crest 杏葉 shows up on Nabeshima family lacquer (花杏葉 for women's and branch-house furnishings, 筋杏葉 for the main house) and on a 1923 Fukagawa Seiji tea set made for the 12th Marquis with the crest in relief. Arita Meiji-period orders also show crests of Japanese households (a c.1910 Tachibana-family tea set), the opposite of export decoration.

A formal kimono or haori carries one (centre back), three (back and both sleeves) or five (adding both chests) crests; more crests, higher formality. A 'dyed-out' crest (染め紋, white reserve with the crest inked or drawn) outranks an embroidered one (縫い紋). A married woman's formal black tomesode and a man's formal montsuki haori-hakama bear the five-crest form with the wearer's family crest (定紋); some women use their natal line's crest (女紋, mainly Kinki). The crest identifies the family of the wearer or the person who ordered the garment, not the maker.

kamon.topic: Presentation silver, cloisonné and cups: imperial gifts (御下賜品, 恩賜品)
kamon.text: Pieces bearing the imperial chrysanthemum were commissioned by the Imperial Household and given, domestically and to foreign guests: the Met's pair of cloisonné presentation vases (about 1906, Andō Cloisonné Co. with Kawade Shibatarō) carry a 32-petal gold-wire chrysanthemum and the catalogue says such pieces were often presented to foreign dignitaries; Philadelphia's 1918 silver vase with imperial-crest chrysanthemums was commissioned by the household for the crown prince to give to guests before his England trip; Edo-Tokyo Museum holds 'gift' sake cups with a paulownia crest. Andō was named a purveyor (御用達) to the Household in 1900. The crest says the channel (household gift), the paperwork says the occasion.

kamon.topic: Crests as decoration on export wares
kamon.text: Crests were also used purely as decoration or as brand cues on Meiji export goods. The Seiji Kaisha (Fukagawa) service made for the Meiji Emperor was ordered with a paulownia crest and company mark, and Fukagawa's surviving export-style dishes use a chrysanthemum-and-paulownia border, 'the crests of the imperial household', so the motif travelled from court commissions to the maker's wider range. Collector references say the Shimazu circled cross is commonly found on export Satsuma (a signifier, not a commission); one dealer-grade page says a stamped piece of about 1947 was mass produced for servicemen. I found no museum catalogue text that states crests were 'added for Western buyers'; this stays as a collector-level claim (see gaps).

kamon.topic: Rules of thumb: what a crest does and does not tell
kamon.text: 1) A crest names a family, house, shrine, state office or institution; it is not a maker's mark and not a date. 2) The Imperial crest has a precise definition (sixteen-petal, two rows) and princes' forms differ; count petals and rows. 3) Edo-period restrictions applied to the Tokugawa hollyhock (strict) but not to the chrysanthemum, which spread to commoners until the Meiji bans of 1868-71; after 1871 non-imperial chrysanthemum was legally barred (law lapsed 1947), but private decorative use continued. 4) The paulownia was left free in 1884, so a 'government' paulownia on a modern object is not proof of an official channel. 5) Kimono, lacquer and armour carry the owner's crest, hence provenance needs documents, not just the mon. 6) Crests such as katabami, mokko, tachibana, kiri are shared by thousands of families (通紋).

Japanese Wikipedia (cross-check only) counts 241 general categories and 5,116 individual crests; kinds of crest include main (定紋), alternate (替紋), representative (代表紋), commonly shared (通紋), shrine and temple (神紋・寺紋), women's (女紋) and paired couple's crests (比翼紋); crests could be bestowed, taken as rewards, or passed by marriage or adoption. Dictionaries record 家紋 as a family sign, first attested in the Teikin Ōrai (c. 1394-1428).

rows.form: round seal 極 alone (no year or month)
rows.how_to_read: No date can be read from the seal; 極 only tells you the impression is not before 1791 (design may be older) and, for a print made from a block carved after 1842, that it is a later copy or an old block. Date by artist, publisher, series.
rows.ambiguity: None, but also no information beyond the 1791-1842 window.

rows.form: zodiac animal + month numeral in a small seal (rectangular 1806, oval from 1807 per Self), often beside 極; from 1811 to 1814 sometimes with a gyōji name seal
rows.years_note: 1805 乙丑 ox ... 1814 甲戌 dog. Self records an isolated rectangular date seal c.1800 and a kiwame+oval-aratame type 1815-1832; both rare. Stewart reads a 'hare seven' seal as 1807 and says the date-seal habit lapsed after 1814 until c.1850.
rows.how_to_read: Read the animal, take the one year of 1805-1814 that has it (no animal repeats in these ten years), then the month numeral. 閏 before the numeral = intercalary month, which must match the intercalary list (1805 閏8, 1808 閏6, 1811 閏2, 1813 閏11).
rows.ambiguity: An animal repeats every 12 years, so 子 1804 / 1816, 丑 1805 / 1817 etc. Seal shape (small rectangular/oval beside 極) and the 1805-1814 window resolve it; do not apply this table to later seal types. Stewart: Tiger year with Bunkwa-period cypher could be 1806, 1818 or 1830.
rows.confidence: medium: the 1805-1810 core is agreed; the 1811-1814 date-seal use and the exact shapes rest on Self alone

rows.form: rare oval seal with zodiac above 改 below (1815-1832 per Self), or round date seal without month (1824-1829)
rows.years_note: Every animal has two or three candidate years; do not use these rare seals to date a print without other evidence.
rows.how_to_read: Treat as a signal that the seal is unusual; confirm with artist's working years and publisher.
rows.ambiguity: Maximal: each animal gives 2-3 possible years; this type is easy to confuse with the 1853-57 seals (Self via JNC).

rows.form: two round 名主 seals + one small oval seal: animal and month
rows.reads: year (animal) + month, and the nanushi pair gives a second check on the month
rows.how_to_read: Two nanushi seals plus a date seal: 子 = 1852, 丑 = 1853 only. 子 + 閏二 = 1852 intercalary 2nd month. Check the pair: 馬込+濱 = 9th month 1852, 村松+福 = 10th, 村田+衣笠 = 12th, 渡辺+米良 = 3rd month 1853 (all attested in Iwata/Koike).
rows.ambiguity: None inside the period (only two animals occur). A date seal 申 or 酉 beside two nanushi seals would be a recut, a forgery or a catalogue error.

rows.form: round seal 改 (aratame) + separate oval seal with animal + month; they usually sit side by side
rows.how_to_read: 改 seal present and a separate oval date seal: 寅 1854, 卯 1855, 辰 1856, 巳 1857; 丑 only for the last month or two of 1853 (11th-12th month, when the nanushi stopped). 寅閏七 = 1854 intercalary 7th month; 巳閏五 = 1857 intercalary 5th month.
rows.ambiguity: None inside the period (five consecutive animals). Beware: the later 1859-71 seals use the same animals 丑 (1865) 寅 (1866) 卯 (1867) 辰 (1868) 巳 (1869) but with 改 and the date merged into ONE round seal; two separate seals = 1853-57.
rows.confidence: high; the exact month the nanushi seals stopped (11th vs 12th month 1853) is disputed

rows.form: oval date seal (animal + month) alone, no 改
rows.how_to_read: Date seal with no 改 and no nanushi seals: 午 = 1858 (巳 only for the 12th month of 1857).
rows.ambiguity: A date seal with no 改 also occurs 1872-75 (round) and on Meiji recuts; shape and design context separate them.
rows.confidence: high for 1858; start month 12/1857 from Lane via Berlin

rows.form: ONE round seal containing 改 + animal + month (layout varies)
rows.years_note: 未 occurs twice (1859 and 1871); every other animal once. Intercalary months: {'1860': 3, '1862': 8, '1865': 5, '1868': 4, '1870': 10}
rows.how_to_read: Single round seal with 改: take the animal and find it in 1859-1871: 未 1859, 申 1860, 酉 1861, 戌 1862, 亥 1863, 子 1864, 丑 1865, 寅 1866, 卯 1867, 辰 1868, 巳 1869, 午 1870, 未 1871. 閏 in the seal fixes the year: 閏三 = 1860, 閏八 = 1862, 閏五 = 1865, 閏四 = 1868, 閏十 = 1870.
rows.ambiguity: 未 = 1859 or 1871 and 閏 cannot help (neither year has an intercalary month); use the layout (JNC/Self: 改 with month top-left and year right 'most often 1859-63'; 改 left, year top-right, month bottom-right 'most often 1864-71'; unreliable) plus artist and series. Sakai ends the 改+year type in 1867 and calls 1867-1875 'date only'; the Kokugakuin paper reads 改・未十一 on a Meiji 4 (1871) print, so 1871 is safer.
rows.confidence: high for 1859-1866; the 1867-1871 end is disputed (see row)

rows.form: small round seal: animal on the right, month numeral on the left; no 改
rows.how_to_read: 申 = 1872, 酉 = 1873, 戌 = 1874, 亥 = 1875. Meiji 5 (1872) month numbers are still lunar months; from 1 January 1873 (Meiji 6) the Gregorian calendar was in use and Wetherall reads 戌 + 9 on a Tokyo nichinichi nishikie as September 1874.
rows.ambiguity: None (no 閏 after 1870). Same animals recur 1860/61/62/63 in the 改+date period; the missing 改 and round plain form separates them.
rows.confidence: high for 1872 and 1874 months by example; Gregorian-month rule for 1873+ rests on one worked example (Wetherall) plus the calendar reform

rows.form: circular 御届 stamp with 明治 N 年 / N 月 / N 日, plus printed publisher and artist names and addresses (no seal needed)
rows.reads: Meiji year, month, day the notification was accepted
rows.how_to_read: Meiji year + 1867 = Gregorian year (Meiji 9 = 1876, Meiji 11 = 1878). The stamp is the date the publisher's notice was accepted, not the day of printing.
rows.ambiguity: Early date only; later impressions keep the notice; recuts print new margin text.

rows.form: Large round seal, ワタナベ in white/black halves
rows.what: Print is 1909-1916; last appearance Shunsen's Kamiya Jibei (1916).

rows.form: Small round seal ワタナベ
rows.size: 6-7 mm (6.5 mm typical 1920s-40s; 7 mm standard from 1989)
rows.what: Does not date a print by diameter or kana variant. A prewar design bearing only this seal (no oblong copyright seal) is a postwar printing; many prints printed in the 1930s-40s were sealed after the war.
rows.note: Pachter's 'earlier = smaller' claim is rejected by Moku-Hanga (Watanabe Shoichiro, Shimizu Hisao).

rows.form: Oblong margin copyright seal 版権所有渡邊庄三郎 (types A1, A2)
rows.what: Prewar print of the later 1920s-30; round seal rare while oblong seal used.
rows.note: Start disputed: 1924 (Pachter via Oregon), 1925 (Shimizu via Egenolf), 1926 (Moku-Hanga), c.1927 (Scholten). A1 not seen after 1933.

rows.form: 版元渡邊版画店 (type B)
'Sausage' seal, copyright (C1, C2)
rows.note: One dealer lists a c.1924 Kozu, Osaka with a sausage seal - unresolved.

rows.form: Watanabe mon + copyright/no-copying wording (D)
rows.what: Prewar; most at risk of imitation by later Doi/other reissues.

rows.form: 'Published by Watanabe in Ginza' (E), 'designed by Watanabe in Ginza' (F), 'designed by Watanabe' (G)
Printer's seal Ono Gintarō (P1, P2)
Postwar round seal (Pachter design A, 6 mm) without oblong seal
rows.what: Postwar printing; a print dated 1931 in the design with a 6 mm round seal is a later edition 1945-1957 (hanga.com note).

rows.form: Type H, 'copyright Watanabe Tadasu' (Pachter design L)
Heisei seal, red, hiragana (I)
rows.what: Printing from older, often partly recarved blocks.

rows.form: Seal J, 'copyright Watanabe Shoichiro' 版権所有渡辺章一郞
Reiwa seals (K1 black without publisher seal; K2 with)
Verso address labels L1-L4
General cautions
rows.what: Seals show when a print was sold, not when printed; forged prewar seals A-G exist; two seals together deserve suspicion; Watanabe seals on a print originally by another publisher (e.g. Doi) are to be disregarded.
