calendar_change.summary: Japan used a lunisolar calendar until the end of 明治5年12月2日 = 1872-12-31. The next day, 明治5年12月3日, was declared 明治6年1月1日 = 1873-01-01 and the Gregorian calendar has been used since. So every date written before 1873 follows the lunar year; only dates from 明治6年 are Gregorian.

facts.text: The calendar reform was announced on 明治5年(1872)11月9日; 明治5年12月3日 became 明治6年1月1日, so 明治5年12月 had only two days (1872-12-30 and -31).
facts.quote: 明治五年十二月三日を明治6年1月1日とし

facts.text: The lunisolar calendar in use in the last decades was the 天保暦 (Tenpō calendar), in force from 弘化元年 (1844); before it came 寛政暦 (1798), 宝暦 (1755) and 貞享暦 (1685).
A lunar year has 12 months of 29 or 30 days (about 354 days), so about every third year a 13th, intercalary month (閏月, うるう月) is inserted; 7 intercalary months per 19 years.

Because the lunar New Year falls in late January to mid-February, the 11th and 12th lunar months (and sometimes the 閏 month) of lunar year Y fall in December Y to February Y+1. Era sources count such a date in lunar year Y: 文政13年12月10日 = 1831-01-23 (this is 天保元年, counted as 1830); 嘉永7年11月27日 = 1855-01-15 (counted as 1854); 天保15年12月2日 = 1845-01-09 (counted as 1844).
facts.quote: 文政13年（1830）12月10日天保と改元

facts.text: Rule of thumb for an object dated before 1873: Western year = year1 + n − 1 for months 1–10, and the Gregorian date of months 11–12 (and 閏11/閏12) is usually in January–February of the following Western year. A museum that writes "1850" for "嘉永3年12月" would be about one month off from a strict conversion: the date lies in January/February 1851.

The Western year labels in Nipponica and the NIJL chart are the lunar-year labels, so 嘉永7年11月27日 is printed as "1854". Conversions of day and month to Gregorian dates differ by one calendar year for the last two months.
facts.quote: 嘉永7年（1854）11月27日安政と改元

facts.text: Dates before 15 October 1582 in the era tables are given in the Julian calendar by ja.wikipedia (Julian up to 元亀4年/1573, Gregorian from the end of 天正, 1593); Western museum catalogues normally give only the year.
The era names were not changed by the calendar reform: 明治 continued; only the months and days became solar.

imperial_count.name: 皇紀 (kōki) / 紀元 (kigen) / 神武天皇即位紀元
imperial_count.rule: Kōki year = Western year + 660 (year 1 = 660 BCE, the year of Emperor Jinmu's legendary accession; 辛酉年春正月庚辰朔 = 11 February 660 BCE). So 紀元二千六百年 = 1940 = 昭和15年; 紀元2533 = 1873 = 明治6年; 紀元2600 = 1940.
imperial_count.formula: Western year = kōki − 660; kōki = Western year + 660
imperial_count.used_on_objects: Kōki was fixed as the official count of years by the 太政官布告第342号 of 明治5年11月15日 (1872-12-15) and printed in the first solar almanac of 明治6年. It appears in the 1930s–1940s on official papers and, above all, on souvenirs, books, exhibitions and commemorative items made for the 1940 celebrations (紀元二千六百年). Items marked 紀元二千六百年記念 are not all dated 1940: dated NDL books carrying the phrase were published 1940–1944.

facts.text: The kōki is counted from the accession of Emperor Jinmu; kōki year 1 = 660 BCE. A kōki date is converted by subtracting 660.
facts.quote: 西暦紀元前660年にあたる

facts.text: The count was fixed by 明治5年11月15日 太政官布告第342号 ("神武天皇即位を紀元と定める"); Nihon shoki dates the accession 辛酉年春正月庚辰朔, converted to 11 February 660 BCE (now 建国記念の日).
facts.quote: 神武天皇即位を紀元と定める

facts.text: The first solar calendar (明治6年 = 1873) printed the kōki year, 紀元2533, beside the era year.
The NIJL cross-reference chart prints the kōki for 1873–1945 beside the Western year: 1940 = 昭和15 = 2600; 1880 = 明治13 = 2540.

Edo-Tokyo Museum holds postcards of the 紀元二千六百年奉祝美術展覧会 dated 昭和15年 (1940). NDL holds many books titled "…紀元二千六百年記念" dated 1940–1944 (昭和15–19), so the phrase marks a commemoration, not necessarily the year of making.
facts.quote: 紀元二千六百年奉祝美術展覧会絵葉書

imperial_count.cautions: Commemorative wares, medals, cups and swords with 紀元二千六百年 are 1939–1944, with 1940 the peak; the phrase can also be used on later reproductions. No open museum record of such a ware was found to confirm the pattern on objects (see gaps).

kanshi.formula: For Western year Y: n = ((Y − 4) mod 60) + 1 gives the position in the cycle (1 = 甲子). Equivalently stem = (Y − 4) mod 10 (0 = 甲, 1 = 乙 … 9 = 癸) and branch = (Y − 4) mod 12 (0 = 子 … 11 = 亥). 1984 = 甲子 (n = 1); 1864 = 甲子; 1924 = 甲子. From a written cycle date to a year: find the n of the two characters, then the candidate years are every year with Y mod 60 = (n + 3) mod 60; each 60 years the same name returns. Pick the candidate that falls inside the era (or the object's known period).
kanshi.with_era: An era year is often followed by its cycle name: 天保十三壬寅 = 天保13年 (1842) and 壬寅 is #39 of the cycle (candidates … 1782, 1842, 1902). A cycle name alone gives only a 60-year series of candidates; the era narrows it to one year. The cycle name of a year changes with the lunar year, so for months 11–12 the Western date may lie in January–February of the next Western year.
kanshi.zodiac_alone: A branch animal on its own (e.g. "子" or "寅", or the animal drawn) is only a 12-year pointer; in print date seals the animal plus month stands for the lunar year of the print (covered in the print-date-seal topic). The candidate years of a branch alone are those with (Y − 4) mod 12 equal to its index in the zodiac table.

facts.text: 干支 is the combination of 十干 and 十二支, 60 combinations (六十干支); when the cycle completes it is 還暦. 甲子 reads こうし、かっし or きのえね.
facts.quote: 六十通りあり、六十干支と呼びます

facts.text: Japanese kun readings of the 10 stems: きのえ きのと ひのえ ひのと つちのえ つちのと かのえ かのと みずのえ みずのと; the e/to endings are 兄/弟 (elder/younger brother) — the origin of the word えと.
The cycle table (n, characters, on and kun readings) matches the zodiacal cycle printed in Bowes 1882 (Kinoye-ne, Kinoto-ushi, Hinoye-tora …; Bowes's old transliterations).
1564 is 甲子, 1864 is 甲子, 1924 is 甲子 in the NIJL chart, which fixes the anchor of the formula.
Bowes (1882) notes that a branch animal alone is not a valid year name except in combination with the stem signs, and is "only used by the illiterate".
facts.quote: only used in Japan by the illiterate

extra: 正月 (shōgatsu) is the usual written form for month 1; 初春・孟春 also mean the 1st lunar month.

months.kana: かんなづき／かみなづき

extra: 極月 (ごくげつ／ごくづき) and 臘月 (ろうげつ) are also names for the 12th month; 臘 appears in 臘月八日 (the 8th of the 12th month).

months.numeral: 閏 + month (閏四月, 閏十二月 …)
extra: The intercalary month repeats the name of the month before it: 閏4月 is the second 4th month. About 7 in 19 years had one. Example dates in the tables: 延喜23年閏4月11日 = 923-05-29 (Julian), 元中9年閏10月5日 = 1392-11-19, 朱鳥元年閏12月30日 = 687-02-17.

days.meaning: 1st day of the month (朔 = new moon in the lunar calendar)

days.kana: きちじつ／きちにち／きつじつ
days.meaning: an auspicious day — not a real calendar day; "正月吉日" or "春吉日" means "a lucky day in the 1st month/spring". Cannot be converted to a day.
a good time, a good day (synonym of 吉日)

days.kana: きちじょうにち／きっしょうにち
days.meaning: in onmyōdō a day good for everything; in objects used like 吉日

days.kana: はる なつ あき ふゆ
days.meaning: Season only: lunar spring = months 1–3, summer 4–6, autumn 7–9, winter 10–12 (i.e. about Feb–Apr / May–Jul / Aug–Oct / Nov–Jan in modern terms). A dated inscription 春日 or 孟春 gives month 1 (初春/孟春), 仲春 month 2, 季春 month 3.

numerals.note: Used for the first year of every era. 元年 = year1; the second year is 二年. Not "一年". 明治元年 = 1868, 昭和元年 = 1926.
廿日 = the 20th day; 廿五日 = 25th; 廿一 = 21. Written as a single character in years too (明治廿年 = 明治20年 = 1887).
卅日 = 30th; 明治卅年 = 1897. Same formation as 廿.
Same formation as 廿 and 卅 (the oracle-bone script writes 30 and 40 this way); rare on objects.
Used for the zero in modern kanji numerals: 二〇一九年. Also 零 or ○. 昭和三〇年 = 1955.
拾 is the daiji form of 十, so 二拾 = 20, 三拾 = 30; also 弐拾 in certificates.

numerals.form: 壱 弐 参 肆 伍 陸 漆 捌 玖 拾 (大字)
numerals.reading: いち に さん し ご ろく しち はち く じゅう
numerals.note: 大字 (daiji), used in certificates and forgery-sensitive documents; old forms 壹 貳 參. 佰 = 百, 仟 = 千.
十一 = 11, 十五 = 15 (not 一十五).
Both occur: 二十五年 and 廿五年 are the same.

numerals.form: 一九五〇年 / 千九百五十年
numerals.note: Western years are written in kanji in positional style (一九五〇年) or additive style (千九百五十年). 二千六百年 is a kōki year (1940), not a Western year: check for 紀元/皇紀.
Era years on documents may be in daiji: 昭和弐拾年 = 昭和20年 (1945).

formats.worked: Cleveland 2022.148 sweets dish: 明治六年五月 → 1873 (museum date 1874).

formats.how_to_read: 元年 = year 1. 慶応元年 = 1865 (元治2年 and 慶応元年 are both 1865).

formats.pattern: era + number + 年 + 製 / 造 / 作 / 造之
formats.example: 天保十三年製　明治六年造　昭和三年作
formats.how_to_read: 製 sei, 造 zō, 作 saku, 造之 kore o tsukuru all mean "made in (year)"; the year part is read as above. A suffix 年製 on its own means made in the year named.
formats.note: 製/造/作 do not change the reading of the date.

formats.how_to_read: Names only the era: "made in the Meiji era" (1868–1912). No year is recorded; for 大日本昭和年製 the range is 1926–1989 (and 1930s–60s export wares). Treat as a period mark, not a date.
formats.caution: Appears on export wares; the same pattern is common on Taishō and Shōwa pieces. No museum text found for this exact pattern (gap).

formats.how_to_read: Chinese Ming mark on Japanese porcelain (Hizen/Arita). Not a date: copied for prestige, often a reign earlier than the real date. Do not convert it.
Era year fixes the year inside the cycle: 1842 = 壬寅 (#39).
60 candidate years; need the era or the object's period.

formats.pattern: era only year in kanji + month + 日
formats.how_to_read: Ansei 4 = 1853 + 4 = 1857; spring = lunar months 1–3 (V&A tsuba M.32-1920 → 1857).
"A lucky day of the 1st month": date with no day; month 1 of the lunar year (about Feb–Mar). Often in a sword mei, e.g. 正徳三年癸巳正月吉日.

M = 明治, T = 大正, S = 昭和, H = 平成, R = 令和 followed by the era year: S30 = 1955, T10 = 1921, M45 = 1912, H31 = 2019, R2 = 2020. Used on modern Japanese forms, labels, bills of sale and on 20th-century objects and paperwork.
formats.caution: Letter codes were not found in an official document opened for this report; the conversion uses the era table (single source). Check "S" versus Western letters on foreign labels.

formats.how_to_read: Old character forms of era names (應 for 応, 萬 for 万, 寶 for 宝, 寬 for 寛, 曆 for 暦); 亨 for 享 (享保/亨保) is a common handwriting substitution. Same era.

age_signatures.chars: 行年・齢・歳・年○十○歳
age_signatures.kana: ぎょうねん／こうねん・よわい・さい
age_signatures.rule: Artists and swordsmiths often sign with their age (行年七十五, 齢八十八, 七十五歳, 年八十八歳, 老人 + age). The age is almost always the Japanese count age (数え年, kazoedoshi): 1 at birth, +1 at every New Year (lunar New Year before 1873). So with a known birth year B: year = B + age − 1. If the signer used the Western count (満年齢) — modern, after 1902/1950 — year = B + age (or +1 depending on birthday). Add one to the Western year if the date lies in the last lunar months and the year runs into January/February.
age_signatures.formula: year = birth year + age − 1 (kazoedoshi); check against the museum range

facts.text: 数え年: age 1 at birth, +1 at each New Year; before 1873 the New Year is the lunar New Year, so a child born in the 12th month is age 2 a month or so later.
The kazoedoshi counting was replaced by 満年齢 in law by 明治35年法律第50号 and by the 1949/1950 law; but the habit survived: "昭和24年(1949)になっても数え年の習慣が残っていた".
facts.quote: 数え年の習慣が残っていた

facts.text: 行年 means the number of years lived so far; 行年 can be read ぎょうねん (= 享年) or こうねん.
facts.quote: これまで生きてきた年数

facts.text: Hokusai's old-age signatures: 画狂老人卍 + age: age 80, 81, 85, 88 (1847) and 90 (1849, a dragon painting dated 嘉永二年 first month; "90-year-old man Manji", seal 百). Hokusai was born in 1760.

age_signatures.cautions: The artist's birth year must be reliable (published birth years of many artists are uncertain by ±1). An age can also be written with a different sign (年 + number + 歳 vs. 寿 for a celebration age such as 七十七歳 喜寿 or 八十八歳 米寿). Age signatures are frequently added by later hands on boxes (箱書).

gaps: Second independent source for the start/end years of 96 pre-1558 eras (645–1557) was not obtained machine-readably: Nipponica is the first source; the Satow table in Chamberlain & Mason (1901) is OCR text with scrambled columns (used as a check for 134 eras; 96 eras remain single-sourced for the year facts, flagged single_source true). ja.wikipedia agrees on all 243 eras it lists but is not counted as a source.

Western day-and-month conversions of era start/end dates (Julian before 1582-10-15, Gregorian after) come only from the ja.wikipedia 元号一覧 table, flagged single_source true. Only the year labels are double-sourced.

Era start-date disagreements recorded: 大化 (Nipponica 6/19 vs ja.wikipedia 7/1), 永万 (6/4 vs 6/5). Southern-court eras from 建徳 (1370) on have uncertain start dates (ja.wikipedia note). 正平 start dates differ among later sources (ja.wikipedia footnote: 七巻冊子 4月, 南朝編年記略 7月24日, 続史愚抄 7月4日 — it calls all of them mistaken); not independently verified.

No museum record was found of an object with 紀元二千六百年 (kōki 2600) written on it (ceramic, sword, lacquer or military item). The commemoration is documented through Edo-Tokyo Museum postcards (1940) and NDL books dated 1940–1944; the claim that commemorative wares and military items carry the phrase is not source-backed here.
No open museum record found for 大日本明治年製 / 大日本大正年製 / 大日本昭和年製 patterns; the format entry is single-sourced from the era table and flagged. Japan Search returned 0 items for these phrases.

The abbreviation letters M, T, S, H, R for 明治・大正・昭和・平成・令和 were not confirmed in an official document opened for this report (several official pages searched; none lists the letter codes). Conversion S30 = 1955 relies on the era table only.

Only one Taishō-dated object (Edo-Tokyo Museum bowl) was found in open data, and the museum does not say where the date is written. Met objects could not be used: the Met API has no inscription field and the Met website blocks automated reading.
卌 (40) and 〇 (zero) are single-sourced (字通 mentions the oracle-bone forms for 30 and 40; no dictionary entry for 卌 was available on コトバンク).

Birth years used for age-signature examples (Sekien 1712, Zeshin 1807, Masayuki 1691, Hokusai 1760, Myōju 1558) come from the museum records (first four) and general references (Myōju), and are not independently checked.

Satow table spellings (Dai-kwa, Kuwan- etc.) show that older Western books wrote the on-readings differently (e.g. 大 = Dai- where Nipponica gives Tai-): the other_spellings of 大-initial eras include both forms, but which reading a given era historically had was not checked era by era.

The date-seal system for woodblock prints (era-less year-animal-month seals) and Korean/Chinese era-style marks on Japanese objects are covered by other topics; only the animal readings and the cycle formula are given here.
